5 Minutes||Short story.text:
“5 minutes.”
	I looked at my brother in disbelief.  “Are you fucking crazy?  No way she’s beating her record today,” I said with the tone of an expert.  “I say 10.”
	“Tom’s right.  I’m down for 12 minutes,” added my sister while putting on her used Mickey Mouse gloves, so torn that the tips of her fingers were exposed.
	“Alright, so Geri, you got 12, Will 5, and me, 10.  Good for everyone?”
	My brother said he agreed with a confident yes, as if he was positive of winning, while my sister just nodded.
	The door to my parents’ bedroom opened and closed with a bang; our jovial mood melted away.  Right on time, as if an internal clock had been surgically installed in her, Grendel the Beast descended the wooden stairs, her sharp heels stabbing the carpeted steps.  It was only 7;50 A.M, and already she was puffing on her Marlboro, the cloud of smoke masking her face except for her bloated blonde hair, visible for miles and miles and miles.  On her way down, after seeing us clustered in the hall like three headless chickens, she shouted, “Qu’est-ce que vous foutez la?  Allez dans la bagnole!”  As usual, my mother was in splendid form.
	My sister opened the front door and led the way to the car; we were trapped, ahead of us, by the arctic, gusty air that made our bodies crave for warmth, and behind, by our mother’s raucous grumbling – putain de froid – that made our minds crave for a surprise visit by child services.  But we reached the car, a deteriorated murky green Mitsubishi Montero Sports whose windshield was colonized by frost.
	“Shotgun,” yelled my sister, running to the passenger seat up front.
	My younger brother pushed me and raced to the left backseat.  In defeat, I slowly walked to the right side of the car and sat next to Will.  In despair, I listened to the tormenting but eager clicks of buckled belts.  In disbelief, I recalled the day that my brother strangled himself with the seat belt which then had to be cut by a fat man with a Crocodile Hunter knife at a highway gas station.  The same cut seat belt which could not protect my dear life in case of an accident.
	I was screwed!
	A cigarette-scented fog followed my mother into the car, her mouth still equipped with a Marlboro.  Then she put her large handbag onto her lap and dipped her hand into its maze, searching for the car keys.
	My sister, who must have had a death wish, risked her life.  “Mom, could you hurry up, we’re gonna be late!”
	My brother and I, dumbfounded, stopped breathing, our hands quietly clawing the banquets, as if we were trying to tear it open and make a hole in which to hide.  But nothing could impede the nuclear bomb that was certain to come.  My mother’s hand froze, her head turning as if in slow motion, her cold deathly stare piercing though my sister’s failed attempt to bravely confront Grendel the Beast.
	“Ta gueule, connasse!” bellowed my mother, in between puffs, smoke shooting out of her mouth and nose like from a dragon.
	My mother finally found the car keys.  The Mitsubishi, engine revving so loudly that birds thought the hunting season was back on and so they flew away in distress, brusquely backed out of the driveway and onto the road.  Then my mother braked, the tires screeched, and I became a tennis ball banged around between the banquet and the rear of my sister’s seat.  Finally, Grendel put the shift into drive, and our rocket of a car was propelled into cyber-road, the oncoming cars only comets that our spaceship had to avoid.  I looked at the clock.  7.55 A.M.
	At an intersection near our destination, when I was ready to vomit my breakfast, an array of obstacles forced my mother to stop, against her will.
	“Ils sont tellement lents, ces putains d’amerloques, on comprend pourquoi ils ont perdu la guerre du Vietnam,” she exclaimed in anger.  Then she looked on her right; the sidewalk was clear of any pedestrians.  She turned the wheel and contoured the cars in front of us by driving on the empty sidewalk.  Although our light was red, and numerous cars were passing by at the intersection, my mother forced her way through.  At first I was petrified, wishing that I wasn’t an atheist so I could pray God for protection.  I was sure if I looked myself in a mirror, my face would be as pallid as the ghost Casper.  Then, I noticed that we were making our way across the intersection, unhurt.  I was incredulous, but let out a sigh of relief.  We were going to make it!
	So close to the finishing line, our Mitsubishi clipped my biology teacher’s red Volvo, which, at such speed, was thrown into the air and landed upside down.  My mom didn’t stop, indifferent, but I looked back at Mrs. Rhomer’s overturned car, small flames flickering, oil leaking onto the road like droplets of sweat from an exhausted athlete.  Then the flames grew in intensity, and the gathered crowd backed away; finally, the car exploded.  Biology class had just been cancelled.  My mom dropped us off in the high school parking lot, just as the 8 o’clock bell echoed in the morning mist.  A new record!  My brother had won.

Carpe Diem||Short story.text:
Carpe Diem

	“So… I guess I’ll see you tomorrow, then,” Sophie said.
	“Yeah, see you tomorrow,” I answered.  For a moment, she stood there, hesitant, and her eyes – blue as the sky on a clear summer day – stared at me, pleading like a dog would for a piece of chocolate.  But nothing happened; the moment passed.  She left.
	And that was my first missed opportunity to ask Sophie out.  Whenever I was with a girl and there was a possibility of going beyond a simple friendship, I always blacked out.  My mind was like a computer.  The problem was that the program GIRLS was never properly installed, and so when the time came to step up to the plate, as with Sophie, a pop-up flashed in my mind: ERROR!  SYSTEM WILL SHUT DOWN IN 5, 4, 3, 2, 1 … and fade to black.  I became as incompetent as the veggies from One Flew Over the Cuckoo’s Nest.
	After I left Sophie that afternoon, I wanted to be left alone, wanted to be in my room, the land of freedom, where I could ponder for hours on end and think of a plan to remedy my disease.  Because that’s what I saw timidity as – a disease.  And I wanted, like any scientist confronted with a newly discovered illness, to find a cure.  So I raced to my room like a Formula 1 car would to the finishing line, only making a pit stop in the kitchen to refuel my stomach.
	My hunger appeased, I listened to Led Zeppelin’s Since I’ve Been Loving You, the loud Jimmy Page guitar solos seeping through the paper-thin walls of my fort of freedom and invading the rest of the tranquil house.  No one cared; the song is great.  Although somewhat soothed, I was still furious with myself.  If I didn’t act soon, I would become the laughing stock of the school.  I decided I couldn’t endure letting this disease live in me like a parasite, taking away so much but giving me nothing in return.  I would fight it and beat it, if that was the last thing I did.
	The second missed opportunity came the very next day, in spite of my warrior-like determination to hunt the parasitical timidity and use it as a punching ball until it bled to death.  I walked Sophie home after school, conversing with her while at the same time wishing we’d be attacked by Ted and Nelly, the school bullies, and that I would single-handedly defend Sophie and beat the two boys.  But the only potential adversary that crossed our path was a cute rabbit.  Sophie being an over-active member of PETA, I don’t think attacking it would have helped my cause.  Upon reaching her house we both stopped, as if eternally immobilized, like statues.  I knew she was waiting for me to act, but my mouth, desperately trying to emit any kind of intelligible sound, only shot blanks.
	The moment was ephemeral.  She turned away and walked the short path to her front door at the pace of a turtle, her slow stride tormenting me as I stared.  I was weakened and disheartened by my new failure, but the predominant feeling, the one that flowed through every vein of my body, rapidly expanding from my heart to the tip of my toenails, was that of anger.  I closed my eyes, took long heavy breaths, and waited.  I thought my bones would grow, that my skin would turn cucumber green, that I would become the Incredible Hulk.  But in the still darkness of my closed eyelids, I remained the simple, timid boy that I always had been.  My head low, my eyes fixed on the pavement, I dragged my feet home.
	On the way, for some inexplicable reason, I thought of the only Latin sentence I knew: Carpe Diem.  Seize the day!  A surprise attack by a faint smile victoriously battled sorrow off my face; I knew what I would do.  If I couldn’t ask Sophie out face to face, I would cowardly hide behind technology to do so.  I reached for my Nokia, proud and confident, but by the time I was dialing the number (this was before speed-dial, ladies and gents), my fingers were trembling.  Still, I managed to finish it.
	After the ring, a voice leapt out of the phone and into my ear.  “Hello?”  It was Sophie.
	I still had the opportunity to hang up and run away to a distant country – the world’s a big place – but the ounce of bravery that had been successfully hiding in me thus far surged out of its hiding spot and usurped cowardice.
	So I asked, “Sophie, will you go out with me?”
	The God called for a time-out.  My body became Niagara Falls as beads of nervous sweat poured down from all over.  My hands quivered and I feared I would drop the phone, while my legs turned French on me and went on strike, so I sat down in the middle of the sidewalk, waiting.
	Then an over-excited voice – Sophie’s voice – answered, “yes.”
	And so that was all it took: gut.  I was as excited as a Red Sox fan must have been when Boston broke the Curse of the Bambino and won the World Series.  The fact that Sophie and I broke up only a week later doesn’t matter; the program GIRLS was finally installed.  But then again, there are always computer bugs!

Child Abuse in Our Backyard||Short story.text:
Child Abuse in Our Backyard

	I remember my last December spent in Rye.  Everyday, a thick sheet as white as milk blanketed the high school parking lot.  And everyday, the senior hallway was as bare of students as the trees were of leaves.   The teachers called it senioritis.  We called it a well-deserved year off.  But as much as slacking was the cool thing to do at the time, there was one dreaded but important duty required of us: college applications.
	Christmas was a fortnight away and, while Santa and his elves were rushing to finish their latest toys, I spent my days burning random pedestrians with a flamethrower in Grand Theft Auto 3.  In school I practiced my secret agent skills to avoid my stalking guidance counsellor, Mr. L.  But one day I failed and he caught me.  As his towering body loomed above me, he reminded me that I had only ten days left to hand in my applications, otherwise I would not go to college, would never get a job, never get married, and would die a piss-poor lonely man.
	“You’ll have them,” I told him so he’d bugger off, but what I really wanted to say was, “Geez, thanks for the added pressure.”  I mean, really, couldn’t he understand that I had more urgent matters to deal with?  Earlier that morning my friend Steve had bragged about how he’d gotten to the 12th mission on GTA3.  I was barely on the 3rd, so if I wanted to keep my dignity among my peers I’d have to pull an all-nighter just to catch up with him.  College applications were the last thing on my mind.
	I got home that afternoon thinking hard on how to plan the rest of the evening.  I would play videogames until 6 P.M, then order Dominos’ – pepperoni and cheese – watch Malcolm in the Middle, and then back to videogames.  Senior year was really the shiznit, man.
	People say I scream like a girl.  As I think back about that December afternoon when I entered my room to see a dust-less spot on the table where my TV should have been, I realize that maybe it’s true.  I shrieked like a kid who sees the monster come out of the closet, I shrieked until my throat throbbed, and even then, I shrieked some more.
	Mr. L had called my mother and expressed his concern about how I would die piss-poor and lonely.  Consequence: my TV had been confiscated until my applications were sealed and mailed.  The comprehension slowly sunk in, but I did not cry.  No, I might scream like a girl, but I took it like a man.
	I stormed to my room, cranked up the radio – it helped me concentrate in dire times – and sat behind my desk.  It felt strange; I hadn’t been in that area of my room since Junior Year.  But I was determined to work because I desperately needed my TV back by the next day.  The biggest event of the year was coming up: the MTV Movie Awards.  I could not, under any circumstances, miss it.  It would be the end of me.  I mean, what if Britney Spears and Madonna kissed?  I would look like the world’s biggest fool if I didn’t see it.
	And how hard could a college application be?  Check a few boxes, write down some words, and voila, you’re off to college.  The first few questions – first, middle, and last name, gender, and birth date – were somewhat easy.  But from there things went downhill.  And when I say downhill, I mean like a speeding avalanche charging down a mountain side and crushing everything on its way.
	First came, possible areas of academic concentration/majors.  I had a vague memory of a conversation with Mr. L as he told me what I should major in, according to my grades.  But I hadn’t been paying attention; as I sat across the stalking guidance counsellor in his office, I was more interested by a bird outside nibbling off a dead rabbit.  So I tried to remember what he had told me.  Something about science.  Surely that couldn’t be it.  I never looked at my report card, but I knew as a fact that my grades in any science class never exceeded C-.  Maybe Mr. L wanted me to fail.  Or maybe, I thought as I looked through a booklet of majors available, he had meant Political Science.  I didn’t know what that was, but that’s what I chose.  If you can’t trust your guidance counsellor, who can you trust?
	Next I was thrown, possible career or professional plan.  I hadn’t thought about my future since I’d been five or six, when I wanted to be a fire fighter during the day and a police officer at night.  I doubt that’s the kind of answer they were looking for.  So I pondered.  What did I want to do?  My long term life goal was to become a billionaire and buy a soccer club.  But how would I get there?  I didn’t want to waste any time – the MTV Movie Awards sere only 27 hours away – so I put down undecided.  I’d have four full years of college to come up with a brilliant plan to gain billions.
	My hand ached – I hadn’t written that much since Junior Year – so I took a break.  A Kit Kat break.  Then after a few minutes of singing along to the White Stripes’ Seven Nation Army, I plunged myself back into the 4-paged demon.  I continued answering personal questions, such as whether I would be a candidate for financial aid, and then went on to give details about my “secondary school you now attend.”
	The next part, entitled Test Information, almost gave me a heart attack.  They wanted to know my SAT scores.  How could they be so cruel?  How could they remind me of those 6 painful months spent memorizing words scribbled on colored index cards and which I’d already forgotten?  I had done everything to forget those stupid SAT tests; when I returned home that night, I had lit a fire in the fireplace and burnt, one by one, all those colored index cards.  And now the SAT’s were back to haunt me.  Whatever.  I slowed my breathing and told myself this was only about the MTV Movie Awards, nothing more.  Forget about college.  Forget about My. L.  Just concentrate on the MTV Movie Awards.  And I did.  I wrote down my SAT scores – 1190 – and moved on.
	They required general information about my family.  What is your mother’s name?  Isabelle.  Is she still alive?  And if not, date deceased.  Damn, I wish my mom were dead, then I’d have my TV back.  But no, she was still alive and puffing those Marlboros day in and day out.  Cancer had to be just around the corner for her.
	Then followed an enquiry about extracurricular activities.  Well, I had played soccer until 10th grade.  I’d also been a member of the chess club.  But most proudly, I had been co-founder of the Director’s Club.  Its goal had been for its members to write a screenplay and then shoot the movie – a goal that had eventually led to failure; we had held only one meeting.  But officially the club existed.  I was asked about positions held and honors won in the said extracurricular activities.  As president of the Director’s Club, I immediately honored myself with the club’s Most Dedicated Member of the Month Award for all the months since the creation of the club a year ago.  That filled some lines.
	After that I was asked to, “briefly list or describe any scholastic distinctions or honors you have won since the ninth grade.”  Because I’m a nice guy and I was asked to, I gave the briefest answer possible: none.  I could have taken the time to make something up – it’s not like they would have called all my high school teachers to check if I’d really won anything – but I was eager to finish the applications and get my TV back.
	After a few struggling questions about Work Experiences and a short answer on my most meaningful activities, I neared the finishing line.  All that stood on my way was the College Essay.
	Please write an essay (250-300 words) on a topic of your choice or on one of the options listed below.  I checked out the choices they offered me and settled on discussing, “some issue of personal, local, national, or international concern and its importance to you.”  I don’t have that many strong convictions in life; I hate politics, I’m an atheist, I don’t even have a favorite movie.  But if there is one thing I strongly believe in, it’s that community service should not be forced upon you.  It defies the whole principle of the act.  But Rye High School didn’t see it my way; if you wanted to graduate, you were obliged to volunteer for 60 hours of community service.  So I wrote my essay on how our local case was actually of national interest, because American teenagers were enslaved to “volunteer”.  Forget about Chinese kids working in Nike factories for 5 cents an hour – at least they were paid.  Ours was a clear case of child abuse.  I typed the essay – word count told me I had only 245 words.  So I entitled the piece, “Child Abuse in Our Backyard,” and printed the 250-word essay.
	I signed the Common Application, my hand trembling from disbelief that soon I would get my TV back.  I also realized that, now, high school was really over.  No more would I have to break a sweat on a Monday night to write a five-page essay due the next morning; no more would I have to hurry to school in frustration because I overslept; no more would I have to care about a teacher threatening to call my parents because of a missed homework.  Well, not until college, anyways!

Jam Session||Short story.text:
Jam Session

	“If you don’t, I’ll slash your throat, then I’ll stand over your quivering body and crush your head with my foot.  Got it?” said Nava.  His over-tinted, $20 CVS/Pharmacy sunglasses covered such a large portion of his bony face that one had to wonder – were they protecting his eyes or his skin?
	I glanced at Ben and D, large smiles stapled on their faces, then returned my gaze to Nava.  His breath had not forgotten dinner – a warm wave of scented burritos, hot salsa, and nachos battered against my face, the repelling odors even finding their way up my nose.
	“Why do you wear sunglasses when we’re in the fuckin’ basement?  You think it makes you look tough?  You think I’m scared of you, Piece of Shit?” I taunted.
	Nava remained immobile, as if a magic spell had frozen him for life, except for small beads of sweat that trickled down his unshaven faced.  Communications Breakdown rippled through the room, Robert Plant’s singing overpowering Ben and D’s snickers.
	“And why do you wear jeans and long-sleeved shirts in the middle of the fuckin’ summer?” I added.  “It’s, like, a 100 degrees outside, you’re gonna melt like a fuckin’ igloo.”
	Still immobile and emotionless, Nava slithered in a whisper, “Are you gonna let me?  Or not?”
	I stared at him hard – I could see my goofy reflection in his sunglasses.  “Well, since you apparently don’t understand English, let me say it for you in Spanish.  No.”
	“Oh, so it’s like that, huh?”
	“Yeah, that’s right.”  I nodded.  “It’s like that.”
	Ben and D’s laughter intensified.  Robert Plant’s high-pitched voice died down.  It was the last song on the CD; therefore, Ben and D’s laughter mastered the basement.
	I was pinned to the spot, unable to withdraw my eyes from Nava’s magnetic sunglasses.  I thought about the situation: me, the “small” guy – although I’m 6’1 – insulting the monster, Nava, the tallest guy in our school, sitting atop his 6’5 tower.  Another David v. Goliath story.  My lips parted and formed a large, Grinch-like smile.
	“Fuck it.  I don’t wanna waste any more time.  You ain’t playing drums and that’s final.”  I backed away and sat on the not-so-cozy wooden stool in front of my Pearl drumset.  “Let’s go, Nava.  Go back to your fuckin’ guitar.  You two, as well,” I said, turning my head toward Ben and D.  “I don’t want any more time of my band being wasted.”
	“Your band?” echoed Nava and D together like a well trained choir, looking at me, startled.  I saw Ben just glance, shake his head, and smile.
	“Since when is this your band?” continued D, in his solo.  His mouth gaped wide open, as if he’d just learnt the miracle of breathing and tried to catch up to all those wasted years.
	“Since the fact that we’ve been here for almost a fuckin’ hour and we haven’t done jackshit except argue.  Someone with balls gotta take charge of this band, and you guys obviously don’t have any, so I’m doing it.  Now get to your fuckin’ guitars.”
	No one moved.  Not even Iggy the Gecko, the lizard D had bought a week earlier.  He dozed on a plastic branch in his cage, just as he had done all week.  Lazy bastard!  Nava and D were boiling, like sleeping volcanoes coming to life.
	D was the first to erupt, his lips tight, the words spurting out like rapid gunfire.  “Ig, this isn’t your fucking band.  Nava and Ben started it, and I’m the lead singer.  You were the last to join.  You’re nothing.”
	Nava remained silent, but smiled and nodded – the flickering light form the ceiling glinted off his sunglasses, on and off, like a coded message.  Ben pulled a UN on us and sneaked away from the conflict, sat on my Model’s blue foldout chair – equipped with a can holder – and turned on the Xbox.
	“I’m tired of this bullshit,” I snapped.  “I quit!”  I got up and back-kicked my stool, which smattered to pieces against the wall.  “You guys don’t give a fuck about the band.  Look – he’s playing videogames all the time.”  I pointed to Ben, who concentrated on repelling an alien attack, his face inches away from the screen, his fingers smashing with violence against the remote like a maniac.  I looked at Nava.  “You’re the guitarist, but all you care about is playing drums.  And you,” I said, turning to D, “you say you’re the lead singer, but you don’t even know how to fuckin’ sing.  Thank God I’m the drummer and that I can’t hear shit when I’m playing, ‘cause if I had to listen to your voice, I’d go insane.  So yeah, I quit, I got better things to do.”
	“Like what?  Go home and watch soccer?” asked D.  He wasn’t just an erupting volcano anymore, but an earthquake, a tsunami, and a category 5 hurricane all in one.  He frowned, causing his eyes to become thin slits, and his skin turned redder than a clown’s noise.  I almost expected fumes to heave off his head like from a Looney Tunes character.  “You know what?  You’re not quitting, we’re kicking you the fuck out!”
	“Yeah, well good luck finding another drummer.  I know I won’t have any problems finding someone who can sing better than you,” I said, but not budging – it would be like admitting defeat.
	“Wait!”  It was Nava.  He stood in-between us, like a ref separating two pumped up boxers in the ring.  He looked at D, then at me, searching for the right words to ease the tension and salvage the friendships that were hanging on a thread threatened by giant scissors.  “C’mon, this is stupid.  We’re not gonna kick you out.  And why would you wanna quit?”
	“Geez, I don’tknow, Mr. I-wana-slash-your-throat-and-smash-your-head.  Maybe ‘cause you’re psychotic?”
	Nava smiled, his teeth, white as milk, contrasting against the pitch black of his sunglasses.  “OK, so maybe that was a little bit extreme.”
	“Fine, we’re not kicking you out, but don’t ever call this your band again.  Ever!  Got it?” said D.  The red from his face had disappeared as quickly as a rabbit in a magic trick.
	“Or what?”
	“Or,” he went on, “I’ll slash your throat and smash your head.”  He grinned.  “Now, Ben, turn the Xbox off and get the fuck back to your guitar!”
	Ben jumped to his feet like a terrorized rabbit and obeyed the lead singer.  Nava went to his Gibson guitar, plugging cords into it and turning on all his equipment.  A low hum escaped his amplifier and camouflaged itself amongst the numerous but indistinct basement sounds: creaking ceiling, water running through pipes, ventilation system.  D went to his mike and took it off its stand.  A high screeching sound attacked our ears.
	“D!  How many times we gotta tell you: take your fucking pimp necklace off before going to the mike!  You’re gonna make us all go deaf, you jackass.  Now, let’s go,” said Nava, “we gotta jam.  Wouldn’t want to disappoint our fans, would we?”
	“And let’s not forget the groupies, the pile of groupies just waiting to meet us.  Well, me at least.  I don’t know any girls who’d wanna meet you guys,” I said, walking away from my drum set.
	“Where you going?” asked Nava, concerned, and following my every move from behind his sunglasses.
	“Well, you know how I am.  I like to play in style,” I said, reaching my blue foldout chair – the one with a can holder – and grabbing it.  “And seeing as how I broke my stool, I need a new seat.”
	Next to my drum set was a small Brandt fridge, like the ones college students have in their dorms.  I opened it.  “D, what the fuck, you’re out of coke?”
	“Yeah, man.  We drank the last ones during dinner.”
	“We gotta go to CVS and buy some right now,” I said.
	Nava, Ben and D all stared at me in disbelief.  “Well, what about jamming?” asked D.
	“Well, fuck that.  I ain’t playing if I don’t have my coke first.”  I threw my foldout chair on the ground and headed toward the stairs.
	The clown nose color was reappearing on D’s face.  “Are you shitting me?  You just bitched a second ago because we didn’t jam enough and how you were the only one who cared about the band, and now you don’t wanna play because you can’t have your fucking coke?”
	“Uh, do you know how tiresome it is to play drums?  And do you know how hot it is right now?  Do you want me to fuckin’ die from dehydration?”
	Ben, always the smart one of the four, knew there’s be no jamming now.  He put down his Gibson guitar and returned to the magnetic Xbox, this time compelled to kneel in front of the TV since my foldout chair was gone.  Nava stayed by in case his refereeing skills would be required again.  But he, too, had lost all hope of jamming.
	“Well, if we go to CVS, by the time we get back my parents will be home, and we won’t have any time to jam,” said D, exasperated.
	“Well, then,” I said, stepping up the stairs, “screw you guys, I’m going home.”

The Foreigner||Short story.text:
The Foreigner

	What a terrible day, John thought.  He had been walking endlessly for the past hour looking for a boulangerie that was not closed for the summer break.  In vain.  John wasn’t happy, and his incessantly growling stomach wasn’t happy, and the delicious pate de campagne that was just waiting to be devoured, patiently waiting in the fridge, was not happy, either.  What’s more, the menacing sky was ready to lash out a battering rain very soon.
	But then John saw an old, hunched man advance at the pace of a turtle, a cane in one hand and, hallelujah, a baguette in the other.  Either the old Frenchman wasted his whole day just to get bread, or there was an open boulangerie around.  It was time for John to test his French skills.
	“Excusez-moi, monsieur, ou est la boulangerie?” John asked in a French accent that would have not made his high school teacher proud.  To emphasize what he was looking for, he pointed to the old man’s baguette.  The Frenchman, at first startled, frowning, finally seemed to understand.
	“La premiere a gauche, jeune homme,” replied the turtle-paced man.  John thanked him and hastened on his quest to find an open boulangerie.  He turned left on the narrow street indicated by the old man and could see farther ahead the sign of the boulangerie hanging above the store.  Eureka!  He happily strolled toward the store like a kid would toward a candy shop, but as quickly as it had appeared, his joy vanished; another obstacle clogged his way.  Walking out of the bakery and heading toward John at an incredible pace was what intrigued historians would call the last remnant of the prehistoric era, a woman so big she could not be considered a woman but a mammoth, at the least.  At the same time, droplets of rain began descending on the city of love.
	John looked around for an exit, to get out of the way of the incoming train, but he was blocked on his left by buildings and on his right by those tiny but numerous European cars.  It was over.  He would be crushed like a crepe on his way to get a baguette.  How triste!  Running back to where he came from was useless because the mammoth-like woman was going faster than he was, gaining momentum as she went along like a bowling ball on its way to a strike.  Nothing could impede her rampage.
	But suddenly the obese woman, now only a couple of inches away from John, stopped dead in her tracks, the pavement screeching under her feet, and she entered into a building on her right.  John sighed in relief: not only was he not flat like a crepe, but the road to the boulangerie was finally clear.
	At last, John entered the bakery, his radiant face taken by the sweet scent of baked bread that gushed out of the ovens in the back of the room and besieged the whole store, while the soft rain, which should have materialized into a big storm, surprisingly ceased, and the sky cleared.
	While John bought his two baguettes, the front door of the bakery opened and entered a woman so stunning that John – for an instant only, let’s not forget that he was really hungry – forgot about his unhappy, growling stomach, and his impatient pate de campagne, and his two baguettes and the crepes and all the delicious French foods, because here was another French beauty he was ready to devour.

The Secret||Short story.text:
The Secret

	The man ran for his life, skipping down the stairs ten steps at a time like a kangaroo running for his life and skipping down the stairs ten steps at a time – except I don’t see why that would ever happen.  A bullet skimmed past his head – the man’s, not the kangaroo’s – and buried itself in the wall.  Another man followed right behind him, except that man acted nothing like a kangaroo but more like an Australian tiger out hunting kangaroos.  Now, you must be telling yourself, Thomas is going to write another clichéd action story with the good guy being chased by kangaroos, uh, I mean, the bad guys.  All right, so replace the first man by my brother Will, the bullet with a Siemens SL65 – that’s a cell phone, for all those I-hate-technology people – the second man by my sister Geri, and the kangaroo by, I don’t know, a chimpanzee, and you got a classic weekend afternoon at our house.
	“I’ll kill you, asshole!”  A mother talking to her son’s murderer?  Of course not! Try: my sister threatening my brother after he guillotined all her Barbie dolls – and trust me, there was a shitload of them.  Enough to ask yourself, why?  But as ruthless as the execution of the sweet and innocent blondes was, it was an appropriate and necessary response by my brother, who barely survived a heart attack when he found, the day before, his collection of soccer trading cards – brace yourself for this – shredded to pieces, becoming as useless as a guillotined Barbie doll.  Of course, that was only a comeback because Will had done something to Geri the day before, who had done something to my brother the day before that.
	The endless conflict started on August 15th, 1987.  Yes, the very same day my brother was born.  Weird coincidence, huh?  I was only two at the time so I don’t remember how it all happened, but it eventually led to that frightful afternoon, and my brother leaping like a kangaroo – sorry, chimpanzee – down the stairs, barely avoiding a Siemens SL65 comet that crashed against the wall and smashed into millions of pieces like a spaceship blown up in any sci-fi movie.  My sister, never the athlete, followed close behind, proving those stupid posters with corny quotes wrong: practice doesn’t make perfect, envy does.  My sister really wanted to kill Will, so she managed to keep up with him.
	Somehow, one of the numerous Barbie dolls’ head had managed to find its way far, far away from its home – my sister’s bedroom – and landed in the vast, exotic ground floor hallway.  My brother running at the pace of a chimpanzee – do they really run that fast? – he did not see the tiny but dangerous obstacle that had camouflaged into its new environment.  He slipped, fell.  Now, imagine a porcelain vase dropping on concrete floor; it would smash like the cell phone earlier against the wall, its tiny debris spreading on the floor around the epicenter.  That’s what would have happened to my brother’s head, because the skull, though stronger, is kind of like porcelain.  Fortunately for Will, though, our floor was not made of concrete, but of a hideous, flamboyant yellow carpet that reminded me of a bee relieved of its black stripes.  My brother lying unconscious on the ugly insect, Geri caught up to him.
	And that is how I lost my brother.  No, I kid.  My sister didn’t kill him.  She was about to, but …
	“Don’t do it!” I yelled, interrupting her in mid-act, her sharp, high-heeled shoe only a few inches away from his unconscious face.
	The femme fatale looked at me.  Quick, I thought to myself, think of a reason, or else she’ll really do it.  “What good will he be dead?  Make him your bitch.”
	She hesitated.  My heart pounded like a lunatic pounding on the door of his cell.  “He won’t listen to me.  He’ll keep pissing me off.  Sorry, he’s got to go.”
	Slow down, Terminator.  “What if you could blackmail him?  If I told you his best-kept secret?  Trust me, he’d do anything you’d ask.”
	“Shoot.”
	I looked at Will, still on the ugly carpet, unconscious, not hearing a word of our conversation.  Sorry, bro.  Best I could do.  So I told her.  It’s such a big secret that I can only write it in Arabic.  Here goes:  تؤخس٤ـكْڞڥٳځڿێےڼګٌُڀ٠ڌ.  Yeah, I know exactly what you’re thinking.  What the fuck was my brother thinking about?  But, what can you do?
	My sister put her heels away just as my brother woke up, dazed.
	She smiled.  “Will, why don’t you go get me a glass of water?”
	“Yeah, sure, why don’t I?  And at the same time, why don’t I glue all your Barbie dolls’ head back on their body?”  Sarcasm runs in the family – except for my sister.  I think it’s more a guy thing.
	“What an excellent idea!  Why don’t you or …”
	“Or what?” my brother exclaimed.
	My sister set up the trap.  “Well, do you really wanna know what I know?”
	“Geri, you don’t know shit from fuck,” said my brother, exasperated.  “OK?  So why don’t you go get me a glass of water, Woman, before I start to get angry.”
	“Or…” said Geri, “I could tell mom and dad about,” the secret.  Refer to above Arabic text.
	My brother shot me a glance that said: traitor.  I looked away, in shame.  Couldn’t he realize I did it to save his life?  To save his fucking life?
	“I’m still waiting for my glass of water,” said my sister.
	My brother, defeated, his head low like the low blow he’d just received, dragged his feet to the kitchen.  He looked nothing like a kangaroo.  Not even a chimpanzee.

The Lie||Short story.text:
The lie.  That damn lie, it torments me.  And I listen to the child cry downstairs, endlessly, his screech resonating in my head, trying to find a way out but continuously bumping my skull, imprisoned.  It won’t go away; the ache, excruciating, accrues.  The pills are useless, like everything else.
	Then a knock on the door.  My mind, perturbed, hesitates.  It could be them.
	“Who is it?” I cry out, immediately reprimanded by a burst of pain in my head.
	“It’s me.”  The soft whisper floats in my skull, battles the pain, wins.  I welcome the soothing calm.  The child has stopped crying.
	I rush to the door and unlock it, desperate, like a prisoner who’s miraculously found the key to his cell.  And find Freedom staring at me.  My savior.  Her magnetic, navy blue eyes gawk at me, I’m drawn to them, and I forget about the rest of her face, her glistening black hair, her pale skin, so perfect it seems it was keenly buttered on.  I try to speak, but she beats me to it.
	“Hi, Tom.”
	I replicate.  “Hi, Sophie.”
	“Aren’t you going to let me in?”  She doesn’t wait for my predictable answer, and forces her way in my grimy apartment.
	“I’m sorry, you scared me.  I thought you were them.  And the child downstairs has been crying all night long, again,” I say, while picking up my dirty clothes colonizing the only sofa of the apartment.  “But please, sit.  Do you want anything to drink?”
	Sophie takes a sit on the sofa, while I pull up a chair.  “When did he stop?”
	I look at Sophie, beautiful as ever.  My head twirls again.  I’m confused.  “When did who stop what?”
	“The child.  Crying.  You said he’d been crying all night long.  But I don’t hear anything, Tom.”
	“He stopped right when you g-.”  My mouth gapes wide open.  I understand, disappointed.  “Oh, you think I’m making it up again.”
	“Look,” she says, getting up from the sofa and walking to me, “have you been taking your pills?”
	 She drops on her knees, we’re face to face.  Her eyes are a deep ocean, I’m lost in them.  Weakening.  Tears build up in my eyes.  “The pills … the pills- they were prescribed by them.  Don’t you understand?  They’re poison!”
	“Don’t raise your voice,” she whispers, her cold hands, gentle, caressing mine.  “We talked about this before.  The last set you got, I thought you agreed they weren’t poison.  You have to take these pills, Tom.”
	Her hands frailly glisten on my cheeks, like two bits of cold steel, make my hair jump.  Then her stare pierces through my last defenses, and the tears start flowing down my cheeks.  The child starts crying again.  Louder than ever.  His high-pitch scream penetrates my head once again.  I abruptly pull myself away from Sophie’s hands and cover my sobbing face in mine.
	“Do you hear him now,” I cry out, fidgeting my head back and forth.  “God, please tell me you hear him!  He’s crying again, fucking crying!  SHUT UP!  Shut him up, please!”
	“Tom,” she says, and for the first time on her face I read uncertainty, doubt.  “Please, take the pills.”  She pulls out a bottle, uncaps it, and a bunch of multi-color pills flow in her hand.  She directs them toward me.  “Please.  Take them.”
	The lie.  Them.  Sophie.  Doubt.  The child crying, the pills.  It suddenly clicks.
	“Why did you come here in the first place, Sophie?  You weren’t supposed to come.  That’s why you scared me, that’s why I thought you were them.  Because you weren’t supposed to come.”
	“What are you talking about?”  Fear.  I could smell it a mile away.  She backs away from me, slowly.  Probably so as to not alert me.  But I won’t be fooled twice.
	“You weren’t supposed to come,” I repeat, slowly and articulate.  The crying has stopped again.  I look up, see her.  She’s paler than usual, still moving slowly away from me.
	“Tom, I told you yesterday I would come, like I do everyday.  At the same time.”
	“You lie!  You lie like them.”
	Her voice falters.  “Tom, you’re scaring me.”
	“Yes, you should be scared.  Because I saw right through your plan.  How much did they pay you?”
	She’s shaking her head now, her hands are trembling.  “What are you talking about?  Why would anyone pay me?”
	“It’s no good pretending, Sophie.  I know.  And you know what I have to do, now, don’t you?”
	“No!  Wait, what are you talking about, Tom!?  I didn’t do anything, I swear.”  Sophie drops on her knees, crying.  I walk to my bedroom.  Sophie gets up.  “Where are you going?”
	“Wait right here,” I say.  “You shouldn’t have done this,” I mumble to myself.  In my room I go to my bedside table, pull open the top drawer and pull out the gun.  Then I go back to the living room.  Sophie stands near the door.
	“Trying to leave, are you?”
	“Please, Tom” she says, turns around.  Her voice is calm again, but then she sees the gun.  “Do you really want to do this?  Do you really want to kill me?  If I worked for them, I would have killed you a long time ago.  I would have killed you when you opened the door.”
	I aim the gun at Sophie, my hands trembling.  What if she’s right?  What if she’s not working for them?  What if I really am just imagining things?  I don’t know what to think anymore, my mind is a boiling pot, too many things pop up, confuse me.  Sophie is still looking at me, but she doesn’t seem scared.  I don’t know what to do.  I need to take initiatives.
	“Goodbye, Sophie,” I say.
	“Wait, To-.”  She doesn’t have time to finish her sentence.  For a split second her eyes glare at me, glare, full of terror, of comprehension that this is the end.  They seem to say¸ how could you have done this?  Then she falls to the floor.  The blood is gushing out of her stomach, drenching her clothes.  It spills on the carpet.  Doesn’t matter, anyways.  Now they know where I live, I’ll have to move.  I walk over Sophie’s body, push it aside to open the door.  I take one last look at the woman to which I said I Do.  That seemed so long ago.  Yet it was only last year.  Then I walk out.  Already in the distance I hear police sirens.  And I listen.  But the child cries no more.

Tiger Land||Short story.text:
Tiger Land

	I attended high school in Rye, in the heart of Westchester County, where the weekends were spent at the local country club.  Fathers and sons battled through the coarse gold courses, booby-trapped with sand bunkers and large ponds, tall trees and wild roughs; mothers and daughters tanned by the pool, slurping their diet cokes and gobbling down club sandwiches, while the younger children giggled and splashed in the water under the watchful eye of a bored teenage lifeguard.  It seemed like golf courses in Westchester County outnumbered schools, hospitals, fire stations, movie theatres, factories – everything!  Driving along I-95 were endless rows of green pastures populated by white flags numbered 1 through 18.  And every weekend, Rye became a ghost town, like one from those Clint Eastwood westerns; everyone fled to Rye Country Club, Appawamis Country Club, Willow Ridge Country club, Westchester Country Club, Saxons Woods Country Club.
	I remember my golf bag.  When I bought it, it was white as milk and magnificent with thick blue letters sewn to the leather fabric and advertising the brand name, Hogan.  The last time I put it away – in our basement, next to our rusted bikes – it was covered in dark grayish grime with streaks of brown.  The “O” from Hogan was gone, but it had left a trace of its existence.  It had been my only bag, in a golf career that lasted almost seven years.
	While most kids wanted – hells, demanded! – that their parents buy them a new bag every two years or so, I kept mine with pride.  The streaks of dirt that accrued over time, deteriorating the bright white of freshness into a faded gray, were like war wounds brought back from the battlefield.  Golf balls and tees and gloves acquired from golf courses in Arizona, Florida, the French Riviera, and California overfilled the front and back pockets of the bag.  It was stuffed, bloated, fattened by what as I conceived as treasures from around the world, as proof that I had travelled to many exotic places.
	“A bullet pierced my kidney in ‘Nam, another one cut through the flesh of my leg in Iraq,” might say a legless, bearded man in a Veteran’s hospital, bragging about his war wounds.  Well, if you want to see my war wounds, zip open the front pocket of my bag and you’ll find a bunch of blue tees bought in Montpellier, France.  Dig deeper in the oblivion of the pocket and you might reach the ones I got in Montpelier, Vermont.
	The bag was, of course, conceived to carry golf clubs

Tribute to King||Short story.text:
Tribute to King

	All this happened, more or less.  The death, the resurrection.  And I’m not talking about Jesus; we all know that didn’t happen.  No, I’m talking about my black cat Michael Myers.  Everything started on October 24th, 1871 – yes, I’m that old.
	I was strolling through the park, my feet squashing the crunchy autumn leaves that blanketed the ground, when my gift – brilliance – hit me yet again.  “It would be swell to have a household cat, wouldn’t it, dear Geraldine?”
	“Oh yes, Thomas,” she exclaimed.  “It would be swell indeed.  What a brilliant idea!”
	The next day, Our Majesty Sir Lord John Francis Igou the 3rd, son of the 1st – you don’t want to know what happened to the 2nd – bought a cat for a penny from some petty street vendor.  A black cat which my father named Michael Myers, for reasons unknown.  You should have seen him before the accident; what a cute little thing – I’m talking about the cat, not my father.  His accident happened years later.
	For a week we gave Mikey-Mike – that’s’ what we nicknamed him – so much love.  Sometimes we even gave him food.  But he must have been in his rebellious teens, or l’age bête, as the French would say, because every time we approached him, to pet him, to talk to him, to hold him, or to shave him – he left his long black hair all over the place – he ran away.  Or tried to, at least.  All the exits of our mansion were locked and double locked, so much to the point that Fort Knox envied our security.  Not that we considered Mikey-Mike our prisoner; only, the world is such a dangerous place for a cat.
	This saddened my dear sister, who was not as strong as me and could not bear it.  But my mother was always, always there to comfort us.  “Give him time,” she told us.  “It’s hard to become accustomed to a new family, but he’ll come around.  Who wouldn’t with such wonderful owners as ourselves?”  Her eerie grin revealed a gapped wall of teeth whiter than albinos.
	So we gave Mikey-Mike some time, we took our distance.  But who could have foreseen that terrible accident on October 31st, a day which will live in infamy in our family?  The previous day a violent storm had battered against the area.  The damage had been minimal: a few fallen trees in the backyard and a broken window in the attic on the thirteenth floor of our mansion.  Of course, at that time elevators didn’t exist yet – the idea would come to me decades later – so we didn’t find out about the window until it was too late.  Mikey-Mike, though, knew about it.
	Always the rebel, he saw it as his opportunity, his one shot, to run away, like Steve McQueen in The Great Escape.  McQueen, in the movie, jumped a fence with his bike toward freedom; Mikey-Mike, in real life, jumped the window his dignity toward death.
	My sister, the poor innocent child, was as angry with God as John McEnroe with a referee.  Thank God she didn’t have a tennis racket; it wouldn’t have lived long.  Kind of like our cat.  To keep the story PG-13, I’ll save you the gory details.  Let me just say that it wasn’t a pretty sight.
	My sister was devastated, but still had the courage to pick up the car – well, the numerous bloody limbs of the cat, splattered all over the yard, some of them with flies already nibbling on the flesh – and buried it – or them, I don’t know how to phrase it – in our little backyard, known today as the Yellowstone National Park in Wyoming.
	Call it the magic of Halloween, call it luck, I don’t know, but the next day at dawn, when 90% of Americans were 10lbs fatter from the previous night’s sweets, who stood in the doorway of my room?  Michael Myers!  And not the Halloween killer – he would have been a day late – but my used-to-be-dead-but-is-now-resurrected black cat.
	“Jesus Christ,” I murmured, shocked.
	“Nooooooooo, “my sister said, picking up the cat and entering the room.  “Don’t you recognize him?  It’s Mikey-Mike.”

					The End

Epilogue:
	Well, I lied: my cat didn’t really die.  He could have, but the thing is, my dad must be some descendant of pharaohs because he’s terrified by cats, so we never had one.  But see, we could have had one, and, as sad as it makes me to think of the death of a potential cat that I could have had, he most definitely would have died, the poor thing, since all cats dies.  And he could have resurrected, because he would have been a special cat, my cat.  So don’t call me a liar.  But if you’ve read Stephen King’s Pet Semetary, you might call me a fraud.

Baude (working title)||Short story.text:
I put my hand over her flat stomach. It's warm and moist and makes a gurgly noise. Is it hungry? I start caressing her skin with the tip of a finger, mapping the shape of an expanding circle until there is no more space and then it recedes. I repeat the gesture absent-mindedly, mechanically. The rest of her body mirrors her stomach: immobile and fragile, yet underneath it's a steaming, boiling kettle. Next to the bed where we lay is the open window, whose gap is so slim that only an ambitious and determined mouse could force its way through -- or the current breeze, rare on this humid day but welcomed, that carries along with it, faintly, the distorted tune of Radiohead's No Surprises. I take a deep breath and devour the ever growing colony of freckles resting on her subtle nose, that small, untraceable and untouchable smelling equipment that lies with an unworried mind between her eyes and her mouth. And even though her eyes are closed, I know that she's not sleeping, just like I know, wasting my gaze out the window, that the moon hidden by the clouds is still shining bright somewhere in the darkness.  ''How did we get to this?''  It doesn't matter whose voice utters this, hers or mine. Maybe it isn't even a voice, deep or high, masculine or feminine, but rather ink on paper, or telepathy. Or a cruising thought in a traffic-less highway of a vast mind.

Silence, in its dominant reign, allows the echo of the last word to be carried by the intruding breeze to the four corners of the room, and even into the chimney, but so weakly that the word gets lost, confused, tangled: this ... iss ... iss ... bliss ... iss ....iss ... kiss. I regret the question and curse the fool that voiced it. Maybe it was me. The question evokes the past when the solution should solve the future; it evokes sins when we're seeking redemption. The question evokes stupidity from the questioner. The question is meaningless because only the answer matters, only the answer dictates our future, only the answer can be split in two and down the middle by a thick fluorescent gray line visible from the abyss of our ephemeral mind all the way to the surface of the ever-expanding and eternal universe. The answer. Only it will torment us for the rest of our lives. It = the decision.  My finger ascends the mount of her breast, earthed mostly by implants, an act committed a decade ago by a naïve 18 year old girl with rich grandparents. The journey to the top begins with a small brown mole that guards the foot of the hill and ends with a long, erect nipple. The whole region is slightly shaken by the steady rise and fall of her chest.  The tiniest of whispers, so close to being thin as air that it is barely audible, escapes from a slit between her delicate and crimson lips: ''Fuck.''  ''What's wrong, honey?'' I express my concern in a three-worded sentence, cutting right to the chase.  ''Fuck! You fucked me, I got fucked by you, we fucked like rabbits, say it however you want. It was fucking. That's how we got to this. Fucking great, don't you think?''  ''Well, personally, I think you're missing a few fucks before you can appear in the Guinness Book of Records.''  It's been a while since the frames on our walls -- filled with pictures of Mick, Madonna, Carla Bruni, Led Zeppelin, our dog Zeppelin, and Johanna and I in Israel -- have witnessed such a lengthy conversation. My jaw could almost ache from the effort. And my mind could almost open-heartedly embrace a cigarette. Almost. Until it remembers that it's one of the few things I don't regret having quit in my life.  Johanna ruffles her feet under our black dots-covered white sheets; the action stirs Zeppelin from his dull, lopsided rest in his wooden basket; our mini-Yorkshire, still in his teething phase, whirls out of his sleeping place, glides across the carpet, and hops onto our low bed. Biting occurs while caressing and boredom continue. Conversation, ephemeral, has ended.

Time to think: I'm too young to be a father but even younger to be a murderer. I'm too young to have regrets and sleepless nights, too young to have quit smoking out of good conscience and even much younger to have picked it up again out of freak nervousness and I can't even explain how far too young I am to consider myself responsible enough to make -- and take -- decisions, let alone life-changing ones, and let even more alone lives-changing ones. Conclusion? I'm too young for this shit. My mother should have kept the notice that came with the product when she gave birth to me; then, I could have gone to page 13 to see when I won't be too young anymore.  ''You're cold,'' she states.  I'm surprised by the comment. Maybe she's gone to the other side. Craziness. I'm sure it's happened before, to another couple, in a similar situation. The girl simply couldn't take it anymore, and so told her boyfriend that he was cold when in fact, he wasn't, because it was the middle of summer and the sun scorched during the day and their apartment was an oven that had been turned off but had cooked all day long.  ''Nah, actually, I'm a bit warm honey. Are you cold, though? I can get you a sweater if you want?''  My finger is stroking in the proximity of the mole, encircling it toyingly, threateningly, like horse-mounted Indians circling around a group of adrift cavalry men in the desert. The jukebox from the apartment below us, still procuring us tunes, has now gone on to Morcheeba wondering What New York Couples Fight About.   ''No, you're cold,'' she says, slowly, accentuating the articulation of the last word. Then she adds, in crescendo, ''Oh, I'm sorry, Mr. Writer, do you prefer indifferent? Stolid? Impassive? Emotionless? You just don't give a flying fuck, do you?!''  The stars remain calm. Always. They're the ones who are indifferent, stolid, impassive, emotionless. They're the ones who don't give a flying fuck, except maybe for the shooting stars. They're the ones who don't have a mind split down right the middle, with each side filled with undesired doubt and an immense ego who are pulling so hard in the opposite direction from each other that the thin invisible cord that holds our minds together -- Sanity -- is ready to snap at any moment. The stars watch the Earth, enjoy the show with a big stupid grin on their faces, and they mock us.

My eyes are like a dam with a tiny but present crack that is unable to hold the tons of water anymore. Soon, a flood. If only, I think to myself. If only I were cold, if only there was a switch that you could turn on and off, if only I didn't have the recurring image of an austere hospital room in which a Johanna covered in sweat and in a green robe had just given birth and a baby was crying in a meaningless doctor's arm and then suddenly crimson blood trickled down the camera screen that filmed the scene and the crying abruptly stopped as the screen turned all red -- if only I didn't have all that, then what the fuck! I'd be happy! But happy is one of the words that vanished from my dictionary.  ''I'm not cold,'' I say, because I must say something, because I must fill the void. But am I cold? Or am I in shock? Am I anything, or just a concrete body empty of emotions? The dam can't hold the water anymore, the crack is spreading, the flood begins, the tears stroll down. As I cry, I amuse myself with one stupid thought that pins one infinitesimal smile across my face: although I'm a rightie, the first tears always pour from my left eye.  ''I'm sorry honey, I didn't mean to hurt you. I know you're not cold, I'm stupid, it's just that--''  ''It's OK,'' I interrupt. Truth be told, it is OK. I understand her. She's a more sensitive person than I am. I don't comprehend yet that in the future I will look back on these few days, this week of reflection, as the most important period in my life. The defining moment of my life, probably. I don't grasp the magnitude of it only because I am still in it, and while I am still in it, the sun still rises in the same place, which is East or West, I don't remember, and it still sets in the opposite direction. In near or distant future, tomorrow or in ten years, when I will look back on today, I will think that time -- that linear, pain-in-the-ass stress machine -- broke down to give me eternal deliberation. But it didn't.  ''Are you mad? You don't love me anymore, do you?''  I look at her and grin at the preposterousness of the question; she beguiles me with the same look Zeppelin gives when he knows he's done something bad and has been caught, a look that says: I'm so sorry and so cute you'll forgive me anything. Right?  ''If I didn't love you anymore, I wouldn't have knocked you up. I would have told my sperm to hold back.''  She takes my hand, squeezes. ''Let's talk about it, then. What do you want to do?''  I know she's naturally weak, I know also that I'm the man and that she awaits me to make the decision for her. She won't ever admit it, and might not even be aware of it on the surface, but deep down she wants me to make the decision because it will assuage her conscience. Scapegoat. That's what I will become. Unconsciously, I am aware. She will never hate me for this.

Small decisions are hard. Suffice to say, big ones are impossible. You can ponder, you can wonder, but you can't squander doubt. You might as well toss a coin. I look at Johanna's face. Her eyes are greenish, scintillating stars. They're calm, like the ones up there, and they always bring a feeling of light and security within me, like a lighthouse would to a ship stranded in a furious sea in the dead of night. I think to myself that these eyes have allowed me to remain at peace these past few days, that whenever I felt my heart ready to burst out of my ribs, all I had to do was look into those two stars, or think about them, and the wave of anxiety would retreat.  And now, I could allow a baby to come into this world, and breathe our polluted air, and walk (or crawl) our shit-covered sidewalks, but most importantly, bring me another pair of stars.  ''I don't know what I want to do,'' I say. ''What I do think, though, is that we're lucky to have the possibility to be scared shitless about making a decision. Some parts of the world, abortions are illegal. That's scary.''  ''So you're scared shitless?''  I nod. ''Of course I am. Look, I've always wanted to be a father, just, I never expected to happen so soon. And you know, I don't really believe in destiny and karma and all that shit, but I have to admit, this is an opportunity presenting itself. We thought our lives were plain, boring, empty of something. This could be it.''  ''So,'' Johanna answers. ''You wanna keep the baby?''  I think back about what I've just said. Sometimes things roll out of your tongue and parachute into the air, gliding to the other person's ear, without you really meaning for it to happen. Sometimes, you just say things, without thinking. Do I really want to keep the baby? Didn't I want to live a few months by myself in Spain in the very near future? Hadn't we talked and accepted that proposition, only a week ago?  ''I'm still not sure, honey. I don't wanna kill it, that's for sure. But I also want to have a bit of freedom in the coming future. Having a dog, that's already being tied down. But a baby, that's like being nailed to the fucking cross. And not everyone gets a resurrection, you know?''  Silence from the two of us. The dog is snoring on the bed. The stars are watching in through the window. My hand is now operating on her neck. Abortion is tormenting my mind, shredding it to pieces. Each second spent contemplating about it is like a dagger in my heart. I run my other hand through my hair, ruffle it, while my stomach growls in anger from the lack of food it's received today.  ''Be honest. You don't want it?''

Breathe in. Moment of truth. Kind of like a time-out. I'm on the spot, which I hate, and I have to give a decisive, honest answer. No curving around that one. Straightforward. No strings attached. No buts or ifs. What do I do? I plunge into the real abyss, my heart, my soul, maybe, and search for what I really want the most. I think about the austere hospital room again, then flash forward to my parents and how I imagine them reacting to the news, then I picture myself watching the World Cup with my son in eight or ten years but I also visualize struggling for money and always searching for perfection.  What I fear the most, though, is slavery. Loss of freedom, loss of dreams, even those I know I'm too lazy to accomplish. It ain't over till the fat lady sings, and a pregnant woman who loves humming along to her Madonna or Rolling Stones album is as close as it gets to a fat lady singing.  ''It's OK,'' she says, not bothered by my silence, maybe able to see through my eyes and into my troubled mind. An army of tears is assembling itself in the field of her eyes. ''If you don't want it, we won't have it. That way, the baby will become a star and be a guardian angel for our next one, just like my brother is my guardian angel.''  The army is still holding back the attack, but not for long. I try to negotiate for peace and hopefully prevent war from breaking out, even if it seems improbable. ''Don't say that. Maybe it would be better to have it. I'm scared, you know. I'm scared of having it, of spending 8 months with you pregnant, I'm scared of struggling for money so that he or she has a good childhood, and I'm scared shitless of telling my parents. You know, society creates an image about everything, about how normal is perfection, and in a normal life a 23 year old uneducated and job-less guy does not have a child with a 28 year old girl after only one year together. So I'm scared of the image. But deep, deep down, even beyond the scared shitless part, whatever happens, happens, and I know I'll be happy once we have it.''  The army is attacking down the field of her cheeks, but instead of shooting bullets, flowers are coming out of the guns. She is crying tears, not of sadness, but of joy. And to welcome the army beyond the field of cheeks, a smile is in preparation. ''You would? Be happy?''  ''Of course I would! I mean, since the choice is ultimately yours, if you decide to keep it then I get to choose the name, so obviously I would be happy. And I'm excited about the idea of arguing with you about what clothes to buy for the baby, of how to raise it, of feeding it, of everything. I love you, and I would love our baby.''

My fingers are now tenderly caressing her face, running up her cheeks and around her forehead, venturing out in the wilderness of her hair and looping around her ear lobe and contouring her lips and slopping down her nose.  My mind is racing through the past, the present and the future; it races through a Spring day, dictated by a scorching sun witnessing a shy boy scared shitless admitting to a beautiful Swede that he really likes her, and when she answers that she likes him, too, he counters in a shaky voice that he means he really likes her, and when he notices the flicker of a smile on her face he draws near her and does the unthinkable: he kisses her; it races through this evening, our conversation, her body and her tears, my mind and my fear, our parents and unasked questions, love and doubt, and eventually, risks; it races through to a father looking proudly and in awe at his son, a blond toddler in diapers with a curious grin on his face, on the floor crawling after a scared mini Yorkshire while the mother is on the couch laughing and Mick Jagger is singing that childhood living is easy to do, the things you wanted I bought them for you. It races and races, eternally and ephemerally, from one thought to the other, from one skull side to the other, from one star to the other.  And then, I put my hand, flat, over her stomach.

The Breakup (Or How I Lost a Girlfriend.text:
‏					The Breakup
‏			Or How I lost a girlfriend but gained a best friend


‏	“What are you thinking about?”  I said.
‏	“Nothing.”  A lie.  “And you?”
‏	Eye for an eye, lie for a lie.  “Nothing.”
‏	The reign of lies was usurped by the one of silence, longer and more cruel.  Silence is pitiless.  Silence is blameless.  Silence is a river of tormenting thoughts.  Silence leads to breakup.  Silence led to our breakup.
‏	“I‘m thinking of us,” I found myself saying.  I paused, searched for strength to go on.  An endless search.  Then, simultaneously as I said the words, a bolt of pain plagued the pit of my stomach.  “I’m thinking about how it’s not working anymore.”
‏	“I know,” she said, her eyes bloodshot, this time not from pot but from the water-damn her eyes were constructing, a damn not strong enough to hold the tears for long, though.
‏	I blew the final whistle.  “I think we should stop seeing each other.”
‏	It was over and the fat lady hadn’t even sung.  A shame.  Amélie and I stared at each other; her face was damp, red.  Or maybe I was looking myself in a mirror, because I knew mine was similar-looking.  I looked her in the eyes, I looked at those five months we had spent together, five months shattered as quickly as a card-castle knocked down by the wind.  Yet was any of this really surprising?  No, I think it was inevitable.  I didn’t cry much, maybe because I wanted to take it like a man in front of my future ex-girlfriend, or maybe because my mind hadn’t yet realized what was happening -- I was still in her bed in her apartment, holding her naked body in my arms, covering her in kisses and drying her tears with Kleenex.
‏	I thought of movies then, of big Hollywood movies with their predictable happy endings.  Couples who breakup always have sex one last time, for old time’s sake.  I don’t know why, but I always thought it would happen to me.  I realized, however, that it was the farthest thing from reality.  How could you take any pleasure, knowing it was your last time?  How could you even be in the mood?  I wanted to grasp her and cuddle her with so much force that she’d suffocate in my arms.  She was mine and I was lucky to have her, John Harland had said so himself.  Except now she’s gone.

Family Dinner||Short story.text:
I coughed.
	Again and again.
	I looked toward the kitchen and saw the thick fog that had formed, that had gained ground and made its way to our living room.  The smoke blurred my vision, tickled my eyes.  Despite the difficulties, an alarm triggered in my head.  THE OVEN!
	“Mom, you forgot th—” I started yelling from the top of my lubgs, but I could faintly see, as the mist started to dissipate, that she’d already gone to the distant, smoky land of the kitchen.  She was a brave woman, my mother.  Meanwhile, having absorbed gallons of smoke – I would have a hard time from now on telling any doctor that I am not a smoker – I hurried toward the window my father had brilliantly opened and upon reaching it, gasped for air.  Liberation, I thought to myself, as I gladly took in the dirty, polluted air of Paris and enjoyed the sightseeing view of those numerous and pointless factories along the Seine River, emanating fearful gray clouds.  Ah, the 21st century!  My incessant cough now gone, I returned to the living room where, around a perfectly round table reminiscent of King Arthur’s, sat the valiant knights of the Igou family, impatient, like hungry carnivores from Jurassic Park, to devour the delicious food awaiting them.  Yep, dinner was ready.
	For a spectator who’d be unconscious enough to observe dinner in my family, I have to admit that it must be a disappointing show.  There’s so much preparation between grocery shopping, cooking the food, setting the table and in the end, all you get is a glimpse of four stomach-growling dinosaurs fiercely gulping down a whole chicken faster than you can say: chicken.  Even an ESPN slow-motion replay used during NFL games would not be of much help.  If the Guinness Book of Records has such a category, we’re it, the ultimate heavyweight champions as fastest dinner-eating family.  No doubt.
	But the night that the living room was besieged by the kitchen’s oven, our apartment was comparable to a zoo.  The smoke – which hadn’t completely evacuated yet, as we’d only opened one window to clear the room – shot out of out apartment as if it were one of those factories along the Seine River, and I feared a neighbor might call the firefighters.  To complete the freak show, the TV set was blasting.  My father, because of the dim vision to the smoke, had put the volume up, as if sound compensated for his impossibility to see the TV.  Incomprehensible logic.  The fact that the roasted beef was, well, roasted, did not impede our usual rapidity.  When eating at such a fast pace, what with the gulping of Evian water, the sticking of large, unchewed chunks of baguette in our mouths if we found space, and the pouring of Maille mayonnaise or mustard, little problems such as the actual taste of the meal do not occur.
	That night, as on any other night, no meaningful talking was made.  This was no political debate; it was dinner.  The closest we got to a debate was when halfway though the meal, my father and mother, in perfect unison, asked me to pass them the mayo.  Perplexed, I looked at the both of them, my teeth chomping hard on a piece of meat, my mind pondering even harder who to give the mayo to.
	Ah, the choices we have to make!

I, Spy||Short story.text:
I, spy

	 A man with binoculars.  Leaning against the metallic ramp of the seventh floor balcony.  Spying on neighbors in the middle of the night.  FBI searching for one of its most wanted?  CIA’s got a leak on Ben Laden’s whereabouts?  No, I thought to myself.  Not in this neighborhood, not with my luck.  Just a pervert trying to get a glimpse because he can’t get any.  His face was hidden but he had long puffy hair.  I stared at him from my foldout chair, wishing I, too, had binoculars.  Because, well, I, too can’t get any.  From my side of the street I couldn’t even see what he was looking at; my vision was blocked by a newly-built church – me and God, long story.
	“What you doing?”  The voice belonged to my sister Geri.
	I jumped.  “Jesus, you scared the shit out of me.”
	“So, what you doing?” She persisted, as she sat on the other foldout chair and tucked herself under the itchy nylon blanket.
	“I’m being a good neighbor by spying on neighbors who spy on other neighbors,” I replied.  Clarity is so my forte.
	“I thought you had work to do?” she asked.
	“And being a good neighbor is part of it,” I answered.
	Geri sipped hot coffee from a white cup with a Coca-Cola Santa Claus logo on it.  “What do you think he’s looking at, with his binoculars,” she said, jerking her head toward the man I had been staring at.
	“Probably a woman getting undressed,” I said.  Definitely.
	“Well, he could be gay – he could be looking at a man getting undressed.  He, he might look at you sometimes.  You should be careful and close the curtains when you undress.”  My sister looked at me with a faint, malicious smile.
	“OK, where the hell did that come from?”  A hesitant pause.  “He’s probably looking at something else.”  My faltered voice did not reassure me.
	“You’re right!  Maybe he’s like Mel Gibson in Conspiracy Theory and he’s watching a woman he swore to protect, and bad guys are after them so they’ll have to run aw—.”
	I interrupted her screeching, high-pitched, ear-unfriendly voice.  “OK, I think that’s a bit far-fetched.  Maybe he’s just a bird watcher.”
	“In Paris?  In the middle of the night?  So, like, what, he wants to know if pigeons are insomniac?”
	“Well, I’m sure some people might be interested by pigeons.  I mean, we see them everyday, so we don’t care.  But people from Africa or Asia, they don’t get to watch pigeons as much.  Maybe they care,” I said.
	“I think people from Asia and Africa have other things on their mind than pigeons,” she said.  “No, I think he’s probably like Mel Gibson in Payback.  He was betrayed by his friends, left for dead, and now he’s back wit—.”
	“Shut up!”  She did, thank God!  My ears took full advantage of this very uncommon moment of tranquility and rested.  Six flights down – according to my ears – two pedestrians walked the street, their feet rhythmically tapping against the dirty, dog-shit covered pavement.
	But then the torture resumed.  “Maybe he’s like Mel,” – by now they were on a first name basis – “in Lethal Weapons.  Like, he’s on stake-out because these Russian mobsters are trying to buy coke fro—.”
	“Maybe,” I cut in, “he’s like Mel in Spy Game.”
	“But, Mel wasn’t in Spy Game,” stammered Geri.
	I grinned.  “I know, and wasn’t it a great movie?”
	“Ha, ha, ha.  Very funny.  Sorry if you have no imagination, Mr. Bird Watcher.”
	“Oh yeah, like running all the plots of Mel Gibson movies is better.  Very creative, Mrs. Gibson,” I retorted.
	The following morning, while I was on my way to school, I investigated the area the man with binoculars had been looking forward to the night before.  I arrived in front of a bland, lifeless edifice that gave off the feeling of an abandoned, red-bricked factory, but on the first floor, through a curtained window, I could see the shadows of movements.  I looked back toward my street; I could see the seventh-floor balcony with the metallic ramp.  But no man, no binoculars peering.  I neared the door of the edifice and noticed a sign: Sexy Ladies Inside!  An arrow pointed to the doorknob.  A whorehouse?  In my neighborhood?  No way!  Well… we weren’t too far from the Bois de Boulogne.  I was so shoked.  So shocked that I reached for the doorknob, so shocked that I tried to turn it.  It was locked.  Just my luck, I thought.

Love, Death (working title)||Short story.text:
‏03/10					So I Can Die Easy

‏	Never forget, he tells me.  In my mind.  Or told me, before it happened.  As if time could slip out a back window in my skull, left slightly ajar to freshen up the room.  As if time was not concrete, was not this handwritten journal he kept and that I’m holding in my hands.  As if time was not engraved somewhere, somehow.  Time, I told him (and tell him still, in my head) is not a keyboard.  There is no delete button.  There is no U or I keys.  Time is a painting of us.
‏	I only listen to Led Zeppelin since he’s been gone.  I randomly put on one of the five CD’s he owned, and by now I know all the songs by heart.  Why wasn’t I in love with them before?  Some days I think I should go buy the ones he didn’t have.  Once, I remember, I even went to the music store down the street, where you can listen to the whole CD without buying it.  I spent four hours there, listening to a Led Zep CD, the one he wanted to buy before he died.  I went to the counter, and the vendor let me buy it with my credit card even though you’re not supposed to use credit cards if you don’t spend a minimum of 30€.  When I walked out of the shop with the CD in my hand ... 
‏	I cried.  More than I did at his funeral.  More than when Joe twisted my arm when I was nine, more than when I was rejected from Yale and even more than when Mufasa died in front of Simba’s eyes.  I brought the CD back home but I haven’t dared open it.  It would be like betraying him, listening and enjoying the music he craved for and that he’ll never be able to listen to.
‏	And now I don’t do anything with my days.  I ripped off the black curtains we got together and leave the window wide open all the time, fixing a spot in the distance just as he used to do, puffing away and thinking.  And when I see an army of menacing clouds approaching, I stroll outside hoping for a pouring rain to drench me.  Hoping to feel cold afterwards.  Hoping to feel.  Anything.
‏	I read over and over the short stories he’d written, his journals, his poems.  I feel his presence when I do, from the smell of the pages, from the style of his writing, from his slapstick humor that reminds me of that smile of his.  Everyday I go over the same routine.
‏	Then my phone rings.  And I know that it’s either my dad or my mom.  Trying to lure me home.  The princess back to the palace, because the peasant she fell in love with died.  They argue that I have nothing to live for in France.  They gave me that same argument when he was still alive.  I think in a way, deep down, they’re right.  But I’ve always had what my mother calls the spirit of contradiction.  If you say yes, I’ll say no.
‏	And somehow, even deeper down, in the place we rarely go because we’re afraid of it, kind of like a kid popping a head in the closet before sleep but not really entering it, something tells me it’s not over.  I don’t know what the it is, but even those days when I’m down, when the spot in the distance I’m fixing is the pavement of the courtyard underneath and in my head I imagine my splattered, bloody body lying near the garbage cans, even during those days something holds me back.  And it’s not fear.  It’s like a lost eternal hope, not of a better future, but maybe of a revived past.  Not that I expect a zombie Thomas to dig himself out of his grave.  I know he’s dead and I’ll never see him.  But something between him and I is not over yet.  Unfinished business.  Call me crazy.  Whatever.
‏	Right now it’s time for my dose of a short story.  I pull my hand in his portfolio and pull out a piece of paper.



‏				Child Abuse in Our Backyard

‏	I remember my last December spent in Rye.  Everyday, a thick sheet as white as milk blanketed the high school parking lot.  And everyday, the senior hallway was as bare of students as the trees were of leaves.   The teachers called it senioritis.  We called it a well-deserved year off.  But as much as slacking was the cool thing to do at the time, there was one dreaded but important duty required of us: college applications.
‏	Christmas was a fortnight away and, while Santa and his elves were rushing to finish their latest toys, I spent my days burning random pedestrians with a flamethrower in Grand Theft Auto 3.  In school I practiced my secret agent skills to avoid my stalking guidance counselor, Mr. L.  But one day I failed and he caught me.
