As his towering body loomed above me, he reminded me that I had only ten days left to hand in my applications, otherwise I would not go to college, would never get a job, never get married, and would die a piss-poor lonely man.
‏	“You’ll have them,” I told him so he’d bugger off, but what I really wanted to say was, “Geez, thanks for the added pressure.”  I mean, really, couldn’t he understand that I had more urgent matters to deal with?  Earlier that morning my friend Steve had bragged about how he’d gotten to the 12th mission on GTA3.  I was barely on the 3rd, so if I wanted to keep my dignity among my peers I’d have to pull an all-nighter just to catch up with him.  College applications were the last thing on my mind.
‏	I got home that afternoon thinking hard on how to plan the rest of the evening.  I would play videogames until 6 P.M, then order Dominos’ – pepperoni and cheese – watch Malcolm in the Middle, and then back to videogames.  Senior year was really the shiznit, man.
‏	People say I scream like a girl.  As I think back about that December afternoon when I entered my room to see a dust-less spot on the table where my TV should have been, I realize that maybe it’s true.  I shrieked like a kid who sees the monster come out of the closet, I shrieked until my throat throbbed, and even then, I shrieked some more.
‏	Mr. L had called my mother and expressed his concern about how I would die piss-poor and lonely.  Consequence: my TV had been confiscated until my applications were sealed and mailed.  The comprehension slowly sunk in, but I did not cry.  No, I might scream like a girl, but I took it like a man.
‏	I stormed to my room, cranked up the radio – it helped me concentrate in dire times – and sat behind my desk.  It felt strange; I hadn’t been in that area of my room since Junior Year.  But I was determined to work because I desperately needed my TV back by the next day.  The biggest event of the year was coming up: the MTV Movie Awards.  I could not, under any circumstances, miss it.  It would be the end of me.  I mean, what if Britney Spears and Madonna kissed?  I would look like the world’s biggest fool if I didn’t see it.
‏	And how hard could a college application be?  Check a few boxes, write down some words, and voila, you’re off to college.  The first few questions – first, middle, and last name, gender, and birth date – were somewhat easy.  But from there things went downhill.  And when I say downhill, I mean like a speeding avalanche charging down a mountain side and crushing everything on its way.
‏	First came, possible areas of academic concentration/majors.  I had a vague memory of a conversation with Mr. L as he told me what I should major in, according to my grades.  But I hadn’t been paying attention; as I sat across the stalking guidance counselor in his office, I was more interested by a bird outside nibbling off a dead rabbit.  So I tried to remember what he had told me.  Something about science.  Surely that couldn’t be it.  I never looked at my report card, but I knew as a fact that my grades in any science class never exceeded C-.  Maybe Mr. L wanted me to fail  Or maybe, I thought as I looked through a booklet of majors available, he had meant Political Science.  I didn’t know what that was, but that’s what I chose.  If you can’t trust your guidance counselor, who can you trust?
‏	Next I was thrown, possible career or professional plan.  I hadn’t thought about my future since I’d been five or six, when I wanted to be a firefighter during the day and a police officer at night.  I doubt that’s the kind of answer they were looking for.  So I pondered.  What did I want to do?  My long term life goal was to become a billionaire and buy a soccer club.  But how would I get there?  I didn’t want to waste any time – the MTV Movie Awards sere only 27 hours away – so I put down undecided.  I’d have four full years of college to come up with a brilliant plan to gain billions.
‏	My hand ached – I hadn’t written that much since Junior Year – so I took a break.  A Kit Kat break.  Then after a few minutes of singing along to the White Stripes’ Seven Nation Army, I plunged myself back into the 4-paged demon.  I continued answering personal questions, such as whether I would be a candidate for financial aid, and then went on to give details about my “secondary school you now attend.”
‏	The next part, entitled Test Information, almost gave me a heart attack.  They wanted to know my SAT scores.  How could they be so cruel?  How could they remind me of those 6 painful months spent memorizing words scribbled on colored index cards and which I’d already forgotten?  I had done everything to forget those stupid SAT tests; when I returned home that night, I had lit a fire in the fireplace and burnt, one by one, all those colored index cards.  And now the SAT’s were back to haunt me.  Whatever.  I slowed my breathing and told myself this was only about the MTV Movie Awards, nothing more.  Forget about college.  Forget about Mr. L.  Just concentrate on the MTV Movie Awards.  And I did.  I wrote down my SAT scores – 1190 – and moved on.
‏	They required general information about my family.  What is your mother’s name?  Isabelle.  Is she still alive?  And if not, date deceased.  Damn, I wish my mom were dead, then I’d have my TV back.  But no, she was still alive and puffing those Marlboros day in and day out.  Cancer had to be just around the corner for her.
‏	Then followed an enquiry about extracurricular activities.  Well, I had played soccer until 10th grade.  I’d also been a member of the chess club.  But most proudly, I had been co-founder of the Director’s Club.  Its goal had been for its members to write a screenplay and then shoot the movie – a goal that had eventually led to failure; we had held only one meeting.  But officially the club existed.  I was asked about positions held and honors won in the said extracurricular activities.  As president of the Director’s Club, I immediately honored myself with the club’s Most Dedicated Member of the Month Award for all the months since the creation of the club a year ago.  That filled some lines.
‏	After that I was asked to, “briefly list or describe any scholastic distinctions or honors you have won since the ninth grade.”  Because I’m a nice guy and I was asked to, I gave the briefest answer possible: none.  I could have taken the time to make something up – it’s not like they would have called all my high school teachers to check if I’d really won anything – but I was eager to finish the applications and get my TV back.
‏	After a few struggling questions about Work Experiences and a short answer on my most meaningful activities, I neared the finishing line.  All that stood on my way was the College Essay.
‏	Please write an essay (250-300 words) on a topic of your choice or on one of the options listed below.  I checked out the choices they offered me and settled on discussing, “some issue of personal, local, national, or international concern and its importance to you.”  I don’t have that many strong convictions in life; I hate politics, I’m an atheist, I don’t even have a favorite movie.  But if there is one thing I strongly believe in, it’s that community service should not be forced upon you.  It defies the whole principle of the act.  But Rye High School didn’t see it my way; if you wanted to graduate, you were obliged to volunteer for 60 hours of community service.  So I wrote my essay on how our local case was actually of national interest, because American teenagers were enslaved to “volunteer”.  Forget about Chinese kids working in Nike factories for 5 cents an hour – at least they were paid.  Ours was a clear case of child abuse.  I typed the essay – word count told me I had only 245 words.  So I entitled the piece, “Child Abuse in Our Backyard,” and printed the 250-word essay.
‏	I signed the Common Application, my hand trembling from disbelief that soon I would get my TV back.  I also realized that, now, high school was really over.  No more would I have to break a sweat on a Monday night to write a five-page essay due the next morning; no more would I have to hurry to school in frustration because I overslept; no more would I have to care about a teacher threatening to call my parents because of a missed homework.  Well, not until college, anyways!



‏	I don’t cry when I read his stories.  They’re the only bright spot in my day.  But I limit myself.  I don’t want to over abuse it and make it mundane.  One short story, one poem, and one entry from his journal.  One baguette traditionnel, one bottle of wine, and one pack of Marlboros.  One true love, one life, and one death.
‏	Occasionally, Steve calls me.  Sometimes it brings me back to the old days.  Before I had even met Thomas.  I don’t like Steve anymore, his arrogance, his dry humor and doleful comments on life.  But I like plunging back to a world with no Thomas.  It doesn’t’t erase him, but puts (him) in parentheses, if only for a few seconds.
‏	I don’t attack the bottle of wine before night, but the pack of cigarette I start unloading pretty early on.  Like he used to do.  It’s a habit he gave up at the end, and that I picked up only recently.  I remember how I would always plead him not to start so early, because it’s bad for the health.  But at the same time, at night he had a sexy raspy voice.  I don’t know about my voice, whether it’s become raspy or not.  I’ll have to try talking, one of these nights.
‏	Right now I put his story back in the portfolio.  And I listen to In My Time of Dying.  And I can’t stop thinking how perfectly it fits the situation.  It was one of his favorite songs, too.	

‏			In my time of dying, want nobody to mourn
‏			All I want for you to do is take my body home

‏			Well, well, well, so I can die easy
‏			Well, well, well, so I can die easy
	
‏			Jesus, gonna make up my dyin’ bed.
‏			Meet me, Jesus, meet me.  Meet me in the middle of the air
‏			If my wings should fail me, Lord,  please meet me with another 			pair


‏	And the tears roll down my cheeks but I don’t cry because I’m sad, I miss him, of course, but I think that he was an angel, and that maybe now he’s in a better place.  He wasn’t religious, didn’t’t believe in God.  Hated religion.  I remember the heated arguments we would have.  Or this one time, my cousin Susie that he’d never met before came to Paris for a week, and Thomas, he was a rather shy person, wouldn’t say much with strangers, and with her he was the same, except this once she started talking about religion, and it led to an argument between them.  But still, I think he’s in heaven now.  Looking down on me.
‏	And when I rarely go out, I always go to Notre Dame.  And pray, kneeling.  Selfishly, maybe.  Because I don’t pray for somebody else’s sake, but for my own.  I pray that I go to heaven, so that I can join him.  We’ll see.  Whatever.
‏	Now I want to read him again.  I pull out a poem.

‏Birdocracy
‏Birds are free to do as they please,
‏			Are we free to do as we please?			
‏			Birds can go here and there;			
‏			We can go here but not there.			
‏			Birds cannot cry but they do fly;			
‏			We cannot fly but we do cry.			
‏			I heard a man the other day:			
‏			He said birds killed for food.			
‏			I heard a bird the other day:			
‏			He said men killed for fun.			
‏			We have laws, but they always are broken;						Birds have naught, and nothing’s ever broken.					Men look to the sky and think there is heaven,					Birds fly to the sky and rise above our lies!

‏	I feel weak.  Tired.  Hungry, but I’m on a strike.  I’m losing grasp on reality, on time, on life, on religion, on dinner and supermarkets.  I don’t know what time it is when I wake up, and when I look at the digits on my cell phone, it (here’s a phony joke) doesn’t ring a bell to me.  I don’t know whether I should say, it’s been two weeks already since he died or, if it’s only been two weeks since he died.  Or maybe, I should go simple: he died two weeks ago.  A fortnight ago.  14 bottles of wine and 15 packs of cigarettes ago (I smoked a whole pack just at the funeral).  20 packs of Kleenexes ago.  Negative 10 lbs ago.  And how many ounces of tears ago?
‏	And the pills.  For every tear that took a slide down my cheeks, probably as many pills took the slide down my throat.  It’s weird, though.  If I had to take a survey, I wouldn’t be able to say which, out of the pills, cigarette, and the wine, helped the most to alleviate the pain.  It wasn’t faith, though.  But I’m not losing hope.  I don’t want to be a quitter.  But I don’t want to quit him, either.  Maybe I’ll join him in heaven.  Sooner or later.  Sooner, I hope.  Whatever.

Promises||Short story.text:
‏	There is no truth.  Take a glass, for example.  Lola picks it up sometimes, half full, to drink its water.  Then she picks it up sometimes, half empty, to throw it at me.  It misses because girls can’t throw (that’s why to insult a guy you say he throws like a girl) and it breaks like little promises.
‏	Little promises.  Let’s take a big one, actually.  Like when Lola, naked and tightly held in my arms in our uncomfortable bed, says she loves me.  I love you, and wanna spend the rest of my life with you, she says, constantly.  And I always believe her, because I’m a sucker for compliments and because I’m naive and because I love her also.
‏	So I tell her I love you.  
‏	But when I come home from work today, I observe she’s not her usual self.  She’s not fidgeting or restless like always.  She’s not trying to pinch or tickle me like always, trying to seduce me for sex then turn away for a laugh like always.  She’s not listening to any music, not even some shitty album by Mick Jagger from his solo 80s career, like always.
‏	She’s pensive as hell, like never.  I have to ring the bell three times (third time’s the charm, right?) before she opens the door, and it’s not like she lives in a luxurious palace where she has to cross a football field-length room to open it.  It’d be closer to the truth saying she could open the door from her bed.
‏	She doesn’t jump on me, doesn’t look at me.  She doesn’t say I love you, or maybe she does, but she mutters it and it’s not audible.
‏	I’m starving.  I’m not sure whether I say this or just think it out loud but she says, I wasn’t in the mood to make dinner, there’s some stuff in the fridge.
‏	Finally I get a good look at her.  I see the damp eyes; I’m no Sherlock Holmes but I know that spells “crying”.  And I ask her what’s wrong.
‏	Nothing, she tells me.
‏	I don’t know why, but whenever she’s got something wrong and I ask her about it, she always says nothing.  And everytime it frustrates me, because I expect an elaborate answer, immediately.
‏	I do have the option of not going further in my inquiry; I could open the fridge and prepare something for my starving stomach.  But then after a few minutes I would be accused of not caring and only thinking about eating.
‏	C’mon, I know there’s something wrong.  Come here, I tell her, opening my arms for her to fall into.  She doesn’t budge, staying a few feet from me.  She doesn’t say anything more, either.
‏	Then she asks the most alarming question possible: Do you have a cigarette?
‏	In our nine months together, she’s never asked me one.  I have seen her smoke a few times, but it was only taking puffs from my lit cigarette.  Once or twice, all of them in the early part of our relationship, she accepted a full cigarette when I offered, but until then I’d never known her to ask for one.
‏	You wanna smoke?
‏	Well, that’s stating the obvious, she curtly says.
‏	I could answer back, God knows I want to as much as any teenager when wrongly scolded by unfair parents, but nine months in a relationship has taught me I know better.  Instead I head toward the sink to get the ashtray and on the way I notice a bottle of wine downed 3/4th of the way and two glasses, one empty and the other half full.
‏	Again, I’m no Sherlock Holmes but by then I’m uneasy.  I ask her if she had company, and when after a minute she doesn’t answer, the unease sets in with ease in my skin and in my head.
‏	OK, I say, trying to take a commanding tone while holding the ashtray back toward her, now you’re going to tell me who was here, and what the problem is.  And right now.
‏	She knows I’m not kidding anymore, and she was probably waiting for this.
‏	Mike came by today, she says, curt again.  By now I’ve handed her the cigarette and a lighter and from the first, deep drag, it seems like this is an event she’s been awaiting for a very long time.
‏	Mike is her ex.  I first met him on our first date in one of her favorite bars.  Bars and ex, two bad omens reunited in one.  Thinking back now, I guess I should have seen it coming.  I’m pissed that she doesn’t go on, that I have to drag out the answers the way she’s dragging on her cigarette.  Her eyes are still damp and she’s still not looking at me.
‏	I move closer to her, my head a melting pot of questions.  Should I yell, be sensible?  Hit her?  Ask her why he came, or what happened?
‏	I move closer to her and say, and?
‏	She looks at me for the first time.  I see the water bubbling in her eyes, the tears ready to roll down her cheeks.  I see the puffs of her cigarette and her fingers fidgeting, I feel my heart beating faster and faster, gaining momentum, pounding like a maniac would on the door of his cell and I say and? again and still she doesn’t answer and now my whole body is shaking and all kinds of thoughts are racing by in my mind like a speed-racer.
‏	So what the fuck happened?
‏	Silence.  I don’t think silence happened between her and Mike but it happens now, between her and me.  And I can’t stand it.  I’m still waiting for an answer, but I’m also trying to calm myself down.  I go over to the stereo and put on Since I’ve Been Loving You, by Led Zep.
‏	I didn’t ask him to come over, you know.  And I certainly didn’t want anything to happen.  I mean ...  She takes a puff again, blows out the smoke slowly, shakes her head.
‏	Yeah, but something fucking happened, then?  Right?  Anger.  It was in me, has been in me for a while, but now the fucker is out.  And furious.  I move closer to her, grab the cigarette out of her hand and put it out in the ashtray.  The music soothes me a bit, comforts me, but not enough to prevent me from grabbing her hands, forcefully, too much maybe, it will probably leave red marks after and I know she’s hurting, I see  it in her eyes, but I know her pride, also, and she doesn’t say anything, pretends she feels nothing.
‏	I let go.
‏	I love you, she says.

Sentence Assignment||Short story.text:
After I finally finished my twentieth big, fat cheeseburger, when there was not an ounce of grease left on the plate, and although I wasn’t yet done with my overpaid warm coke, I quickly left the so-called restaurant, my stomach twisting in pain from the undigested food and my mind, dumbfounded, trying to think of a reason why I had accepted this stupid dare.

	In a packed arena where the crowd is savagely going wild, on a distant planet that resembles our own, near the end of the fifth round, where the tension is so strong that it could rip you apart, I incredulously see, on the left, Snow White, her pale face covered in blood and bruises, her eyes fiery, and on the right, Cinderella, her beautiful face hindered by a black-eye, her jaw locked, pounding at each other as if there was no tomorrow.

	The food I had in my plate was a cheeseburger, but it was not the kind of cheeseburger that you ordered in restaurants; it was so greasy that the first bite accidentally slipped out of my tongue and down my throat like a burning comet ripping into the atmosphere, the large lump of unchewed meat crashing into the oblivion of my stomach like a lost treasure chest thrown in the bottom of the ocean.


					Privilege: Food

	10:30 A.M.  Time to wake-up.  First thing I do is check my phone to see if anyone was drunk enough over the night to leave me a message.  I do have one.  It’s from God!  God?  But I’m an atheist!  Whatever.  He tells me that I’ve sinned and as a result I’ve lost the ability to eat.  Damn! – and me who thought I’d go get a big, fat greasy brunch across the street.  Whatever.  I go to school my stomach growling, making noises I never thought possible.  If I can’t eat, I’ll die of hunger.  I read in an article – and by article I mean the internet – that you could only survive seven days without food.  Is that true?  Well, I’ll find out soon enough.  So I go to school, to room G-32 and Professor Gunn’s Post-War European Lit. Class.  Of course, I forgot to read Muriel Spark’s Territorial Rights, so I won’t be able to take part in the class discussion – not like I ever do, anyways.  My stomach keeps making inhumane, embarrassing noises that sound like multiple dogs barking.  Professor Gunn asks me if I’m hungry.
	“Hell’s yeah,” I tell him.
	“Well, why don’t you go get some food?”
	“I can’t,” I say.  “Doctor’s order.  No food until I die.”
	“Why?”
	“I don’t know.”
	Then something hits me.  Seven days to live?  I don’t have to be in this stupid classroom.  I can do whatever I want.



Disciplined, without any emotion, not pity, not malice, with a swastika pinned on his uniform, without over-eagerness, the Commandant climbed onto the wooden platform, grabbed the loudspeaker, and bellowed in German: “Back to your barracks!”

The Child||Short story.text:
I listen to the child cry downstairs.  His parents are dead, now two cadavers decomposing on a blood-drenched bed, their brains splattered all over.  The cries echo in the otherwise silent house, they seep through my skull and echo in my head.  I take a white cloth to sweep my gun, then place the weapon in my holster.  I won't need it for the child.  Then I make my way out of the room, but am confronted by a man.  A tall stranger in timber baggy pants and long black raincoat.  His face is veiled by a hood, but he uncovers it to reveal his face.  An eerie scar freely runs along his left cheek to disgust women away, while men are kept at bay by his menacing look, eagle eyes that creep out of thin slits.  I stare at this stranger and my eyes are drawn to his, like magnets.  I punch the stranger in the stomach, and the mirror shatters.  Under my glove, I can feel the warmth of my hand bleeding and my knuckles hurting.  I exit the room
	And I listen to the child cry downstairs.  The resonance in my head intensifies, evicts out all my thoughts.  I now stand at the top of the stairs; I have to lower myself to another level.  My hands tremble a little; my nervous tick kicks in; I tap my fingers rhythmically against the ramp; I take a deep breath; I take a first step.  And another.  This will be my first child.  The stolidness is gone, the self-confidence that allowed me to burst in the parents' room, and empty my cartridge in seconds without doubt, without second thoughts – that self-confidence is gone, has left the building.  A child is something else, it has none of that putrid corruption adults have, the corruption that, in the end, justifies it all.  I remember my innocence, and the premature loss of it, when, at nine years old, solitude heartily welcomed me after my parents were shot dead while robbing a grocery store.
	And still, I listen to the child cry downstairs.  Maybe he knows it's coming, like I knew it was coming while I did my tour in Vietnam.  Except I was wrong, it never came for me, only for the others.  I was avoided by the Grim Reaper.  But not by the Vietcongs.  I was in a hole for three years in POW camp, before being traded back to America, the land of the braves.  Except the braves are a dying breed.  They cry because they know death is coming, like the child cries because he knows I'm coming.   My footsteps creak against the wooden floor.
	Again, I listen to the child cry downstairs.  Tomorrow the headlines will read: Virtuous Judge And Family Murdered In Cold Blood.  But they will leave out the father's alcoholic problems, or the mother's affair with her doctor.  No one is perfect in this world, not I, not my employer – who left a red sticker in the envelop, meaning no one is to be spared.  Not even this child, twirling in his crib frantically, yelling.  I advance in his territory, marked by light blue wallpaper, boxes flooded with broken toys, shelves full of bedtime stories.  I stand over him now, his stare locked into mine.  I take out my cloth.  At first there is struggling, but then it quickly stops.  Only a few twitch of the arm or leg here and there.  Then it completely stops; immobility.  I look at his lifeless eyes, lifeless body.  I leave the room.  And I listen, but the child cries no more.

Thought||Short story.text:
‏Finally.
‏I see the stars.  Gone for a long month, hidden in the darkness behind the clouds.  But today the sun pierced through and tonight they tease me to play a mental game of connect the dots with them.
‏A drag.  A puff.  
‏My dog is watching me through the window.  He wants to join me on the balcony, but I leave the door closed.  Alone time means alone.  From men, from women, from my sleeping baby, from my dog.  From my thoughts, if I could.  
‏But I can't.
‏My fingertips still hurt from the hours I spent burying them in the metal strings of my guitar, but the more pain I feel the more joy I get.  I gave, I took.  I wish I could take a snapshot of this moment and lock myself in it for eternity.  Away from everything and everyone locked out on my balcony with a cigarette under the stars and Noir Désir singing that I'm lost but I'm not stranded.
‏But if these moments were eternal, I probably wouldn't enjoy them as much, down the line.  Like everything, they would fade, slowly, and disappear into the vast kingdom of boredom.  A treasure thrown into oblivion and turning to dust.
‏I look at the stars.  Underrated.  I've always loved watching them.  Maybe it's the thing I've loved for the longest time.  Who knows?  I don't.  I remember, as a younger kid, I could sit on a long chair during summer nights and stare at them.  Just stare, lost in my thoughts.  They're peaceful, the stars.   Soothing.  Trustworthy.  They come back every night.
‏My girlfriend's not back.  Yet.  She'll be drunk when she comes back.  And hungover tomorrow.  She complains that her weekdays are boring, cycles stuck on the repeat button.  Diapers, laundry, groceries, dinners.  But her weekends are the same.  Drunk nights and hungover tomorrows.
‏But she's not back, yet.  So let's not think about her.  Otherwise I'll over overdose.
‏I wonder about stupid things, sometimes.  Like, how many people are looking at the stars, right now.  This very second.  And how many of them are thinking exactly like me, whether anyone else is looking at the stars wondering if other people are doing the same thing.  Then I think about the fact that there are over a billion people in China so someone there must be doing that .  But I guess it's stupid, because with the time difference, it's not night there.  So they can't see the stars.  But maybe someone in China is looking at the sun, with sunglasses, of course, and thinking if anyone else is doing the same thing as him.  I am.  Kind of.
‏Stupid thoughts.
‏Another one: today on the bus I went to the bathroom because I needed to pee, and when I went I was flabbergasted by the size of the bathroom.  It was by far the biggest bathroom I've ever seen on a bus, train, and airplane combined.
‏I probably have as many stupid thoughts as there are stars dotting the blackness over my head.  Does that make me stupid?  But what if, then, out of thin air, I have the smartest thought of all times?  Would that make me the smartest man ever?  Would both extremes balance each other out and make me ordinary?
‏Are thoughts confined only to the realms of our minds?  If I start explaining a thought, does it end being a thought, since it leaves my mind?  Aren't thoughts for our minds, only?  Is that another stupid thought, or the smartest one of all times?
‏I can see the clouds moving pretty quickly, in a hurry.  Maybe there's a place that's been getting too much sun, and they need to go there, to piss the people off and give them a bit of grey in their lives.  And rain, too, maybe.
‏I haven't dragged for a while.  I do.  I puff.
‏Zeppelin is still staring at me through the window, with pleading eyes.  He knows better than to bark, though.  I give in a gentle shove at the door so that it stays ajar.  I take my earplugs out and put my ear closer to the door.  I hear silence.  Leo's still sleeping.  My alone time has won another battle.  But eventually it always loses the war.
‏Oh, I got another stupid thought:  I'm happy I don't know squat about science and that I don't really know what stars truly are.  That would kill it for me, like finding out who the killer is in a detective story.  I like them how they are.  Mysterious.  Alight.  Far away.  And above, like they're better than us, not in a stuck up way but humble.  I think if stars were men, they would be humble.
‏I hate people who ask "why".  And even more those who answer "because".  "Why not" is the way to go.
‏Why not?
‏It's a cheap method out of anything, a nice getaway when backed up in a corner.

Weather||Short story.text:
Then there was the bad weather.  I say then, as if another outcome was possible; but I didn’t see myself going there, under a torching sun reigning over a blue sky as empty of clouds as a beach is of swimmers in winter.  No, the weather was bad; terrible, in fact.  So bad that the thought of having an accident and joining her was ever present in the back of my mind.  The rain was pouring, the thick drops battering against the hood and rooftop of my Montero, banging continuously, incessantly, as if it desperately wanted to get in my car and tell me something.  Maybe they were sent by her, maybe they were her tears.  Crying, because of our last time …

					*	*	*

“I’m leaving you.”

					*	*	*

The muffled sound emanating from the radio was so incoherent, it could have been either Beyonce or The Beatles.  Or maybe it was some new pop group, called The Static.  The rain, knocking to get in, added a nice rhythmic beat.  Amélie had told me ages ago to fix the damn radio, or have a CD player installed, for times we’d be stuck in traffic.  Like today.  Except, today, I was the only one stuck in traffic.  The highway, flooded by a few inches of rain, looked like a colony of snails slowly edging forth.  At this pace, it would be hours till I reached Boston.
On my left, impatiently waiting like everyone else, was a coaching bus.  Some passengers were looking out the window; they seemed happy, sad, young, old, bright, stupid, funny, boring.  But most of all, they seemed alive.  I could imagine an explosion taking us all away, or I could imagine nothing happening.  Either way, nothing was fair.  It wasn’t fair that Amélie hadn’t taken this very bus that I was staring at, this bus that radiated safety, that radiated life to all its passengers.  They knew nothing would happen today.  Good for them. 
My ears ached again.  I turned off The Static.  Good for me.

				*	*	*

	“I’m leaving you,” she said, tears already flowing down her damp cheeks.  She had nothing on but the radio, this time distinguishably neither Beyonce nor the Beatles – not even The Static – but Radiohead’s Creep.  Her visible belly paraded her recent urge to simply stop any kind of diet.
	“Why?” I asked, weak, meek.  Like always.  And that was why she was leaving.
	“You already know why, do we have to go over it again?”  She glared at me; she was in a rush, but at the same time, she was not budging.  Maybe deep down inside her she was waiting for a rebellion inside me, maybe she clung on the hope that I truly loved her and would fight for her.  A bleak hope.
	“Don’t go,” I said.  Because I had to.  What else was I supposed to say?
	“Don’t go?”  She scuffed, picked up her bags, looked me in the eyes.  She was hesitating, I knew it.  I still had time to seize my chance.  I could grab her arm, by force, throw her on the bed.  She would resist.  At first only, though.  
	The scenario of what could have happened was still running in my head when she stormed out of her room, when she stormed out of my life.  Without a bye, without a look back.

					*	*	*

	I could have grabbed her arm, by force, throw her on the bed.  She would have resisted.  At first only, though.  Then she would have smiled that stunning smile of hers, yelling, “my tommyyyyyyy!” and throwing her arms violently around my neck.  And she would have lived.  I could have taken the car, driven to the bus station, and stopped her from getting on the damn bus.  I could have changed, like she had asked me to.  I could have cared more.  But I didn’t.
	I was running low on fuel, and I was even lower on cash.  I didn’t even remember if I’d taken my credit card.  I could always leave my car in Boston and take the bus back to New York.  A road sign indicated that Boston was only 75 miles away.  And the traffic was getting lighter.  There was no need to hurry, though; Amélie would be eternally waiting for me, now.
	I suddenly realized that I was the only one to know.  Her mother, her father, her friends: none of them had been alerted yet.  Would I have to do it myself?  I’d have to ask once I arrived.


					*	*	*

	I waited in a silent corridor.  It was austere, the walls were cracked, decaying; here and there were traces of its original color, a bright white, but now it was coated by grime.  I didn’t wonder if these walls could talk, but if they could listen, and how many cries had they heard?  Would they hear mine, soon?  The silence was a surprising guest, because the dozen chairs or so around me were all occupied by people.  Yet, not a word, not a cry, not even a whisper dared contest the reign of silence.
	After a while, police officers came in the room.  I didn’t count how many.  Everyone looked up at them, as if intensely waiting for barked orders.
	“We’re now gonna proceed to the identification of the bodies,” said a fat one.  He called a name out loud, and a frail lady, her face livid, stood up.

					*	*	*

	“Sir, are you Thomas?”
	“Yes,” I said, putting the phone closer to my ear and a finger in the other so I could hear better.
	“Do you know an Amélie Wallach?” asked the monotonous voice.
	“Yes.”
	“I have the regret to inform you that her bus was in an accident.  There were no survivors.”
	At first I did not understand what he meant by that.  I wanted to say, there are no survivors, fine, but how’s Amélie?  Is she OK?  Then, it sunk in, slowly, and the phone slipped out of my hands, quickly; my heart burst out while the phone shattered, throwing small debris all over.  I didn’t care; these I could pick up, throw away, and the phone I could replace.  But my heart … Nothing could replace that.  

					*	*	*

	“Sir, are you Thomas?”
	I was lost in my thoughts, and couldn’t hear what the cop was saying.  I only looked up because he blocked the light.
	“Are you Thomas?”
	I nodded.
	“I know this is hard, but could you please follow me for the identification?”
	I didn’t nod, but I got up, which was as good an answer, if not better.
	The first thing I noticed when I entered the room was the smell; then, I saw the table and a body draped over by a single white sheet.  I approached, slowly.  The fat cop stayed by the door, while a man dressed like a doctor stood by the table in the center of the room.  When I stepped up to him, he looked at me.  Before he could say anything, I nodded.

					*	*	*

	Orange was the color.  Balloons, flags, jerseys, everything.  Everyone was wearing orange.  The streets were filled with jovial people, all the restaurants had set tables outside, and already it was impossible to find seats anywhere.  But we didn’t care, we weren’t hungry.  Not for food, anyways.  We only craved to get to the end of the street.  So that we could get on another and get to the end of that one.  We felt like Columbus or Armstrong, discoverers, awed by every detail processed by the iris of our eyes.
	Beautiful was the word.  She was beautiful.  Smiling that stunning smile of hers.  The people, even the ugly ones, were beautiful.  The buildings, the streets, the canals.  Beautiful.
	It was our getaway weekend, a surprise weekend, a last-minute weekend.  Our parents would kill us on our return, but we didn’t care, we were lost deep in space, in another galaxy, and our ship was nowhere close to getting back.
	It was a weekend of drugs: the shrooms, the joints.  But the biggest one was love; the love that chained us together and drove us to the Bulldog, the Red Light District, the Alice-in-Wonderland bathrooms.

					*	*	*

	The girl under the sheet was Amélie.  I clearly recognized her face, the thick traits of her jaw, the creamy pale skin smoothly buttered on, her perfectly-shaped nose, the bright red of her lipsticks, which she had put on this morning just to piss me off because she knew I hated it.
	Then I blinked.
	Suddenly, Amélie was blonde.  Her nose lost its perfection, replaced by a long and twisted downward road that dipped right, then swerved left, to come to a screeching stop only inches away from pallid lips, stripped naked of its lipstick.
	“It’s not her.”
	“Are you sure?” asked the doctor, taken aback.
	I wanted to say something cocky, like, yeah, I’m pretty sure I’d be able to recognize the person I’ve been sleeping with for the past 12 months of my life.  But this wasn’t the right time, nor the right place.  It wasn’t the doctor’s fault, and anyways, since this wasn’t Amélie, it meant someone else would be coming later to identify this corpse.  And this time, the identification would be most likely positive.
	“Sir, can you please follow me?” said the fat cop, still not moving from the door.
	We left the room for another one, filled with desks and other cops.  My fat guide walked to a drawer, pulled it open, and brought out a phone.  Amélie’s phone.

	
					*	*	*
					
I waited in a true silence, in a fake darkness.  Sunrays pierced through the curtains, the bright sliver of light slicing the darkness like the blade of a razor, emitting enough luminosity for my eyes to clearly distinguish, for example, the curves of a large bellied – but otherwise slim – woman lying on my side.  I looked at her; her chest heaved up and down, up and down, slowly, while her mouth gaped wide open.  Then she turned on her side and opened her eyes.
“Hello, you,” I said.
“Hello, you.”
I asked her if she had slept well.
She told me she had.  “What about you?”
	“Yeah, but I had a horrible dream.  We broke up, then you left me to go to Boston, by bus.  I got this phone call, telling me there had been an accident.  So I drove up to Boston to identify your body.”
	“Well, now I really know what you think of me!  You want me dead.”  A thin smile was stapled on her face.
“No.  But right before I had to identify your body, I thought about our trip to Amsterdam.  Then I went in the room to identify you and it was you, then your face disappeared and it was someone else.  It was a pretty weird dream.  I remember the part when I drove up from New York.  I was so sad and pissed because I thought you were dead, and there was huge traffic.  Then there was the bad weather…”



						The End

A Tale of Two Sarahs||Short story.text:
A Tale of Two Sarah’s


	I snored like a jackhammer, tired from the night-long jamming.  Then a tiny beep emitted from my Nokia woke me up.  I read the text message: hey, it’s Sarah, I’ll be in Paris this weekend, wanna go to a movie?  Two keywords about Sarah: blonde and Swedish.  Therefore she didn’t need to ask me twice.  I went to the kitchen, got me a coke and a cookie, then went back to my room.  Now I could ponder with complete serenity with the problem at hand: what to answer.  After a debated half-hour, I came up with, “Yeah, I’d love to.”  My creative writing major was paying off.  I nervously typed my answer, and sent it.
	A few minutes later, a second beep from my Nokia proposed to see Munich on Saturday night.  I sent a search party to my brain to find the perfect answer.  It found, “Good for me.”  I was on a roll.
	The next day I woke up happier than a dog who’s found a bag of bones.  I had a smile pinned on my face as I entered the kitchen, ready to devour a bowl of Frosties.  Then I saw my sister.  Somehow I knew something wrong would happen.
“Tom,” her eerie voice said.  “Why didn’t you tell me you had a date with Sarah?” 
That question was like a thrown bowling ball that had knocked all my pins on its way to a strike.  My smile was gone.  “How the fuck do you know who Sarah is?”
“Well, duh, I only introduced you to her.”
“No, you di-.”  then the nightmare began.  My knees buckled, my heartbeat came to a screeching stop, then kicked again as if it was running a marathon.
“What’s wrong?”  My sister must have noticed my pallid face.
I took a moment to breath a bit, and calm myself down.  “Well, I thought it was a different Sarah that sent me a message.  I didn’t even know your friend Sarah had my number.  I never gave it to her.”
“I know, I did.  But what’s the problem, don’t you like her?”
Two keywords about this my sister’s Sarah: not bond and not Swedish.  “She’s nice, but…” I had no need to finish the sentence to make my point.
“Well, sorry.  Guess you’re gonna have to cancel your date.”

You’re gonna have to cancel your date.  That idea stayed in my mind.  Did I have the balls to call a girl – that I didn’t like – and tell her, well, I’m sorry, I took you for someone else, I actually don’t wanna go to the movies with?  No, I didn’t have the balls to do that.  So I didn’t cancel the date.
A Tale of Two Sarahs||Short story.source: Incomplete Short Stories/A Tale of Two Sarah.doc

Advice (Because I Just Broke Up with My.text:
Advice

			Because I just Broke-Up with My Girlfriend


	I need advice because I’m as lost as a kid looking for the How To Ride a Bicycle For Dummies in the Science Fiction section.  I’m looking for the How to get my stuff back from my ex for dummies and I’m in the very inexperienced section.  If, for example, you were to compare me to a fruit (not that kind, my ex is a girl), then you could say you have the ripe, the unripe, and then me.
	The said stuff is a bunch of CDs, including the Jimmy Page Experience (which, actually, is a funny story because it’s a CD that belonged to my previous ex, and I never gave it back to her) and two books, one of which, Kurt Vonnegut’s Mothernight, is my favourite.  Needless to say I care deeply about these precious possessions of mine, inadvertently fallen into the wrong hands.
	Before I go on, and before people bombard me with advice, I should add that it took long hours of consideration and many cups of coffee and countless coin tossing before I finally took the decision to break up with my girlfriend.  The reason for this is that while I visited her this summer in Sweden (yes, she’s Swedish, but guys, I swear, there IS a good reason to break up with Swedish chicks), I don’t know how it came up, but one day she bluntly told me with her darting eyes black as a crow shackling me to the spot, “If you break up with me, I’ll make your life a living hell.”  It’s even possible that she whispered this, and then that her head turned round once on its neck like in the exorcist.  Not saying it happened, but given the situation, could have been possible.
	Anywho, I had the exorcist scene in my head when the coin toss landed in my cup of coffee that sleepless, starful night.  Then another scene spurted out of nowhere: this one included a butcher knife, and lots and lots and lots and lots – well, let’s just say a (giant) truckload – of blood.  And it was all mine.  Again, obviously not possible, but sometimes an over exaggeration of an image gets the point across.  Across what, I don’t know.  Maybe my dead body?  But the point is across: My ex is a maniac.
	So.  I need advice.  I’ll even give up on the CDs, I can always download them off the internet.  I do truly care about the book, though.  I should maybe add that I have not one but two books of her right here in my Fort Knox of a home.  Maybe, unlike the Israelis and Palestinians, we can come to some sort of agreement for an exchange.  I’ll even forget about the other book, as well.  But this is as far as I’ll go.  I do have some dignity … left … somewhere.
	So, advice, anyone?

Breaking Down Is Easy||Short story.text:
Breaking Down Is Easy


	Things are inevitable, I think.  If I am what I am today, it’s because of who I was yesterday.  And today I am shaping up what I will look like tomorrow.  That’s a scary thought.  Tomorrow in the papers you will read lies from the pit of hells, offensive words that will say I was always a little monster, because that’s how journalists are.  They embellish stories, to sell.  I don’t blame them; we live in a society dictated by money.  The rich aren’t necessarily happy that they have money, but the poor are depressed that they lack it.  For those few of you that still read the papers, and for the rest that watch the news on TV or surf it on the net, let me tell you how it all happened.  From the beginning.  Let me give you the exclusive.

	There are so many ways to begin a story.  I could say it began the day my family and I moved to the US because those were happy times as I remember them, and not happy only because we had money, not happy times because we flew in business class with Air France to JFK, and not happy times because from the airport we took two limousines, one for my mother, brother, and sister, and one for my dad and I, which is, I agree, totally useless; no, those were happy times because we were about (and here comes a cliché) to embark on a new journey.  I could also say, and it wouldn’t be lying, that it began in 9th grade, when I met Dion, who went on to become the lead singer of our band, the co-director of a club we created together, a golf buddy, a videogame buddy, a senior year spring break mate, but most of all, my best friend in high school, which allowed me to feel fit in, which I hadn’t until then.
