Conversation of Premeditation||Short sto.text:
Conversation of Premeditation

	2200 hours, sundown.  The five-men (well, actually, three men and two women) commando team assembles at the previously agreed upon rendezvous point, the second floor of the Kleptomaniac Bitch’ apartment, where silence and darkness reign in harmony.
	“Is it safe to speak in here?” murmurs Disney Phobia.
	“As safe as eating a pretzel,” responds codename Atheist Mastermind.
	“Well, apparently that’s pretty hard for Americans.”
	“Yeah,” retorts Atheist Mastermind, “well, good thing we’re not Americans, then.”
	“Then why are we speaking in English?  We won’t even be able to understand Dad.”
	The commando leader shakes his head in disbelief.  “Goddamnit!!!  Use codenames.  Codenames!!!  And we’re speaking in English because this story is going to be read by English speaking people.  You’ll just have to do your best to understand Blind Man.”
	“Don’t say Goddamnit, you’re a goddamn atheist.  Makes no sense.”
	“He’s right,” confirms Grendel, the smirk on her face revealing a gap in her yellowed teeth.
	“Whatever!  Can we get on with the mission?”
	“Vell, I av too go too basroom furst,” declares Blind Man.
	“Negative, Blind Man.  Don’t you see the importance of this mission?  Especially you.  Don’t you want to watch the Gunners attack the Toon Army at 1300 hours on Saturday?”
	“OK, Atheist Mastermind.  That’s going a bit too far.  We don’t need fucking codenames for soccer games.  We can just say Arsenal play Newcastle at 1 pm,” says Disney Phobia.
	“Wait,” interrupts VIP Vodka.  “Is this story going to be read by Americans or British people?  Because should we say soccer or football?”
	“Oh my God, you guys are retarded.  You’re deviating the story so much.  We’ve already wasted half a page and we haven’t even gotten to the topic of this meeting.”
	“Hey, did you hear me say, ‘hello, my name is Disney Phobia, and I’m an alcoholic?’  No.  Because this isn’t AA.  It’s not a meeting, as you say.  It’s a rendezvous point.  So get your vocab right, wannabe writer.  Why not make it a 20 year family reunion, while you’re at it?”
	“Hey, consider yourself lucky, you only got 20 years.  I got 24 in this stupid famil…  Hey!  What the hell is this mist?  Why can’t I see you guys anymore?”
	“Grendel!” snaps Atheist Mastermind.  “Stop smoking.”
	Grendel obediently puts out her three lit cigarettes.
	“Vy in ze ell vould yoo smoke sree cigarettes at the sem tam?” asks Blind Man.
	“Blind Man, can’t you see?  She’s not smoking sree cigarettes, whatever that means, she’s smoking three cigarettes,” says Disney Phobia.
	“Zats vat A said.”
	“Whatever!  No one cares.  Let’s talk about the business at hand.  How do we go about it?”
	For a few seconds, Silence’s ferocious armies regain control of the room, and It reigns, but not in harmony; Darkness’ rule is being challenged by piercing light from the luminous queen of the night, Moon.
	“Well, we can’t do it now,” declares Disney Phobia.  “They’re watching TV.  They’re probably watching the Discovery Channel.”
	“No, that’s a porn festival for animals.  Too much sex for them.  They’re probably watching family feud or who wants to be a millionaire.”
	“Oh, speaking of who wants to be a millionaire, I have a great video from Youtube to show you, VIP Vodka.  There was this guy on the show, and the question was, ‘what gravitates around the Earth?’ and the choices were Moon, Sun, Mars, and Venus.  The dumbass didn’t even know the answer, so then he asks the audience’s advice, and around 40% said the Sun, and another 40% said the moon.  It’s hilarious, people can be so fucking retarded.  And you know what he answered as his final answer?”
	“Well, the correct answer is the Sun, isn’t it?”
	The other four members of the commando team look at each other, incredulous.  “Damn, that’s right up there with your comment about Gandhi being a Muslim,” says the team leader.  He then adds, “Alright, now, can we discuss our situation?  We have to go about it carefully.”
	Grendel raises a closed fist, out of anger, and in an excited voice, says, “What does it matter?  I say we go in there, rip her heart out, and make her eat it.  As for him…”
	“Grendel, Kleptomaniac Bitch doesn’t have a heart,” utters Disney Phobia.
	“Huny, evrybodee as a hart.  But yoo zust can’t make er eat stone.”
Disney Phobia looks at Blind Man, as bewildered as James Cameron was when he found out there were millions of stupid rich teenage girls to con with a stupid movie about a blond kid dying on a sinking ship.  “Wow, Blind Man.  That was actually an OK joke.  Too bad your shitty accent ruined it.” 
“Holy mother of Shit, I swear to God, planning anything with you guys is harder than taking over the world with a bunch of 5 year olds,” admits Atheist Mastermind.  He takes a deep breath, and then adds, “Need I remind you, fellow commando-mates, what awaits us in the not-so-far future?  A poor, helpless family of five confined to suffer locked up for weeks all because you guys couldn’t take two seconds to use the few brain cells you didn’t kill with your alcohol and tobacco to think up of a plan.  Are you guys admitting defeat to a couple of 80 year olds?  Is that truly what the Rambo Commando motto is?”
“Rambo Commando?  What the fuck is that?” protests Disney Phobia.  “I thought we’d agreed to call it the Chuck Norris Commando!”
“Chuck Norris blows.  We should call it the Jack Bauer Commando, coz Jack Bauer kicks ass,” proposes VIP Vodka.
“What are you talking about?  Chuck Norris rocks.  He went to the Virgin Islands, once.  Now they’re referred to simply as the Islands.”
“Yeah, well Jack Bauer counted to infinity.  Twice.”
“So?  Chuck Norris knows two speeds: walk and kill.”
“Yeah, but Jack Bauer could kill Chuck Norris, any day, any time.”
“Doesn’t matter.  Chuck Norris is already dead.  The Grim Reaper’s just afraid to tell him.”
Grendel has already lit two Marlboros again, and between two puffs, she says, “I didn’t even know we had a motto.”
“Yeah, Grendel, doesn’t matter, you’re always two trains behind anyways.

PEP: Pink Is the New Black||Prose fictio.text:
Chapter 1:
			               Pink is the New Black


Private Eye Patton was half blind and a 75 year old, Nancy of first name.  She had shortly-trimmed hair tinted metallic silver, and a non-trimmed mustache not tinted metallic silver.  She had two passions: her love for guns (she was always packin’) derived from her father’s life; her love for intrigue came from her father’s death.  By the way, her father was General Patton, of fame from the sequel to World War I.  Another by-the-way:  Nancy is a city in Lorraine that went back and forth like a ping pong ball between Germany and France (match won by France … until rematch), and the General decided to honor the people from Lorraine by naming his daughter Nancy.  Had he had a boy, as he wrote in his unpublished memoirs, he would have named him Strasbourg, after the similar-fated city in Alsace.
Nancy had a dog, and a frog, and an online blog.  But one day, while the P.I typed away on her blog, the groggy dog saw the frog hop after an insect into the burning log.  No need to clog the story by naming the frog, then, but the dog’s name was AC/DC, and he got flogged for the frog’s death (reasons unknown, though we could assume that being half blind, Private Eye Patton did not witness the incident and thus blamed the dog, but then again, we’re only assuming).
Then one day, while Nancy was pressing keys on her keyboard relating precious information proving the plot of the assassination of her father (go to: http://pep-talks.blogspot.com/) on her blog, PEP TALKS (Private Eye Patton Talks), fog crept in through the windows and Elspeth walked in – strangely enough – through the front door.  And thus began the story of:


	      Private Eye Patton and the Mystery of the Pink Lighter


	“You see, it’s a pink lighter.  It’s so fucking rad,” said Elspeth while handing out two large black and white photographs of the object to Nancy.
	AC/DC, a 10 month old Yorkshire whose hair was silvering, barked.
	The two women sat opposite each other on two similar-looking wooden armchairs, beneath a whirling ventilator hanging from the ceiling. Nancy’s left arm dropped down on her side to pet AC/DC, who calmly rested next to her chair while she looked at the photographs.
	“I’m sorry, young girl, I do not see that it is a pink lighter.  To me it looks white.”
	“Oh,” said Elspeth, “don’t call me young girl, please.  I’m 19.  Call me Elspeth.  And here, give me the photo back, I’ll color it in with my Hello Kitty Pinky Crayon.  Maybe you’ll see it better that way.”
	P.I Patton handed the photograph back to Elspeth.
Nancy: “So you want me to find that pink lighter for you.  Is that it, Elspeth?”
	A nod.
	Another bark from AC/DC.  
	“I will need you to give me three things, then: a week, the name of the last person who saw the lighter, and 500€.”
	Elspeth said, “Well, I’ll give you three answers, then: ok, Luke, and I’ll send a check.”
	Silence reigned.  Awkwardly.  Elspeth fidgeted in her seat, unsure of what to do, what to say.  Unsure of why Nancy sat immobile in her seat, barely breathing.  Sweat trickled down her forehead, unsure which route to take, the nose or the cheek.  It chose the cheek.
	Nancy had fallen asleep, actually.  But with her eyes open.  Then AC/DC barked for the third time since the beginning of the story and she was snapped out of a dream in which she had been on the verge of igniting a cigarette with a pink lighter.  The weird thing is, Nancy had not smoked in 25 years.  And even weirder, Nancy had never owned a pink lighter.
	“How can I find this Luke?  What is his last name?”
	“I don’t know his last name.  I think aa-nn-dd, if I deduce from his email address.  But warmtalk is meeting next week.  He’ll be there.”
	Nancy had pulled out a notepad from a nearby table, as well as a mechanical pencil, and she was pretending to scribble down information on a blank page when actually she was doing nonsensical squiggly lines.
	“So,” Elspeth said, “Do you think it’s possible for you to recuperate my pink lighter?”
	“Yes.”
	“How will you do it?”
	Nancy got up from her seat and walked across a creaking floor to a counter, on which were two empty glasses and a bottle of water.  She took the bottle and drank from it.  “I will follow Luke to his place, then go on a stake-out and wait for him to go to work.  Then I will break-in to his apartment and thrash it upside down until I find the lighter.”
	“Sounds like a plan, granny,” said Elspeth.  “Luke works from home and he’s a heavy smoker, so he would presumably be carrying the lighter on him at all times, but other than that I don’t see anything wrong with your plan.”
	Nancy gulped.
	AC/DC barked.














Interlude:
		                    Peach is Actually the New Black  
Important!  The author of the story has learned that the actual color of the lighter is not pink, as was mentioned in the first chapter, but peach.  He would like to personally apologize for the mistake and assure the readers that it is not a sham.  He would also like to apologize to Marcel Bich, the CEO of BIC enterprise, the company that manufactured the peach lighter.  In no way is the author implying that BIC's peach lighters are actually pink.  However, because of the change in color from pink to peach, the author recognizes that there are incongruities in the story line, most notably the fact that Elspeth colored the lighter in the black and white photograph with a Hello Kitty Pinky Crayon.  There are no such things as Hello Kitty Peachy Crayons.  Please make believe that the Hello Kitty Pinky Crayon is a Hello Kitty Peachy Crayon.  Thank you for your attention.  You may now go back to reading the story.  Or not. Your choice.  However, the author would like to raise one other point.  Does BIC have a monopoly over lighters, or are there other brands that manufacture lighters (Zippo’s don’t count, they’re not in the same price range)?  If you know of others, please email the author at  HYPERLINK "mailto:bic-is-my-bit.ch@hotmail.fr" bic-is-my-bit.ch@hotmail.fr.  Thank you.  Now you can go back to reading the story.  Or not.





























					Chapter 2:
             	         Why Do We Even Say a Color is the New Black?


	Nancy needed a plan.  And there was no better place to come up with one than in her car.  Her Smart had a special aura that made P.I Patton feel … smart.  So right after Elspeth left (the morning after from Chapter 1 actually, because they ended up playing Cluedo the whole night, thinking it would be good practice), Nancy went to her car.  Peach-colored.
	How could she get the lighter away from Luke?  She did a recap in her head of things that would seem important to the final equation:  she was a woman, old thus experienced, Luke was a man, British thus always drunk.  You couldn’t neglect the fact that Nancy was attractive (to at least one person’s standard in the history of mankind having standards), and even if she hadn’t been wooed by a man (internet-ordered male gigolo, consequence of sexual frustration mixed with boredom) in 5 years, she had a great memory.  All this led Nancy to one conclusion: seduction.  But not à la Basic Instinct.  She would use tact.  And not wear a skirt.  But would wear something under whichever she would be wearing that would not be a skirt (most likely jeans, but to be confirmed).
	Game on! 
	P.I. Patton got out of the Smart – which actually wasn’t hers but belonged to someone who always parked it right in front of her apartment building – with what should have been a grin stapled on her face, but she had so many wrinkles that her skin sagged and she did not have enough lower facial muscles to bring it back up into a smile.  Thus she smiled on the inside.
	Nancy also realized that to solve the intrigue, she had to follow the principle rule of mystery solvers, used by such artists of fame like Sherlock Holmes and even fakes like Hercule Poirot: immerse yourself into the subject.  Become it.  Of course, it was pointless to become Luke.  He was just a tool, like Carson Daly.  She had to become the peach lighter.  And in order to become the peach lighter, she first had to become peach.
	Eureka!!!
	Back in P.I Patton’s apartment/office, locked up in the detective’s bedroom – because otherwise he gnawed on and minced the rug in the living room – AC/DC barked.
	And back in the street now (sorry for the back and forth and consequential headaches), Nancy raced to her ride with no care whatsoever for the pedestrians in her path.  On the way, the following were injured: two young boys (a few broken bones), a pregnant woman (a few broken twins), and a cat (lost his life, so 1 down, 8 to go).
	Now, of course, Private Eye Patton was the definition of cool.  But a cool detective was only as cool as his/her ride.  Ask Batman and his Batmobile.  Ask J. Bond and his Aston Martin.  Ask Wyatt Earp and his fine stallion.  Nancy knew this and thus, last month, had subscribed for a yearly Velib’ pass.  Unfortunately, her account balance was hanging low like her saggy skin, and so she had been denied a pass.  That’s why the night, after she went to the closest Velib’ station and, equipped with a sledgehammer, stole a bike.  It would be a bit too much to say she had painted it peach, so let’s pretend that she went with fluorescent green.
	Nancy climbed her bike and pedaled away.  Destination: unknown.  And useless to the plot.

					*	*	*

	It was four days after P.I Patton’s useless bike ride in the streets of Paris.  She had bought a peach every single day since then.  She had eaten two of them, given one to AD/DC, and one – rotten – had been thrown in the garbage.  Thus had she began her Immersion Program into becoming a peach.
	“It’s too slow a process,” she told her friend, psychiatrist B.D Wong.
	The good looking Asian, famous himself for his recurring role on Law and Order: Special Victims Unit (every Tuesday’s 9pm on NBC) – whose name one can only assume stands for BaDass Wong – said, “Why do you feel that way?”
	“Because I don’t feel like a peach.  Not even a fruit.  I feel straight as a cross country highway.  My plan is failing and warmtalk is meeting in two days.  I need help.”
	B.D Wong sighed.  He was sitting in his black couch, an arm around Nancy’s shoulder, to console her.  The blinds were down, and only a few rays of light pierced through here and there like multiple, small spotlights.  The volume of the stereo was down to level 4, Tinariwen’s Amassakoul ‘N’ Ténéré barely audible and almost drowning out the scattering mice in BaDass’ kitchen.  But not quite.  
	“Listen to me,” BaDass said, grabbing Nancy’s face by the chin and directing it so they were facing eye to eye.  “You’ve never failed before, and you won’t start now.  I can ask Munch and Elliot to help you, if you want.”
	“No, it’s OK.  Thanks for the help.”
	Again locked in the room, AC/DC barked.  And peed.  On the floor (a good ole floggin’ awaits him).
	Simultaneously, an alarm ringed in BD Wong’s office.
	“Oh, our time’s up, I think,” said the Asian, getting up from the couch and looking at his watch.  “OK, we only did 20 minutes today so I’ll give you the session 50% off.”
	“Thanks, BaDass, that’s nice of you.”  Nancy took her leopard-skinned wallet out of her purse and pulled five 100€ bills, which she gave to her friend.
	As the P.I was walking out the door, B.D Wong said, “And if you ever find that peach lighter, gimme a call.  I think I might have some clients who would be pretty interested in acquiring a peach lighter.”
	Nancy thought that was weird. 










					Chapter 3:
				Prequel to Chapter 4

	Nancy was on Facebook.  After having read a few lines from the group What Would Chuck Norris Do? (i.e. Macgyver can build an airplane out of gum and paper clips, but Chuck Norris can kill him and take it), she joined the group Le Génocide des Pigeons, whose profile picture was that of a pigeon squashed on a road.  Suddenly, the floor in her living room creaked.  Nancy picked up her AK47, the one that stood close by her computer.
	AC/DC barked (# 7 of the story).  Out of cowardice.  Then he ran and hid behind the AK47 that was in the kitchen.
	Nancy: “Who goes there?”
	It was night and the lights of the apartment were off because P.I Patton was cheap and wanted to save money on her electricity bill.  A man with long fluffy hair (it wasn’t that long, but it was no crew-cut either) and ripped jeans walked into the doorframe of the bedroom, where Nancy stood pointing the gun barrel of her AK toward him.  At the same time, lightning struck, illuminating the apartment for a split second.
	“Oh my God!  A fucking Hippie!!!” yelled Nancy, but it was quickly drowned out by the trouncing noise of bullets spat by the AK.  Thankfully for the man in the doorframe, a half blind 75 year old granny shooting in the darkness has very little chances of attaining her target.  And P.I Patton did not get lucky.  This time.
	After her clip emptied, and before she could reload, the stranger walked forward and said, “I’m not a hippie.  My name’s Thomas.  I’m from warmtalk.”
	“Oh,” said Nancy, dropping her gun.  “So you’re a wannabe writer.  What are you doing here?”
	“I need to talk to you.  Is it possible to turn the lights on?”
	“It is.  But that’ll cost you.  5€/hour.”
	Thomas thought about it, then walked over to the switch and flicked on the lights.
	“I want you to find my lighter.  It was stolen from me a few weeks ago, and I suspect one of the members of warmtalk did it.”	
	“Warmtalk?” P.IPatton asked.  She was confused.  So many thoughts raced through her mind: who was this man?  Could it be a coincidence that he was from Warmtalk as well?  Or was it all a big conspiracy by the powers that be to try and shut her up about her father’s assassination?  And would he stay long enough to prevent her from watching tonight’s Wheel of Fortune?
	“Now look, lady,” said Thomas.  “Lemme tell ya somethin’.  Sure, I don’t smoke no more.  Sure, I could use matches to light my candles.  But it was my lighter, goddamit!  My fucking lighter, that I paid two full euros for.  That’s why I’m ready to pay you twice as much as Elspeth for you to drop her case and work for me.”
	Nancy contemplated.  Or pretended to, actually.  Of course she would take this young man’s case.  She had already taken Elspeth’s money, and now on top of it she would get twice as much.  It must be her lucky week.
	But maybe she could squeeze a bit more money from him.  “Why should I trust you?  Elspeth seems like a nice enough young girl.  We played Cluedo together, had fun.  AC/DC even became fond of her.”
	“Well, don’t believe everything she says.  She’s a playwright.”
	“Oh, no…”
	“And, what do you really know about Elspeth?  Did she tell you her full name?”
	“Yes, Elspeth Walker, like the Texas Ranger.”
	By now, the two of them were sitting down in the bedroom, Nancy by her computer and Thomas on the bed.  AC/DC had also run back into the bedroom and sat by Nancy’s side.  An eighth bark should be coming from him soon.
	Thomas: “Ah, yes, that is what she told me as well.  And that’s what I thought, for a long time.  Until I found her facebook profile, and saw that she omitted a wee bit important detail.”
	Gasping, Nancy asked, “What is it?”
	“She has a middle name.  Kathleen.”
	“Oh my god!”
	AC/DC barked.
	At the same time, lightning struck outside (well, obviously, it didn’t struck inside!)
	And again at the same time, but with the time difference included, California was shaken (but not stirred) by an earthquake.  Richter’s scale was broken so magnitude unknown, but Ripley’s Believe It or Not said you better believe it was a biggie.  Swarchzinator concurred.
	“Yeah, I know, it was quite a shock to me as well.  When you think about her predecessors – John Wilkes Booth, Lee Harvey Oswald…  Gives you shivers down the spine.”
	“Well, I don’t have a spine anymore, young lad.  They implanted an artificial stick to hold my back together.  But I get what you mean.  It does change my perspective.  Would you like some tea?”
	They both rose up from their respective seats and headed in unison toward the kitchen.
	“Yeah, tea would be nice,” Thomas answered.
	“Ok, then, could you run out to the grocery store and buy some?  I ran out.  Thanks.”

Part I: The Hospital||Short story.text:
‏					Part I
‏			                     The Hospital

‏	I feel dirty.  Unshaved, unshowered for such a long time.  Time, an endless hallway with headache-giving flickering lights.  Like dreamy hospital hallways.  I haven't slept much, or anything actually.  Or so it seems.  My hands are trembling.  My heart is pounding like a maniac pounding on his cell door, trying to burst it open.  I've been sitting for so long that my legs are completely numb; for all I know, I could be handicapped from the waist down.  I look down at the dots on the linoleum floor, try and count them.  Headache thickens and spreads; I stop.  17.
‏	Nothing that you ever imagine happens the way you imagine it.  In my head I was thirty-something, with a good job, my parents and siblings would be waiting in the hallway, my wife would be pushing in terrible pain and crushing my hand or something, like in the movies.  There would be life, movement.
‏	I'm alone in a hallway, she's getting a C-section, my parents and siblings are not here, I'm ten years younger and soon out of job, and she's not my wife but my girlfriend.  I guess the only resemblance to the imagination is that it is happening in a hospital.
‏	They said it would only take ten minutes but it feels like, fuck.  I don't know what it feels like.  What do ten minutes, when you're out-of-your-mind nervous, feel like?  This is supposed to be a life changing event.  I'm still waiting for something to snap in my mind.  To make it seem that way.

Baby Story||Short story.text:
Over the hills and far away, in a distant land and distant time, stood a kingdom high and tall whose people were glad and brave.  Glad, because they were ruled by benevolent rulers, King Thomas and his Queen Emilia, and brave because they were under the protection of the most courageous knight that ever lived, Prince Leo.
The prince had a boyish face, with blondish long flocks of hair and piercing dark blue eyes, and his courage was only matched by the kindness that reigned in his heart.  Although young, he had already been on many perilous adventures, and was always accompanied by his faithful companion: Zeppelin the Hairy Dragon.  Although flying beasts that spit fire out of their mouths are commonly known to be evil, Zeppie was kindhearted and devoted to his master, Prince Leo (and his parents, King Thomas and Queen Emilia).
One day in early spring, Prince Leo stood on the balcony of the highest tower of Slott, his parents’ castle, overlooking the vast land of the Kingdom of Utopia.  The sun commanded a clear blue sky as no clouds dared challenge his reign on this beautiful day.

Backgammon||Short story.text:
“Take off your glasses, you fucking asshole!”  Grendel’s piercing shriek silenced everything: my two siblings and I stopped playing videogames, the construction workers outside our window stopped drilling, even the bells from the church across the street stopped chiming.  Forget about the Middle East, the world spotlight was on our 80m2 apartment.  I wouldn’t have been surprised to see a CNN or BBC reporter on the spot, ready for the exclusive news break.
	“Bon, pour une fois, arrête de gueuler et joue,” responded by father, unimpressed.  30 years – 10950 days – of marriage, with an average of a dozen shrieks per day, you do the math.  He’d heard them all.
	“Take off your fucking glasses!  That way I won’t break them when I hit you,” retorted my mother, a Marlboro already lit in her mouth and a spare one waiting on standby in her hand.  Angry but conscious enough that we were on the low side money-wise.  A big improvement from years past.
	The two of them were glaring at each other, Grendel’s chest heaving louder than a pig snoring while in contrast my dad tried to remain calm.  I had a strong urge to go to the bathroom, but I was nailed to the spot.  Not because this was a nail-biting, edge-of-your-seat, suspenseful situation.  No.  But because this was Grendel against my dad, and if I moved, I could become a potential collateral damage.  And despite all the misery in my life, I clung to the hope of one day breaking away from this crazy family and conducting a normal life.  A happy life, a life in which I could see parents playing a game of backgammon without one of their lives being threatened by the other, a life in which the three children didn’t live in constant terror.  Good thing we never owned a gun.
	“Bon, tu vas jouer ou pas, merde?  Moi j’ai pleins de coups de fils à passer, alors tu fais vraiment chier.”

Depression||Short story.text:
They were bored out of their minds.  They sat all day long in their apartment, which they nicknamed “the cave”, sitting like zombies on their puked-on, pissed-on, shit-colored sofa and with their pupils scotched to the dusty computer screen.  Time meant nothing to them.  It was as distant as a third world conflict or a robot exploration of Mars.  Their only clock was the needs of their three months old son: cry, hunger, bath, diaper change, sleep.  Unfortunately, the latter was becoming rarer and rarer as Leo grew.  Their depression was a torrid one, and any wee bit of joy or happiness dried up quicker than Edward’s sperm on his stomach after a hand job or masturbation.
	They had been at the café for a while now, on the covered terrace, watching each other, Leo sleeping in his stroller, admiring the indecisive rain going about on and off for most of the afternoon with no self assurance.  He wanted to write something serious, about life, his life, and all the weights on his shoulders and all the things that hammered away constantly in his head, which he hadn’t done in forever.  She wanted to read something light, about sex and celebrities and their stupid incessant love stories and addictions to drugs, which she did every so often.
“You’re starting to irritate me,” he said, the words hidden in a puff of his cigarette, the words hidden of any emotion and of any meaning.
	She stared at him, grinning.  Unhurt.  Depression forced her to take everything as a joke, as if she were on the verge of delirium.  Maybe she was.  He didn’t know.  Her eyes were wide open, green and teasing.  Her hair was long and light-brown, straightened earlier that day but usually a bit fluffy and curly.  She could have been a model.  Had a prettier face than most runway walkers and definitely the silhouette for it (she was obsessed with her line).  He knew he was damn lucky to be with her.  “You mean I’m irritating you now, or have been for weeks, or what?”
	“I don’t know.  I guess you’re starting now.  I mean, I know it’s not your fucking fault.  It’s weird.  I don’t know.”
	The grin on her face.  It was there, and then it was gone.  She said: “I know.  Don’t worry.  You bore me to hell, as well.  But less than the others.  And I mean,  I have to breastfeed Leo every four hours, so I’m on a clock, I can’t go around and do what I want.  You can, though.”
	He put out his cigarette in the ashtray, thinking.  Took a sip from his Heineken, still thinking.  He was sitting with a jacket because of the cold, even though it was June, but he quite enjoyed it, even the rain.  It fit with the mood.  It was a calm weather.  And he was a calm person.  His hair was long for a guy, and curly.  He used to be blond as a kid.  Golden hair, in fact.  Then over the years it darkened, like a man’s soul who loses his childhood innocence and naiveté.  “What can we do about this?  I mean, soon we’ll be in Sweden, and that will be boring as hell in a way, but also challenging for me.  But now there’s three weeks left in Paris, and if we keep this up, I’m gonna shoot myself before we get to the end of the month.  That would be ironic.  Suicide from depression even before I move to Sweden.”
	“Wouldn’t be so ironic.  Logical, actually.  Your stupid jokes with suicides in Sweden is retarded.  There are way more suicides in France, even when you factor in rates according to the population.”
	“Nonetheless.”
	A sigh of despair.  A large gulp from her glass of Champagne.  “Well, what’s your magical solution to our problems?  What is it that you want to do?”

First Date||Short story.text:
First Date

	We’re in line; I’m trembling.  Inside, of course.  I can’t show her I’m scared, nervous, and sweating like a pig.  No, no showing any signs of weakness.  Why?  Because: j’suis un homme.  Un vrai.  I look at her, she seems happy.  So far, so good.  We’re now at the booth.
	“Two tickets for Syriana, please.”
	She moves for her wallet, but I’m faster than Billy the Kid.  Despite being a greedy Jew, I pull my wallet faster than any one in the wild wild west.  She thanks me, and while I pay the overpriced tickets -- in the corner of my mind I now regret having paid for her place -- I notice a sign warning that the movie contains a scene of extreme violence.  I can already picture it: a Humphrey Bogart-version of me sitting next to Amélie during the scene of violence, she brusquely rushes into my arms, crying, I take hold of her, we look each other straight in the eyes -- by the way, all this is happening in black and white, of course -- and I say, “frankly, dear, I don’t give a damn.”  Oops, wrong quote.  I mean, I don’t say anything, I just stare at her with that killer look of mine, then I go in and kiss her, then a big The End sign comes on screen and credits start rolling.  Perfect!
	We go in the theater and she chooses the back row.  Is that an indication she has the same thing in mind, and wants to sit in the back so that no one will see us kiss?  Or does it just mean that her eyes hurt if she sits too close to the screen?  Questions, questions.  Sometimes I hate them, yet my mind is always filled of them, they keep coming and coming just like stupid pop-ups when you surf the net.  But there’s no anti-virus for questions.  Except answers.
	We sit.  Shit!  I forgot to ask her if she wanted anything to eat or drink.  Is it too late, now that we’ve already taken our seats?  Or do I still have time?  Now I’m sweating like four pigs combined who just ran a marathon.  The stupid elevator music stops and the lights are lowered.  Then an overloud commercial about ice cream comes on.  OK, someone is going to have to explain to me why ice cream commercials are always about sex.  When I think of ice creams, I think of the white truck, the bell, the kids chasing the truck in the summer heat, laughing, tumbling, getting back up and running again.  I don’t think of a half naked guy looking at a beauty queen across the street licking the chocolate like she would lick … something else.  Then the guy takes an ice cream, and the girl goes crazy for him?  Because they eat the same ice cream?  Maybe I should leave Amélie for a second, go get us some ice creams.  Then we’d end up in the theaters’ bathroom doing some licking and other such things.  Whatever.  Commercials, commercials, oh, here comes a preview for a Tom Cruise movie coming out in a year and a half.  The preview lasts thirty seconds, of course, hip music, a glance of Tom’s face, hot girls, cool cars, explosions.  Yeah, it’s gonna be a classic.  And it’s by one of the producers of The Rock.  Wow.
	I take a quick look at my date.  Hopefully she didn’t see me looking at her.  I don’t know why I don’t want her to know I’m looking at her.  Wouldn’t I want her to know I’m interested in her?  Well, I wouldn’t be here if I wasn’t, would I?  Fucking questions!  They creep up out of nowhere.
	Then I get this idea.  Maybe -- just maybe -- I should make my move now.  I mean, the movie is supposed to be good but hard to understand.  And I kind of want to see it -- I did pay two full-priced tickets for it.  If I make my move now, there’s still a good fifteen minutes of commercials -- thank you, Coca-Cola, Pepsi, McDonalds’, Toyota …  Fifteen minutes is long enough.  Wait a minute.  There’s a stupid commercial now about this fucking sick kid, and it’s asking the audience for donations for research so that in the future other cute kids like this one can get treatment.  Yeah, now the kid is playing in the yard with a cute puppy.  No way I’m making my move now.  This doesn’t compare to the extreme scene of violence of the movie, where Clooney gets his nails plucked out.  Nails plucked out does it much better than cute sick kid dying from incurable disease. 
	I’m not in the mood anymore.  I’ll have to wait for the gory violence.  Better to stick to the plan, anyways.  The movie starts.  Blah, blah, boom, blah, bang.  The movie moves along well.  It’s not hard to follow, but you have to stay concentrated. Which I’m not.  When you have the kind of girl that Amélie is, sitting next to you in a dark room, you don’t stay concentrated on the movie.  But I do have to follow the movie a little.  I wouldn’t want to miss the torture scene.  All I know is that it comes after Clooney gets kidnapped by the bad guys.  Come on, Georgie, get kidnapped.  Oh, come on, don’t escape.  Like that would really happen.  This isn’t batman, it’s supposed to be a true story.  Wait a minute, why did that kid die electrocuted in the pool?  He couldn’t have betrayed the bad guys, he’s kind of young.  He looks more like one of those kids who would tumble chasing the ice cream truck.
	Eureka!  The bad guys stormed in Clooney’s room, and he didn’t even try to escape.  That’s my man.  Now he’s tied in to a chair in a very, very dirty bathroom.  The expert torturer comes in, talking about some kind of Chinese torture.  Come on!  Too much blah, blah, blah and not enough extreme violence in this movie.  Oh wait, what’s this nice looking instrument?  Yes, I think he’s gonna pluck them!
	Amélie is shifting in her seat.  I look over, she’s got her hands covering her face.  This is it.  Time to make my move.  I take a deep breath.  I put my arm around her neck, and pull her to my chest.  We stay like that.  I can’t remember for how long.  Was it an eternity, or just a few seconds?  All I know is that after, we’re kissing.  We kiss for a bit, then stop.  Watch the movie.  Kiss, movie.  Movie, kiss, kiss.  I miss a good chunk of the movie, but when I’m watching it, I miss kissing her.  I’m pretty sure we kissed for a long time, because when we started, Clooney was getting tortured, and now he’s apparently escaped, and chasing some guys in pick-trucks in the desert.  Whatever.
	I turn back to Amélie.  We kiss.  Then the lights come back on.  The movie’s over.  Already?  Damn it!
	“Pretty good movie,” I remember having said.
	“Yeah, though some guy kind of distracted me, and I had a hard time to follow,” retorts my date, a thin smile pinned on her face.
	“What guy?  Show him to me, I’ll beat the shit out of him.”
	Our teasing conversation ends, we walk out of the theater into the icy March nights of Paris.  Like bugs we follow the hypnotic lights of the Champs-Elysées while our hungry, carnivorous stomachs guide us on a quest for a restaurant.  Pizza, proposes Amélie, so Pizza it is!
	We cross the most beautiful avenue in the world, my hands rubbing Amélie’s body to fight the cold.  We make a few kiss stops on the way, to refuel.  Refueling is good.  Expensive for cars -- way overpriced, kind of like movie tickets -- but this kind of refueling I could do all day.  And all night.  I point to a pizza place.  Amélie doesn’t want to go to that one.  Doesn’t like the setting, she says.  Now, I’m a big eater.  They don’t call me the vacuum back in New York for nothing.  I should have realized there and then how big a pain in a huge, Jennifer lopez-like ass Amélie is for choosing restaurants.  I should have realized, but then another stop.  To refuel.  And I forget.  We move on.
	Now it’s been fifteen minutes.  Finally we find a place appropriate for Cheap Queen Amélie, who wants a cheap, undirty, nice-looking place which serves good food.  But no, she’s not picky.  We walk in the pizza joint.  We order, eat.  I pay.  I’m broke.  Whatever!  At least they can’t call me a greedy Jew.  They can’t call me a racist Jew, either, because she’s Lebanese.  We leave the restaurant, stomachs appeased.

First Time||Short story.text:
‏	This is our fourth date.  Well, fifth if you count the party, but it wasn’t really a date, since we met there for the first time.  Is that a good number, four?  Four, four, four, let me think … Fourth of July!  That’s a pretty big Four.  The Incredible Four!  Even better.  If only four could mean the same: fireworks, incredible.  I’d settle for that.  She opens her door, my body sweating like a black cloud in a storm battering rain.  Oh my God, what is she going to think?  Is this really it?  Is she the one?  She’s smiling at me.  Why is she looking at me like that?  And why are her lips moving?  Oh, wait, she’s saying something.  Come on, ears, translate!  It’s processing to my brain, slowly -- I must look like Rain man, right now.
‏	Finally, her words are fedexed to my brain.  “Would you like to come in?”  
‏	Panic!  What do I do?  What do I do?  Uh, Duh!  I have legs, don’t I?  Let’s see what these babies can do.  One leg forward, nice and easy.  So far, so good.  Now, we have one foot in.  Let’s pull the second leg in.  Mission accomplished!  We’re in.  The apartment, of course.  Not in in.  That mission is for later.  Now, I’ve used the skills I learned when I was one; let’s use the ones I learned at three.  But what should I say?  That her apartment is nice?  Shouldn’t I at least pretend looking around, first?  I walk in and … damn, what a mess!  Dirty glasses, empty bottles, papers, open books, ash trays full of ashes.  And the floor …  Maybe for her birthday I can offer her a vacuum.
‏	“Sorry for the mess, I meant to clean, but I was busy these past few days.”
‏	Shit!  Can she read my mind?  Then that thing stapled on my face and rivered by lips says, “No problem.  I’m used to it.  At home we’re a lot worse than this.”  Which is true.  Amelie’s an amateur compared to my family when it comes to messy apartments.  Then I venture deeper in feminine land, in enemy territory.  And I see it, her pink-covered bed, her queen-size sleeping furniture.  So is that it?  Is that where I’ll do it for the first time?  I’m in my fantasy world, trying to imagine what it would be like for the first time, in here, when she interrupts me.
‏	“So why were you ignoring me, today?”
‏	Wow, wow, wow.  Say what?  Definitely not the conversation I thought I’d be having.  Honesty is key.  Tell her the truth.  “Uh, I don’t know.”  Nice one, ladies’ man.  Very smooth.
‏	“You don’t know?  You don’t know why you ran away at the end of class, why you ignored me at Grenelle, why you wouldn’t kiss me in front of anyone?”
‏	How are you going to dig yourself out of this one, genius?  “I didn’t run away, I just had to go home.  And I wasn’t ignoring you at Grenelle, I was just doing work, coz I had a shitload to do.  I didn’t have any time over the break to work.  Look, I’m sorry, really.  It’s just that I’m kind of shy, and in public, I don’t know…”  Not bad.  There’s a touch of sincerity, there’s regret, there’s a valid explanation.  It’s good.  But with women, sometimes good is just not good enough.  And it doesn’t seem that Amélie is delighted with the answer.
‏	“Yeah, but still.  I missed you so much when you were in Montreal, then I saw you today, and you acted so strange, I thought you didn’t want me anymore,” she flurried in an innocent and endearing whisper.
‏	“I know.  I’m sorry, really.  And I still want you, more than ever.  You’re beautiful.  I couldn’t stop thinking about you in Montreal.  The best times were when I talked to you on MSN.  I promise I’ll act differently in public with you, from now on.  OK?”
‏	She nods, it’s in the bag, case closed.  Now that that’s over…  She takes my hand and leads me to her bed.  My head is as close to hers as a golf ball from the hole after a Tiger Woods approach.  I’m a hunter now.  A hunter with a million questions running multiple marathons in his mind, granted, but a hunter nonetheless.  And my prey is there, defenseless, in front of me.  I lock.  Our lips touch.  And load.  My tongue gently caresses its counterpart.  We move onto the bed, tongues still glued to each other, eyes closed.  It’s my first time here, I don’t know where the bed is, but I know where it is.  We move in unison, I lay on top of her.
‏	So.  What now?  I mean, do I let her initiate it, or should I?  And if I do it, is it appropriate?  It is what she wants, isn’t it?  Or did she invite me here just to give me a moral lesson about acting better in public with her?  She is a woman, after all.  They love lecturing us.  Maybe I should wait a little.  Hold the trains!  I did bring ‘the condom,’ didn’t I?  I think so.  I mean, I’m pretty sure I’d remember if I’d used it recently.  If I’d used it ever, in fact.
‏	It’s going to come soon, I feel it.  The moment I’ve been waiting for.  20 fucking years and counting!  Almost 21, in fact!  I’ll finally be able to write in my journal, ‘Bouya, Grandma!  J’me suis vidé les couilles!’  We’re still laying on the bed, kissing.  My hands contour her body, fondle her breast.  My penis becomes erect.  Hopefully she’s an apprentice at putting condoms on.  Because if you count on me, well, I am a fast learner, true, but a learner nonetheless.

Happyworld||Short story.text:
‏Day 1
‏	The Bus.  8 hours.  Which turned into 11 hours because of a stubborn driver who drove from Paris to Amsterdam but spoke neither French nor English.  The Bus.  Full of people, going off at Brussels only to be replaced by other strangers.  The Bus.  And its backseat.  The conversation that made the trip an illusion, that made the trip seem 5 hours shorter than it really was, that connected Amélie and I even more than we already were.  Boredom didn’t exist yet.  The backseat.  And the pleasure.  The soft moans, muffled by one of my hands so that the other passengers couldn’t hear the pleasure my other hand was giving Amélie.  The bliss I felt from scrutinizing every detail of Amélie’s ecstatic face: her fluttered eyes and bitten lips and slow, agitated body.  The excitement, anticipation of discovering a new city, new experiences.
‏	The Holy City reached.  We thought we were lucky, that Lady Charm was keeping a keen eye on us like a Jewish mother codling her only son.  But She was actually teasing us, playing with us.  We managed to get in the subway for free, on our way to the hotel.  Only to notice, halfway through, that I’d forgotten our only bag with all our stuff at the Bus Station.  Amélie went ahead to the meeting with her Canadian friends, while I made a slow U-turn back to the station.  I did get our bag back, but having to pay for the subway and paining to get to the hotel, located fifteen minutes away from the center of Amsterdam according to the brochure but really stranded in the asshole of nowhere.
‏	Then, tired and dirty, I tried to meet with Amélie and her friends, in a foreign city where a phone call was taxed 1€/min, in a foreign city where all streets were named blahblahstraat, in a foreign city where it was not making its 62€ bus ticket worthwhile, in a foreign city where so far my problems were as numerous as its canals.  It seemed that Amélie and I were playing an unwanted game of hide-and-seek.  I would call her asking where she was, only to find out when I got there she had moved to another place.  My nerves were short-fused.  A foreign city which brought me nothing good that first day, except when my pupils closed and I began snoring and burying the past of a horrible day and readying myself to prepare for another tomorrow.
‏Day 2
‏	I was supposed to be home, watching soccer.  Instead, I was in Disneyland in the state of Florida in the country of Germany in a city called Amsterdam.  And bright colors blinded me as wave after wave of Orange people swarmed Mickey’s streets.  The sun blazed like it might commonly do in June – I’m not sure, it was my first time in Holland – and although I knew I was supposed to be hot and sweating like I do in Parisian metros during summer, I didn’t feel anything.  My throat was dry but I couldn’t feel it, I was melting like an igloo stuck in an oven but I couldn’t feel it, my legs should have felt heavy from the alcohol and especially from the six hour walk we had just made, but still, I couldn’t feel it.  I was numb.
‏	I was like a wooden doll with a clown smile painted on its face, because as hard as I tried, I couldn’t stop smiling and snickering and laughing.  We walked down a crooked street that seemed out of place with Disneyland – or maybe they were building a Rated-R theme park – because graffitied on the wall was a school girl dressed in a blue uniform, her fiery eyes staring at me, staring at all, her eyes screaming “Death! Kill! Murder!” and her hand holding a blood-dripping shiny blade, her posture hunched forward as if ready to leap out of the wall, ready to spend the rest of her life hunting you, hunting until you wouldn’t rest, hunting until you were buried six feet under.  I moved on, but paranoia betook me and I spent the rest of the afternoon watching my back, on the lookout for the crazy bitch with the knife.
‏	Amélie was more space than me.  Nothing troubled her; she was calmer than the Dead Sea.  She was like a new-born baby, her curious eyes wide open, amused by everything.  Time meant nothing to us.  Time did not fly by, did not slow down.  Time did not exist.  This was the twilight zone.  Nothing meant anything.  The city was a ride and our legs were the carts dragging us from place to place.  Anastasia and Tyson were leading us like Santa Claus leads his reindeers from rooftop to rooftop.  Yet Amélie’s Canadian friends were definitely not in the twilight zone.  I think somewhere in the afternoon our carts derailed, and while Amélie and I followed the mushroom tracks, Tyson and his girlfriend followed the tourist trail.  And they seemed exasperated by our lack of interest in everything, or by our over-interest in everything.
‏	Canadians are not renowned for their athletic skills, and soon Amélie’s friends were tired from the sun and the walk and the heat and the people and the noise and the bright colors.  We stopped at a coffee shop.  Amélie and I headed to the bathroom, which the waiter indicated to us was in the basement.  We walked down, leaving Mickey’s Disneyland for Alice’s Wonderland.  Although a sign clearly stated, ‘Beware of low ceiling,’ my body was uncontrollably stiff, almost like a walking tree trunk.  I could not bend, and my 6’1 size made it hard for me to make my way to the bathroom.  But finally, I reached it, Amélie by my side.  A large, clean wooden door awaited us.  I opened the door and walking through the doorway was like being transported by a portal.  We entered a tiny room, barely big enough for the both of us.  I looked on the left and saw a large grimy mirror covered with cracks.  Amélie already had her pants down and a cigarette stuck to her lips.  Behind me, the door was covered with graffiti.  We had just been sent to the Parisian ghettos – or the 9-3, as they call it.  We spent an eternity in there, Amélie peeing, smoking, while I laughed like a maniac in a psychotic hospital.  Then Amélie got up, we switched positions so I could go, then I realized that my bladder wasn’t full.  In fact, it was full, but like everything else, I could’t feel it.  We left.
‏	Time forwarded, and we found ourselves in front of the Ann Frank Museum.  Anastasia and Tyson wanted to go in.
‏	“Wait,” I yelled.  “I don’t know if this is the best time to visit this place.”  I was already paranoid by the school girl; I didn’t’t want the Gestapo after me, as well.
‏	“Fine, then.  Where do you want to go?”  Anastasia sighed, obviously pissed.
‏	“I don’t know.  I don’t care, really.”  I looked around.  On my left I saw Orange balloons.  Balloons are fun.  “Let’s go that way,” I said, pointing toward the balloons like an over-excited kid.
‏	Anastasia grimaced.  “We already went that way.  Let’s go to the Red Light District.”
‏	Why the fuck do you even ask me, I thought to myself while nodding as my smile widened: red is a good color.
‏	We got there quickly – or maybe not, I’m not sure.  The sun still blazed and Mickey still reigned in the city.  Then we got to the NC-17 part of the city, where prostitutes of all sizes enslaved behind glass doors teased passer-bys.  A 15 minute ‘Suck and Fuck’ for 50 euros?  No gracias.  Anastasia seemed bothered by the vulgarity of the place, and she kept whispering to Tyson’s ears.  Her words floated back to me, sizzling murmurs.  What was her problem?
‏	“Anastasia doesn’t’t like us.  She’s pissed at me,” I said to Amélie.
‏	My girlfriend was staring at a building.  “Who cares?  Just pretend they’re not there.  Look at that building!  Is it me or is it slanted?”
‏	I looked at the wooden – and indeed, slanted – building, then looked at Amélie.  Our eyes met for a second, then we broke in laughter.
‏	“Yo, Tyson, Anastasia, come look at the building.  It’s fucking slanted.  That’s hilarious.”
‏	The Canadians approached, slowly, and gave a quick glance at the building.  “Yeah, that’s hilarious,” one of them said, with a tone that couldn’t’t lack any more enthusiasm.
‏	Did he just roll his eyes at me?  I was spaced but paranoid, I cared but didn’t care.  The Canadians were getting on my nerves, yet at the same time I had no nerves.  It was day and night in my body.  We kept on walking, to the Kiev exposition and the Madame Tussaud building with the oval window on top and to the giant sculpture that looked like an erect penis.  We walked so much and I was so little tired that I thought we were on wheelchairs and were journeyed around the city.
‏	The mushroom effect was waning.  It was fighting to stay in control, but as time went on, its resistance dissipated, and little by little it lost dominion of my arms, then legs (the tiredness hit me at once), my face (the wooden doll smile retreated with the defeated resistance), and eventually my whole body.  Amélie came back to the real world at around the same time.  We wanted to be away from the citizens of Canada (the loft upstairs a great party, as Robin Williams said) who pretended to be our friends but did not fulfill their role of one (that of wanting our happiness).
‏	Nervous.  “Maybe we should each go our own way.”

The last step was always the glasses.  He took them off his slanted nose and put them in the large pocket of his tattered jacket, like always, then he descended the cement steps into the metro, just as the first rays of light descended onto the streets of Paris, pushing back the darkness into the corners.  He moved unto the platform amongst a crowd of Parisians: of students going to school, of men going to work, of tourists going to explore.  He and the others didn’t have to wait long before an all too familiar rumbling emanated from the tunnel, followed by lights, and then a sweeping wind that led the train like horses lead a carriage.
	He entered the first car, his stench following close-by.  Already the gazes of the other passengers, some of them sitting, some of them standing, were turning away from him.  He was used to it, by now.  He didn’t care; he had a job to do, and he would do it.  The alarm warning the closing of the doors blared, then the doors closed.  That was his cue.
	“Ladies and gentlemen, I’m sorry to bother you.  My wife and I are both homeless, forced to sleep on the street.  It’s winter, cold, and our 7 year old son hasn’t eaten in a day.”
The car was half-empty.  Only one person, a woman dressed in a black blouse, looked up at the man in tattered clothes.  She looked up at the orator, at his unshaven face, yellow teeth, his dirty hands – she could even see, from her seat, filth hiding under his fingernails. She looked up at him as if she were trying to locate an annoying fly buzzing around her, as if he was a nuisance.  And if she could have squashed him like a bug, she would have.  She looked up at him, and then looked back down, back to her gossip magazine describing Paris Hilton’s interesting week.
The tattered man, who hadn’t seen the woman look up, never stopped his speech.  “If you would be kind enough to give me a coin, a ticket-restaurant, a metro ticket, or even a cigarette, I’d greatly appreciate it.  Thank you.”  He took off his hat, and started walking around the train, going from person to person, the hat upside down in his hands to collect money.  Only a frail woman with a tender smile threw clanking coins in the abyss of his hat.
At the next stop, the man in tattered clothes joined the horde of blasé mammals forcing their way out of the car against a stampeding pack making its way in, then he moved on to the second car.  He continued the same routine, the same speech, until he was done with that whole train, until no more than a few coins jingled in his hat like a bell chiming around a cow’s neck.
He followed the reeking, urine-scented corridors of the subway to transfer onto another line, to hop on another direction, to solicit the generosity of more metro users.  Again he waited on the platform for the train, and again it came, although this time with a longer delay.  Apparently, there was a problem on the line, at the République station.  The announcer wouldn’t say more than the word “accident”, but the man in tattered clothes knew what that meant: someone had jumped.  Someone had stepped to the edge of the platform because their mind had gone over the edge of sanity, had waited until the rumbling revealed itself, until the lights blinded his eyes, until he had felt the wind rush past his face, then he had made the last step.  Maybe he had heard the driver blaring the horn, warning him – urging him – not to jump.  Or maybe not.  The body would have been rushed off the tracks by paramedics, the witnesses on the platform would have a story to tell their spouses or colleagues later in the day, and traffic would go on.  Nothing to worry about; only a miserable life gone.
The train did arrive for the man in tattered clothes, and he climbed onto the first car, like always.  The sirens blared, the doors slid clothes, the people read their magazines or newspapers or rhythmically moved their head while listening to their iPods.  And he started his speech: “Ladies and gentlemen, I won’t bother you with a long speech.  I’m homeless, I have nowhere to sleep and it’s very cold outside.  If you could please give me some money so I could rent a room for the night, or at least buy myself something to eat.  I also welcome ticket restaurants, metro tickets, or just a cigarette.  Thank you, and have a good day.”
The hat, again.  The same trajectory, from person to person.  And this car was packed!  But not a single coin made the hoop of his hat, not a single person dared look him in the eye.  He got to the end of the car, empty-handed.  He found a seat, sat, and wailed.  The echoing shrill was like a thousand daggers in each of the passengers’ hearts.  Even the most cold-hearted felt some kind of sympathy for the man in tattered clothes, and if they didn’t get up and wait on line to give money to fill the wailing man’s hat, the other passengers did.
The man in tattered clothes’ hat was as full as a treasure chest bursting with gold coins.  He got off the car, entered the maze-like corridors of the Parisian metros and stumbled upon a legless woman and a child, sitting on the floor, both of them looking down at the ground, as if they were unworthy of looking the mighty Parisians straight in the eyes.  A small box, filled no more than with a few coins, was in front of them.  The man in tattered clothes threw all of his money into that box, and then walked away, to another platform.
On the next train he had another speech, another walk down the aisle to collect money into his hat.  At one stop, two RATP security officers climbed onto the car.  A woman in a white chemise, sitting rigid, barked at the officers.  “There’s a disturbing beggar over there.  Please, do something.  He reeks.”
The two officers approached the man in tattered clothes.  “Sir, it’s illegal to solicit money in the metro.  Follow us,” said one of the two officers, brusquely grabbing the man by one of his arms.  At the following stop, the two officers dragged the beggar out of the train, under the attentive eye of a woman in a white chemise, who couldn’t hide a victorious smile from her face.  The man obeyed, and he was escorted out of the metro, back into the blinding sunlight of the polluted streets.
He wandered the streets mindlessly, until he found another entrance into the metro.  He bought a ticket, and soon found himself waiting on another platform.  For a while he continued his routine, and made little money, hopping from train to train.
