Kid||Short story.text: ‏	There’s this kid, you see, he’s tired from the misery, from the wars and massacres and deaths and bombs and terrorists and conspiracies.  He’s tired, you see, and he doesn’t care who started it, he doesn’t care about promises made fifty years ago, about treaties not respected, about broken words, captured soldiers, fallen towers, collateral damages.  There’s this kid, you see, who’s got a pure heart, shielded from evil thoughts, who only wants people to live and peace to dominate.  There’s this kid, you see, who’s not a Christian, not a Muslim, not a Jew, not a Buddhist, nor an atheist; he’s just a kid.  He’s neither black, nor white, nor yellow, nor red, nor a green Martian; he’s just a kid.  He doesn’t understand why other kids cry on TV, why his older brother is in the military, why governments argue and resign.  There’s this kid, you see, who’s tired, and it’s not even bedtime, he should be out playing soccer with friends, but he’s tired, you see, tired from it all.  He wants it to change, but he’s too young, he wants it to change, but no one listens, he wants it to change, but apparently no one else does, he wants it to change but … you see, he’s just a kid.

Love||Short story.text: ‏I don’t know what to write.  I want to say so much, but I can’t find the words.  How to express my relationship with Amélie?  Everything was perfect, too perfect, oddly perfect.  Scary perfect.  Then it all changed, quickly, unexpectedly.  I was surprised, deceived.  Whatever.  Now I don’t know.  I’m sure I’m in love, because  I constantly want to be with her, I constantly want to make her jealous, I want her to be my constance, I want her and me, all the time, or nothing else.  I want her to be bored with me, I want to deprive her of joy with anyone else.  I want her to be numb with other people.  Of course, I’m not an asshole, and I realize I can’t have that, so I let her go.  But I’m also constantly scared, afraid that our relationship is going to end.  I don’t know why, whether I’m scared she’ll break up with me, or that I will end it.  It’s a feeling I hate, but I can’t make it go away.  I wish I could rip it apart, because it’s constantly growing in me, and it’s ripping me apart.  It’s making me doubt more and more.  But despite that feeling, right now I’m excited.  I have a faint smile invading my face, because I know in three days I’ll see Amélie, and that’s the most exciting thing.  I can’t sleep at night I’m so eager to see her.  I love her, I want to hold her in my arms.  I was afraid for a while, after she talked to me Porte de St. Cloud, that she had broken everything in me.  I was afraid that, like a thief, she had sneaked in my heart and stolen away all my feelings, had made me become numb, because for a while after that, I couldn’t cry, especially at times when I really should have.  I was afraid I wasn’t in love with her.  But now, in the living room with my mom, sister, and brother, listening to Led Zeppelin’s Street Corner Girl, I’m fighting back the tears.  I don’t know why, but I want to cry, and it actually feels good.  I was scared, but not anymore.  I love her and that’s all that matters.  I just felt this crisping sensation in my stomach, the same one I felt when I told Amélie she could cheat on me.  I felt it right now because I wrote: I love her and that’s all that matter.  It’s not true!  Far from it.  What matters most, what scares me most, is whether she loves me or not.  I’m young, inexperienced, and stupid, I know nothing about love, but right now I feel like saying I couldn’t possibly live if she didn’t love me.  I’m writing nonsense; it’s not really a story, not really a journal entry, I know Amélie, you’re going to read this, so I hope you like it.  I might write a lot more, or stop right now, I don’t know, I like to ramble on.  I love you.  I want you.  You know that when a guy and a girl have sex, the girl takes the most pleasure.  What is pleasurable for the guy is the end, the ejaculation.  That’s why we fight so hard for it, that’s why we’re ready to do whatever a girl wants so that we’ll be able to ejaculate.  Sex is physically exhausting for a guy.  But what I like most about sex -- and I don’t know if it’s the same for other guys -- what I like most about making love with you, is the sensation that I’m in you.  For a little while, you and I really make one person.  And I enjoy that so much.  More than ejaculating, more than watching you moan.  I love you so much, right now, right this minute, I want to cry because you’re not by my side, because I can’t hold your hand, I can’t touch your face, I can’t see your smile, hear your laugh and listen to your soothing voice.  I can’t caress that body of yours.  I can’t carry you and throw you on your bed, jump on you, cover you in kisses.  I can’t get a grip on you, bring your face close to mine, feel your warm breath, and tell you straight in your eyes that you’re not only the love of my life, but the most important person in my life.  I’ve known you for barely five months, but I can’t even think of how I survived almost 21 years without having known you, and I can’t fathom the rest of my life without you.  I would do anything, anything, to keep you by my side, honey, because you’re my princess and I can’t live without you.  Life without you is bland, useless, meaningless.  You’re the center of my universe.

Max||Short story.text:
The phone never rang.  And that bothered Max.  Why didn’t she call?  A week ago, she couldn’t see enough of him, she acted like a two year old, crying whenever he had to leave, whenever her toy was taken away from her.  And now, was she bored with him?  The idea sent chills down his spine.  He looked at his watch.  She had been out of class for at least an hour.  Plenty of time for her to have taken the bus back home, to have eaten something, and to be able to call him and ask him to come over.  Or simply call him to tell him she loved him.
	Max knew what the problem was.  He knew he was delirious, too.  He had no friends.  Or very little.  And because of that, she was bored of him.  She was bored of always taking him out.  She didn’t even mind paying for him all the time: she just hated his absence of initiatives.  He always followed, never led.
	Max looked outside.  It battered so much that despite the time, it was dark.  But at least, the rain was fair, he thought.  It battered against everyone and everything: expensive cars, shit-looking cars, white people, black people.  Inside him, it seemed like a thousand daggers battered against his heart.  Should he call her?  What was the big deal about that, he thought?  He was ridiculous, and that shamed him.  He knew exactly why he didn’t want to call her, and that reminded him of a pointless story of when he was six, and he didn’t even know why he remembered that story.
	He had been in the South of France with his parents and siblings.  They were staying at their cousins.  One night, his two cousins and his two siblings, Geri and Will, were playing a card game.  Max couldn’t remember what the game was, only that it could be played with four players.  He came to the table, where the four kids played and laughed, still wet and in their bathing suits because they had spent the whole afternoon in the pool (playing and laughing, too, actually), and Max, who at that time still had hair as yellow as gold, asked them, kindly and watching the game with envy, if he could play, too.
	One of his cousins, Rebecca, the oldest of them all at 9 years old, too concentrated in the game, had absent-mindedly said no.  Max, very sensitive, didn’t take the negative answer really well, and ashamed of the rejection, locked himself in the bathroom.  It took the whole household – his cousins, siblings, but also parents, ant and uncle, and grandparents – pounding at the door for half an hour and promising that he would be able to play if he came out, for Max to open the door.  Jonathan, Max’ father, was the happiest when Max finally gave in, not because he was glad to see his son was alright, but because he had a short bladder and desperately needed to use the only bathroom of the house.
	That story was a constant reminder to Max that he always had been afraid of rejection.  He simply couldn’t stand it.  He thought that instead of calling her, he could go on MSN to see if she was logged on, that way they could talk without having to listen to the tone of her voice.  Anyway, Max was better with writing than talking.  He cancelled the plan, however, because he thought that if she was logged on, but refused to talk to him online, that would be a painful rejection.
	“Ridiculous,” he whispered to himself.  He grabbed his cellphone and dialed Sophie’s number.  It rang twice.  Then three times.  He thought it would go to the answering machine.  He was almost glad.  That way he could tell himself he had at least tried.  But after the fourth and before the final ring, she picked up.
	“Hello?”
	“Hey, it’s me.  What’s up?”
	“Oh, not much.  And you?” she asked.
	“Not much, I was just calling to see how you were doing.”
	“Oh, that’s nice.  Well, I’m going to a concert with Sarah.  What about you?”
	Silence.  Well, that had been stupid.  He hadn’t talked to her in three days, and had absolutely nothing to say to her.  And it all came back to the same thing: he had no friends, and nothing to say.  So now he had just called her to shove it in her face, to remind her that her soon-to-be-ex-boyfriend (at the rate it was going) was friendless, boring.  “I’m kind of in a writing mood, I think I’m gonna stay home and work on my story.”  As opposed to what, he thought to himself?  Stay home and watch TV?
	“Oh well, that’s cool.  I’ll talk to you later, OK?  Bye.”
And she hung up even before he could say bye.  Not even an I-love-you, not even some hint of tenderness.  They had experienced this kind of periods in their relationship before, but the frequent repetition of them made it clear to Max that it was soon going to end.
The crazy, ironic part of it was, when things were well between them, he wasn’t sure he really loved her.  He only wanted things to be perfect all the time because he didn’t want to be alone, to be bored.  He didn’t have friends, not because he didn’t want to, but because he didn’t know how.  There were no manuals on how to make friends (unfortunately for him), not even a “making friends for dummies”.  Every time he tried, he simply failed.  And Sophie was exasperated.
But if they broke up, what he would miss the most was not the lost love, but rather, the lost friendship.  Maybe the lost sex, too, if he really thought about it.  But Max, although no expert on the matter, thought that love was more than sex added to friendship.
He was also unfortunate, he thought, that Sophie was such an impatient girl.  Because otherwise, she would have given him more time to make friends, more time to change.  Although, he knew it was completely his fault.  One year was definitely long enough to change.
Still, Max hated it when someone hurt him.  And Max had a great memory.  He decided that he wouldn’t forget Sophie’s choice to let him rot in his rat hole of an apartment, which he shared with his sister, parents, and grandparents.  If Sophie came back running to him, he would simply ignore her for a few days.  Of course, that’s what he liked telling himself.  But he knew he wouldn’t be capable of doing it.  He knew, deep down, that if Sophie came running back (and he hoped she did), he would also run back to her, and they would crash into each other.  He would do that not because he’d be tired of being bored (he’d be used to it by then) but because he wouldn’t stand hurting Sophie.
Sometimes, Max wished he could be meaner.  He loved watching romantic comedies, then imagining different endings that would be darker.  For example, a woman would cheat on her boyfriend in the beginning of the story.  They would break up, and for the rest of the movie she would try everything possible to get him back, from buying him the greatest gifts to humiliating herself in front of him.  And in the end, the guy would always welcome her back.  If Max ever wrote such a story, the guy wouldn’t welcome her back.  He would throw her out like garbage.  Because, he might still be in love with her, but it wouldn’t be fair that he suffer and not her.  He couldn’t let her get away like that, because there was a little word that counted too much for him: dignity.
Maybe Max wasn’t nice.  Maybe he simply didn’t have enough dignity.  Who knows?  Whatever.
Max spent the night thinking, not sleeping.  In a way, his nights resembled his days.  He thought about his future, which was unclear; he thought about his bizarre family, which, in a way, was also unclear; he also thought about his relationship with Sophie.  That was, in contrast,  pretty clear: heading straight for a breakup.
Maybe, he thought, he should go out.  Forget about Sophie.  Cheat on her.  It wouldn’t be cheating, because they had an agreement.  They were in an open relationship.  Though, in their one year together so far, no one had dared opening it.  But he could, if he wanted to.
He considered he had one great advantage: Sophie was truly in love with him.  During these times, she was less.  But if he were to call her and tell her; “It’s over, we’re through.  I’ll talk to you later, OK?  Bye,” then hang up, she would burst in tears.  She would call him back immediately and tell him, “We don’t have to break up, you just need to change, but I love you, I want to spend my life with you, please, why can’t you change so that everything is perfect?”
He had that advantage.  So he could try and cheat on her, maybe that would also work in making her jealous, make her come running back sooner.
Then, out of nowhere, he fell asleep.
The next day at breakfast, his sister was there.  This was rare enough to note down.  Max felt ambiguous about Geri.  First of all, she was a woman.  And in his vast experience, women were manipulative toward men.  If they were smart enough, of course, because there was always the example of Max’ paternal grandmother, who was too stupid to manipulate her oven, let alone a man.  But Geri, although Max didn’t consider her the smartest woman alive, was manipulative.  She was also schizophrenic, like a lot of other women.  Maybe it was related to their manipulativeness.  Sometimes she was extremely nice, somewhat (very somewhat) generous, laughing, and pleasant to be with.  And sometimes, she was a stupid mean bitch.  She was always talkative, though.  So talkative that her family sometimes called her Radio Geraldine, because she would talk and talk without catching her breath, only to say useless stuff, like people on the radio.
Geri was also a very imaginative person, who loved making up sad stories.  When she was younger, she loved telling her younger brothers Max and Will stories whenever they were in the car, and most of the time, Max and Will would end up crying because Geri’s stories would always be about an unlucky family who loses a kid during the war, a father to cancer, a mother to a car accident, and then the last member, little Katie, would grow up to be beautiful Katie, who would marry handsome Jack, and have three children, but then one day they would all be wiped out by AIDS.  Of course, there’s no way AIDS could wipe out a family like that, but AIDS was a complex disease when Geri grew up, and no one knew much about it, other than that there was no cure, and so Geri incorporated the new, mysterious disease in her stories.
Anyway, Geri was at the breakfast table that morning, and she was in a good mood, and she liked her brother, so she started talking to him.  Radio Geraldine would have talked anyhow, even if she hadn’t liked her brother, even if she hadn’t been in a good mood.
“Last night I went out to the VIP and you wouldn’t believe who I met it was so crazy there was Fergie from Black Eye Peas I mean could you believe it she was standing five feet from me and I can tell you from up close first of all she’s very short and not that great looking like she has very bad skin and Julien took his camera out and he took a picture of me with her and then we started chatting she’s a really cool girl she’s really nice then Julien’s friends got a bottle so we got a table and I got so wasted his friends are like so rich they got three bottles of vodka and two bottles of champagne and they didn’t even finish them so they left  and gave them to us Julien and I look–” 
Max didn’t give a shit, of course; he didn’t really listen to what his sister said, but he nodded once in a while, and even added a few, “oh, that’s cool,” when it seemed appropriate.  Then he asked her: “Are you going to the VIP again tonight?”
“Yeah, probably, because– ”
Max interrupted her before she got into another of her overlong monologues on the greatness of the VIP, the best nightclub in Paris.  Why was it the best?  Because, man.  Entry is free!  “Can I come with you guys tonight?”
“Yeah, sure, no problem.  We have to meet Julien at around 11pm in front of the McDonald’s so he can drive us there.  By the way, last night I also saw a player from PSG weren’t they supposed to play last night it was weird he would go out on the night of a game anyway I talked to him and he was pretty co—”
The words lost themselves in Max’ mind, like an out-of-control ship roaming around aimlessly in space.  He nodded.  Sipped his hot chocolate.  Whatever.
Sophie would not be impressed, even less happy, that Max would be going out with his sister to a nightclub.  They were in an open relationship, so she wouldn’t care if Max flirted with girls on the dance floor; in fact, if that was the only way he could meet people, she wished he would do so.  She didn’t like, however, the fact that Max was going out with his sister.  Sophie and Geri hated each other.
It all started back even before Sophie was going out with Max.  By then they were simply friends that didn’t talk to each other outside of school, although they already had hooked up at that French House party.  Geri needed a job, and Sophie needed to get rid of hers.  Should have been simple.  Except that, with women, nothing ever is.  Geri at first agreed to take the job, which was taking care of a 10 year old every day after school, then changed her mind because she didn’t like the fact that she would be paid every month by check.  She would have preferred being paid cash at the end of each week because she needed to fund her numerous escapades at the VIP.  Sophie was pissed because she had at first gotten rid of her job, which had pleased her, then had found out she was stuck with it again.
Oh yes, there was also that one time where Geri had called Sophie a dirty Arab (Sophie is of Lebanese descent).  Geri wasn’t racist; simply, sometimes she was a stupid mean bitch.  In retaliation, Sophie had called her exactly that.
Max, though, would still tell Sophie he was going out with his sister.  Not to piss her off, but to show her that he didn’t need her.  It was a message: I may not have friends, but I have a sister.  So I don’t need you to have fun.  Stupid relationship wars.  Max hated them, was ashamed of them, found them extremely ridiculous.  He even remembered the time before he had a girlfriend, when he was an observer of his sister’s incoherent love life, and he had always believed he would never be so stupid about love.
He had had lots of beliefs, when he was younger.  A lot of them were shattered by Sophie.  That he would never smoke joints, that he would never smoke cigarettes, that he would never do drugs (Max didn’t consider joints to be drugs).  He also believed that he would never have sex, or at least not for a while longer, though not because he didn’t want to, but imagine that, for a guy who fails at making friends, how hard it must be to get a girlfriend.  He also had had the belief not to drink, though that was shattered before he met Sophie, in his first year of college in Boston.  A belief that had been shattered by Geri.
Max didn’t particularly liked nightclubs.  It was dark, stuffy, the music was too loud, and Max was no Michael Jackson when it came to dancing.  However, he did like to drink, and that night the five of them – Max, Geri, her boyfriend Alex, Julien, and a friend of Alex – got a table and a bottle of vodka.  They had also consumed a little bit of alcohol before coming.  Max liked drinking only because, probably like a lot of guys, it gave him some sort of “special power” that enabled him to overcome his timidity and talk to girls.  And that was what he did, wearing a black jacket over a white shirt.
Lorie was 23.  She said she was married and had a two year old son.  She didn’t like nightclubs, because they were dark, stuffy, and the music was too loud, but her friend was depressed and Lorie had wanted to take her out.
“Bullshit,” said Alex.  His friend and Julien said the same thing.  Geri said she was a whore.  Max said nothing.  He only stared at her, because she was blonde and beautiful, she had a warm smile that revealed perfectly white teeth.  She was sitting across from him, and she was talking to Julien, who had brought her to the table to offer her a drink.  The old trick.  Get a girl wasted to get a chance with her.  But while she talked to him, she kept throwing glances at Max.  After a while, Julien lost interest with her and left.  She stayed.  And after another while, Max got up and sat next to her.
He wasn’t drunk, or not that much, and he wasn’t thinking (other than, she’s beautiful).  He was certainly not thinking about Sophie; in fact, she was the farthest thing in his mind.  If his mind was a map of the world, he was thinking Paris and Sophie was Tokyo.
“Hi, I’m Max.”
She smiled at him.  “I’m Lorie.”
Max didn’t believe her story.  Or rather, he didn’t know if he believed it.  But he went with it, to start a conversation.  “I think it’s great you found a guy you really loved.  And that you had a child with him.  That must be so exciting.”
The smile never left her that night, it was as if she was a doll and she had been painted with it.  “Thank you, that’s really nice of you.  But I don’t think your friends like me too much.”
“No, they don’t.  Well, Julien, he only brought you here because, well, he’s a guy and you’re a girl.  Well, he’s a single, desperate guy, and he hoped you would have turned in a single, drunk girl.  But if you’re married, I guess it kind of changed the picture for him.”
She laughed.  “Yeah, I guess.  What about you?  Are you single, or married?”
“I’m neither,” answered Max, and this time it was his turn smiling.  “I have a girlfriend, but we’re not getting married.  If we were anything, we’d be more in the process of filing for divorce.”
“Oh, I’m sorry.”
“I’m not.  Well, kind of, but we’re only in the process of, we haven’t divorced yet.”  Max added a forced smile.  It didn’t suit him.  The two of them kept talking for another hour, laughing, enjoying each other.  Then Alex, his friend, and Julien came back to the table.
“Hey, you’re still here,” said Julien.  “So how’s the husband?”
The smile washed off the doll’s face.  She looked at the three arrivals, then looked back at Max.  “Look, it was really nice talking to you.  But I think I’m gonna go.”
She got up and made a step to leave.
“Wait,” said Max, holding her back.  He stood up.  He was much taller than her, and had to look down.
She searched in her bag for something.  Max finally saw her take out a pen.  She sat back down and wrote something on a napkin that was on the table.  She gave the napkin to Max, gave Max a kiss, and left.  Max hesitated.  Should he go after her?  He looked at the napkin.  A phone number was written on it, as well as her name.  Maybe she thought he’d be too drunk and forget it the next morning?  He decided not to go after her.  He wanted to, but at that same moment his phone rang.  It was Sophie.
“Yeah?” he said, picking up.
“Hey, honey, how are you?”
“I’m good and you?”
“Well, I’m home and kind of bored.  So how’s the club?  Are you having fun?  Are you gonna leave anytime soon?”
Manipulative bitch, Max thought.  Are you gonna leave anytime soon, he mimicked in his mind.  Are you gonna come over anytime soon, she meant.
“Well, actually, I’m having a lot of fun, I think I’m gonna stay for a while.  Listen, the music is kind of loud, I can’t really hear you well, so I’m gonna go, OK?”
“Well, call me when you get out.  Maybe you can come over after, even if you leave late, I don’t mind,” she said.
“Alright, well, I’ll talk to you later, OK?  Bye.”  And he hung up.  He was happy, spawning a large smile on his face.  Finally, he hadn’t given in.  He wouldn’t call her when he’d leave the club.  He’d let her sleep alone.  Hell, he might even call her just to tell her he had kissed another girl.  Let her even ponder the possibility he might be spending the night with that girl.  Instantly, though, Max felt ashamed.  Of everything.  Of the bad things he had thought a second ago, of having kissed another girl, of his stupid jealousy and envy and hate.  Sophie loved him, and she was bored because Max was a boring guy.  He shouldn’t take it out on her, she had done nothing to deserve it.  It was all his fault.
He took his phone again and dialed Sophie’s number.  She picked up after the first ring.
“Hey, honey, I’m gonna come right now, OK?”
“No, stay if you’re having fun.  It’s OK, I’ll see you later,” she said.
“No.  I love you.”  A lie, or at least not a whole-hearted truth.  “I love you and I wanna see you right now, I wanna lie next to you in bed and feel the warmth of your naked body against mine.  I’ll be there in less than half an hour, sweetie pie, I promise.”
“Really?” she asked in a sweet, excited voice.
“Yes, I promise, honey.”
“Thank you, honey.  Hurry, I can’t wait to see you.”
He hung up.  He still had the napkin with Lorie’s phone number in his hand.  He threw it away, and then walked away.  He stopped.  He was confused.  He didn’t know what to do.  He hated not having friends, because he often got bored.  But he always found things to do: read, write, videogames, a job.  But he also hated not having friends, because he needed people to talk to, people to ask advice from.  Sophie was such a person, but he couldn’t ask her advice now.  Hey, honey, should I pick the napkin so I can call the girl and cheat on you, or should I let it on the floor and run back to your arms?
Fuck it!  They were an open couple.  Anyways, he would only call Lorie to ask her to a movie, as a friend.  She was married, with a child.  She wouldn’t want to have an affair.  He turned back, put the napkin in his wallet.  He said goodbye to the people at the table, then he ran.  He ran out of the club, he ran to the taxi stand, where a huge line was waiting.  Damn people!  Sophie didn’t live far, so he ran to her place.
Max kept his promise of making it in less than half an hour.  They were both overjoyed of seeing each other, and spent an amazing night – or what was left of it, anyways – together.  Ashley, Sophie’s roommate, couldn’t say the same; her room was adjacent to Sophie’s, and the noise from the nightlong sex prevented Ashley from sleeping.  This lack of sleep caused her to fail an important exam in her psychology course the following day, and consequently even caused her to drop her psychology major because that failed midterm made her fail the course (she wasn’t an over all good student).  More importantly, however, the heavy panting made her realize there was an even bigger lack of something that she desperately missed: sex!
The next day, while Ashley was failing her midterm and while Sophie was doing likewise in her econ course, Max was enjoying his semester off.  He was conducting an intense, televised debate inside his own brain.  To call (Lorie) or not to call (Lorie), that is the question!  One part of him wanted to call, wanted to cheat on Sophie.  Again, it wasn’t technically cheating.  Let’s say that this one side of him wanted to open the door of the Open Relationship.  Max called that side the Left Party.  The other side wanted to be faithful, because that was the last important belief Max had held when he was young which hadn’t been shattered yet.  He didn’t feel (that) guilty about having broken the other ones, but he felt, in a way, that if he cheated on Amélie, if he broke the last belief he had held, then he would, in a way, break with his younger self, he would break with that boy and his long hair as yellow as gold.
The thing is, Max never had like that boy.
For the first and only time in his life, Max voted for the Left Party.  He got dressed, left Sophie’s apartment, and called Lorie.
“Hey, what’s up?  It’s Max, from last night.”
A sleepy voice answered, “Oh, hey.  I never thought you’d call me.  Especially this early.”
“Oh, sorry if I’m waking you up.  I didn’t mean to.”
“Don’t worry.  By early, I didn’t mean in terms of hours, I meant in terms of days.  I thought you would call me at the end of the week, to show me you don’t care that much about me.”
“Well, that’d be stupid.  I care a lot about you.”  Max regretted saying it almost immediately.  An awkward silence ensued.
“You know, I was gonna go catch a movie tonight and my friend cancelled,” said Lorie after a while.  “Wanna come with?”
“Yeah, I’d love to,” he answered.  His heart was running faster than an escaped convict who was being chased by cops.
	“I’ll text you the exact address later in the day.”
	Max said OK, then he said bye, and then he hung up.  He had a large smile pinned on his face.  He spent the whole day waiting to receive the text message.  As time passed and the text message didn’t come, his smile weakened.  At one point his phone beeped.  Max was excited, too excited, and rushed to look at the message.  It was from Sophie: “I love you, my life, and I can’t wait to spend the rest of eternity with you!  LOVE YA!”  Max felt the chains shackling around his heart.  For eternity?  This relationship was going too far.  He felt guilty, though.  Sophie truly loved him.  But Sophie also allowed him to see other girls, he consoled himself.  True enough.  And what if she saw other guys?  Then Max would break up with her, he thought.  He couldn’t stand betrayal.
	It was hypocritical, he knew.  But not to him, not completely.  Sophie had had plenty of adventures and relationships before him, but not Max.  He had been a virgin.  And when he heard Sophie say their relationship was “for eternity,” well, it scared him.  He believed in monogamy, but he also believed in fun.  And he felt like he hadn’t lived fun.  Not yet.  He felt as if, during his first years of college, he had only been an observer.  Because of his timidity.  And he knew that, thanks to Sophie, his timidity was (slowly) wearing off.  Only a year ago, he would never have been able to hold a conversation with a girl like he had had the night before with Lorie.  Whatever.
	He sent a message telling her he loved her as well, and then waited.  After what seemed like an eternity, his phone beeped again.
It was Lorie.
He met her at the address she had sent him, arriving a little bit early.  He was pleased to notice she was already there.  Sophie’s always late, he thought to himself.  Max found Lorie even more gorgeous than the previous night.  And he told her so.
“Thank you,” she said.  “You’re not too bad yourself, tonight.”
Before he could say anything, she grabbed his hand.  Hers were fragile and cold, yet powerful enough to lead him inside the theater to the cashier.  They waited in line, in silence, bought the tickets.  Throughout the movie, Max was tempted of putting his arm around Lorie’s neck.  But he didn’t.  The fear of rejection rising in him, again.
They walked out of the movie theater into the icy cold nights of Paris, and like bugs they followed the hypnotic lights of the Champs Elysées, on a quest to appease their rumbling stomachs.
“How about pizza?” offered Lorie.
They settled on Pizza Pino.
“So, tell me about your girlfriend,” asked Lorie, after the two of them had ordered a Margherita to share.

Mystery||Short story.text:
‏Doug

‏	He was looking through his binoculars across the street, at the blonde girl.  Naked, on top of a stranger with shades of grey in his hair.  An old fart, he thought to himself.  Doug threw the binoculars on his single bed and moved to the room’s minibar.  He took out a small glass bottle of vodka and downed it in a gulp.  Then he moved to the bathroom.  His piercing blue eyes stared at their opposite in the mirror.  Ventured around, to his dark ruffled hair, his unshaved scrawny face.  Huge lines had formed under his eyes, wrinkles sieged his mouth.  All the result of exhaustion.  He turned the faucet on and splashed cold water over himself.
‏	‘‘This is it, Doug,’’ he mumbled to himself and the otherwise silent room.
‏	As he walked out of the bathroom he checked -- yet again -- that his briefcase was still there, a black leather case sitting by the foot of the bedside table.  It was still there.  Paranoia was a new thing for Doug.  Hell, in the old days, Helen always reproached him of not caring about anything.  At all.  But now he cared about things, constantly thinking about them.  Like the blonde girl across the street, Kelly.  Like the old fart with shades of gray hair.  Like that asshole Jason.  Like the 50,000 € in the leather suitcase.  Which gave more than a few reasons to be paranoid about its location.  It gave him 50,000 good reasons, actually.
‏	The bedside table.  Doug walked toward it and opened its drawer, containing a Bible and a Beretta.  He took the gun and left God in the darkness.  Tucked the weapon around his waist.  Picked up the briefcase.  Turned the lights off.  Walked out.  The door to his hotel room closed with a bang.

‏	He waited outside for a while, enough for four cigarettes and a few drops of rain.  The air was like his mind, full of doubt.  At times, an ephemeral gush of a chill breeze came over him, as if a gigantic freezer was being opened for an instant, then an interminable current of heat took over, the humid kind that made all the pores of your body sticky.  Doug was torn, not between right or wrong, not between moral or immoral, but between breaking with the past and embracing the future or hiding in the past and avoiding the future. 
‏	A storm would come soon.  And Dough was still lost in thought, his environment as trifling as last year’s weather.  He needed Helen.  Missed her.  He wondered how he had managed to live so long without her.  All those years of loneliness, of pretending, of engorging the sins and doing nothing to relieve them.  Finally, he had gotten the courage to act and be a man.
‏	Doug’s eyes were fixed on the door to the two star hotel across the street, a shabby old place.  Cheap.  Anonymous.  A place people would choose if they wanted to stay incognito.  And Doug could wait a long time.  He was a very patient person.

New (Schizophrenia / breakup draft)||Sho.text:
I’m schizophrenic.  I tried to tell my parents I loved them for the first time today, but failed.  Earlier I told my girlfriend I loved her for the millionth time; soon after, we broke up.  It was one too many.  There’s still a long way to go before I break up with my parents.  I don’t remember which came first though, my failure or the break up.  But it doesn’t matter, time doesn’t matter, life really is timeless.  All I remember is at one point the church bells chimed nine times and nine birds flew away from the bells at the same time, as they always do.  But time doesn’t matter, because I looked at my watch then, and it told me – confidently, of course – that it was actually 8:54.  I didn’t know who to trust, God in the sky (with diamonds?) or the plastic band on my wrist.  Time doesn’t matter, of course, but there’s a lot you can do in six minutes: good sex, heat food in the microwave for exactly six minutes, watch a lot of commercials on TV, write the beginning of a shitty poem or even a shittier story.  But time doesn’t matter; life really is a flow of feelings, we accept or reject.  Whatever.
	As I said,  time doesn’t matter.  For example, I couldn’t say how long the ride from New York took.  I remember the bad weather.  So bad, in fact, that the thought of having an accident and joining her was ever present in the back of my mind.  The rain was pouring, the thick drops battering against the hood and rooftop of my Montero, banging continuously, incessantly, as if it desperately wanted to get in my car and tell me something.  Maybe they were sent by her, maybe they were her tears.  Crying, because of our last time …  Whatever.

The muffled sound emanating from the radio was so incoherent, it could have been either Beyonce or The Beatles.  Or maybe it was some new pop group, called The Static.  The rain, knocking to get in, added a nice rhythmic beat.  Amélie had told me ages ago to fix the damn radio, or have a CD player installed, for times we’d be stuck in traffic.  Like today.  Except, today, I was the only one stuck in traffic.  The highway, flooded by a few inches of rain, looked like a colony of snails slowly edging forth.  At this pace, it would be hours till I reached Boston.
On my left, impatiently waiting like everyone else, was a coaching bus.  Some passengers were looking out the window; they seemed happy, sad, young, old, bright, stupid, funny, boring.  But most of all, they seemed alive.  I could imagine an explosion taking us all away, or I could imagine nothing happening.  Either way, nothing was fair.  It wasn’t fair that Amélie hadn’t taken this very bus that I was staring at, this bus that radiated safety, that radiated life to all its passengers.  They knew nothing would happen today.  Good for them. 
My ears ached again.  I turned off The Static.  Good for me.

				*	*	*
	
	“I’m leaving you,” she said, tears already flowing down her damp cheeks.  She had nothing on but the radio, this time distinguishably neither Beyonce nor the Beatles – not even The Static – but Radiohead’s Creep.  Her visible belly paraded her recent urge to simply stop any kind of diet.
	“Why?” I asked, weak, meek.  Like always.  And that was why she was leaving.
	“You already know why, do we have to go over it again?”  She glared at me; she was in a rush, but at the same time, she was not budging.  Maybe deep down inside her she was waiting for a rebellion inside me, maybe she clung on the hope that I truly loved her and would fight for her.  A bleak hope.
	“Don’t go,” I said.  Because I had to.  What else was I supposed to say?
	“Don’t go?”  She scuffed, picked up her bags, looked me in the eyes.  She was hesitating, I knew it.  I still had time to seize my chance.  I could grab her arm, by force, throw her on the bed.  She would resist.  At first only, though.  
	The scenario of what could have happened was still running in my head when she stormed out of her room, when she stormed out of my life.  Without a bye, without a look back.

					*	*	*

	I could have grabbed her arm, by force, throw her on the bed.  She would have resisted.  At first only, though.  Then she would have smiled that stunning smile of hers, yelling, “my tommyyyyyyy!” and throwing her arms violently around my neck.  And she would have lived.  I could have taken the car, driven to the bus station, and stopped her from getting on the damn bus.  I could have changed, like she had asked me to.  I could have cared more.  But I didn’t.
	I was running low on fuel, and I was even lower on cash.  I didn’t even remember if I’d taken my credit card.  I could always leave my car in Boston and take the bus back to New York.  A road sign indicated that Boston was only 75 miles away.  And the traffic was getting lighter.  There was no need to hurry, though; Amélie would be eternally waiting for me, now.
	I suddenly realized that I was the only one to know.  Her mother, her father, her friends: none of them had been alerted yet.  Would I have to do it myself?  I’d have to ask once I arrived.  Whatever.
	I thought again, because loneliness makes you think.  Loneliness forces you to think.  Loneliness supplemented by the absence of good music, of course.  And so I thought.  How long would the identification take?  Would I be back before they brought my father in the hospital?  Maybe I should warn my mother.  But she already had a plate full, I didn’t need to add Amélie’s death to it.


					*	*	*
	I waited in a silent corridor.  It was austere, the walls were cracked, decaying; here and there were traces of its original color, a bright white, but now it was coated by grime.  I didn’t wonder if these walls could talk, but if they could listen, and how many cries had they heard?  Would they hear mine, soon?  The silence was a surprising guest, because the dozen chairs or so around me were all occupied by people.  Yet, not a word, not a cry, not even a whisper dared contest the reign of silence.
	After a while, police officers came in the room.  I didn’t count how many.  Everyone looked up at them, as if intensely waiting for barked orders.
	“We’re now gonna proceed to the identification of the bodies,” said a fat one.  He called a name out loud, and a frail lady, her face livid, stood up.

					*	*	*

	“Sir, are you Thomas?”
	“Yes,” I said, putting the phone closer to my ear and a finger in the other so I could hear better.
	“Do you know an Amélie Wallach?” asked the monotonous voice.
	“Yes.”
	“I have the regret to inform you that her bus was in an accident.  There were no survivors.”
	At first I did not understand what he meant by that.  I wanted to say, there are no survivors, fine, but how’s Amélie?  Is she OK?  Then, it sunk in, slowly, and the phone slipped out of my hands, quickly; my heart burst out while the phone shattered, throwing small debris all over.  I didn’t care; these I could pick up, throw away, and the phone I could replace.  But my heart … Nothing could replace that.  

					*	*	*

	“Sir, are you Thomas?”
	I was lost in my thoughts, and couldn’t hear what the cop was saying.  I only looked up because he blocked the light.
	“Are you Thomas?”
	I nodded.
	“I know this is hard, but could you please follow me for the identification?”
	I didn’t nod, but I got up, which was as good an answer, if not better.
	The first thing I noticed when I entered the room was the smell; then, I saw the table and a body draped over by a single white sheet.  I approached, slowly.  The fat cop stayed by the door, while a man dressed like a doctor stood by the table in the center of the room.  When I stepped up to him, he looked at me.  Before he could say anything, I nodded.

					*	*	*

	Orange was the color.  Balloons, flags, jerseys, everything.  Everyone was wearing orange.  The streets were filled with jovial people, all the restaurants had set tables outside, and already it was impossible to find seats anywhere.  But we didn’t care, we weren’t hungry.  Not for food, anyways.  We only craved to get to the end of the street.  So that we could get on another and get to the end of that one.  We felt like Columbus or Armstrong, discoverers, awed by every detail processed by the iris of our eyes.
	Beautiful was the word.  She was beautiful.  Smiling that stunning smile of hers.  The people, even the ugly ones, were beautiful.  The buildings, the streets, the canals.  Beautiful.
	It was our getaway weekend, a surprise weekend, a last-minute weekend.  Our parents would kill us on our return, but we didn’t care, we were lost deep in space, in another galaxy, and our ship was nowhere close to getting back.
	It was a weekend of drugs: the shrooms, the joints.  But the biggest one was love; the love that chained us together and drove us to the Bulldog, the Red Light District, the Alice-in-Wonderland bathrooms.

					*	*	*

	The girl under the sheet was Amélie.  I clearly recognized her face, the thick traits of her jaw, the creamy pale skin smoothly buttered on, her perfectly-shaped nose, the bright red of her lipsticks, which she had put on this morning just to piss me off because she knew I hated it.
	Then I blinked.
	Suddenly, Amélie was blonde.  Her nose lost its perfection, replaced by a long and twisted downward road that dipped right, then swerved left, to come to a screeching stop only inches away from pallid lips, stripped naked of its lipstick.
	“It’s not her.”
	“Are you sure?” asked the doctor, taken aback.
	I wanted to say something cocky, like, yeah, I’m pretty sure I’d be able to recognize the person I’ve been sleeping with for the past 12 months of my life.  But this wasn’t the right time, nor the right place.  It wasn’t the doctor’s fault, and anyways, since this wasn’t Amélie, it meant someone else would be coming later to identify this corpse.  And this time, the identification would be most likely positive.
	“Sir, can you please follow me?” said the fat cop, still not moving from the door.
	We left the room for another one, filled with desks and other cops.  My fat guide walked to a drawer, pulled it open, and brought out a phone.  Amélie’s phone.  He extended his arm holding the phone, suggesting I should take it.  Then he added, “Is this your girlfriend’s phone?”
	I refused to take it.  As long as I didn’t acknowledge that this was indeed her phone, then Amélie was not dead.  As long as I refused the phone, I still had a chance to change, to make her come back.  She couldn’t come back if her phone had indeed been on the bus.  You don’t come back from the dead.

	
					*	*	*
					
I waited in a true silence, in a fake darkness.  Sunrays pierced through the curtains, the bright sliver of light slicing the darkness like the blade of a razor, emitting enough luminosity for my eyes to clearly distinguish, for example, the curves of a large bellied – but otherwise slim – woman lying on my side.  I looked at her; her chest heaved up and down, up and down, slowly, while her mouth gaped wide open.  Then she turned on her side and opened her eyes.
“Hello, you,” I said.
“Hello, you.”
I asked her if she had slept well.
She told me she had.  “What about you?”
	“Yeah, but I had a horrible dream.  We broke up, then you left me to go to Boston, by bus.  I got this phone call, telling me there had been an accident.  So I drove up to Boston to identify your body.”
	“Well, now I really know what you think of me!  You want me dead.”  A thin smile was stapled on her face.
“No.  But right before I had to identify your body, I thought about our trip to Amsterdam.  Then I went in the room to identify you and it was you, then your face disappeared and it was someone else.  It was a pretty weird dream.  I remember the part when I drove up from New York.  I was so sad and pissed because I thought you were dead, and there was huge traffic.  Then there was the bad weather…”

I’m lazy.  I know that, and I admit it.  Some might say it’s a first step, acceptance.  But I’m lazy, so a first step is all I’m gonna do.  It’s a big dilemma.  I’m not only lazy, though.  Don’t worry, the list is long.  My ex told me I was also indifferent.  I asked her what she meant by that.
	“Well, you don’t give a damn about anything.”  Then she pinched me.  She does that a lot, pinching.
	I contested.  “I care.  About you, about a lot of things.”
	“Oh yeah?  Explain, then, why you didn’t say anything when I spent an hour flirting with Romain at the bar?” she replied.
	I was taken aback, then, of course.  I couldn’t even say why.  Was it because she was telling me she had been flirting with another guy in my presence?  But I had known that.  I had seen it.  And of course, I’d been a little pissed.  So why hadn’t I done anything about it?  Why hadn’t I gone in there, my tough guy face on, and say, hey baby, leave this jerk and come home with me, or something like it?

New Story (EU allegory)||Short story.text:
At the beginning of the third Millennium A.D., rose the small tribe of the European Unionians, a pool of 500 million self-conscious humans.  It was a decadent “society”, paranoid of being sandwiched (a tiny region called France used another term: baguetted, or sometimes, but more rarely, paninied or creped) by the rising star of the era, a slightly larger tribe called the One-Child Chinese and its nemesis, the Yes-We-Can Americans.  Slowly, however, a devastating epidemic crept throughout the European Union: socialism.  And over the years, as the paranoia and the pressure increased while conditions of life for the European Unionians worsened, reports of terrorizing strikes broke out left and right (mostly left, since we’re talking about socialism).  This crescendo led to the inevitable: a massive, European Union-wide strike. 	The whole Union was paralyzed, and the politicians were so exasperated by the people that they joined in on the strike and refused to do their job, which was, mainly, to sit in a semi-circle shaped chamber called a senate and attempt difficult sudokus while an artist, more commonly known as the chamber speaker, recited poems. Nights||Short story.text: ‏	I used to love sleeping alone in an empty bed, spreading my arms and legs every which way, taking the sheets for myself, moving around, using all the space.  Now I dread sleeping alone in an empty bed, because it means the love of my life isn’t there, it means I can’t touch her, kiss her, finger her, make love to her.  It means she can’t fall asleep in my arms, she can’t bother me by taking the whole bed and cornering me to a small spot, keeping the whole sheets for herself and making me freeze the whole night.  It means I can’t watch her sleep, gaze at her beautiful face for countless minutes, countless hours, and realize how blessed I am to have her.  It means she could be in bed with someone else, it means I’ll spend the whole night tormented, jealous, nervous.  It means I love her.

Rachel’s Party||Short story.text:
‏Honesty is key, I think.  Therefore, I will not lie: the first time I laid eyes on her, time did not stop, the world did not quiet down.  In fact, it was quite the opposite; as I entered the French House apartment, Amélie was in the hallway – arguing with Robin about Sarkozy, gulping down a bottle of wine like a person stranded in the desert would, being filmed by Leah because otherwise the over-abuse of alcohol would prevent her from remembering anything the next day – and Baby Hit Me One More Time (an oldie, I know) was ripping through the paper-thin walls.  Then an atrocious reek – the kind that makes your nostrils twitch and your mind wander why you didn’t bring your gas mask to the party – invaded the room and took my attention away from the dark-haired girl who would soon change my life.  Then I realized I’d been in the apartment for thirty seconds and I was still alcohol-free.  Time to go hunting.
‏I made my way through a crowd of drunk college students like I would through a crowd of harmless zombies, and after a never-ending quest, found my holy grail: a bottle of Sancere.  Lady charm was with me when I found a spot on the sofa.  Sofa is a big word, actually.  The piece of furniture which served as seating arrangements for guests, for watching TV, for occasional sex, or for meeting random girls was actually a beaten old thing and which, similar to snakes, had lost its original skin to now have become wan and, more importantly – and unfortunately – uncomfortable.
‏Although I eventually got up, met Amélie in the hallway, walked with her to a bedroom to listen to Sublime and roll a joint, it was on this very couch that we both made our way back and sat next to each other, at the time still perfect strangers, or maybe more fake friends, hypocrites, her sitting next to an old crush, me sitting next to a girl I barely remembered was in my European History class.  Then a discussion appeared as quickly as a rabbit disappearing from a tricky magician’s hat.  Topic?  Politics, of course.  Best way to impress a girl who’s an AI major.  Unless you’re a complete moron, which, luckily, I was not (hopefully).  We sat there for an eternity, our bodies not touching but dying to do so, my eyes lost in the pallor of her eyes, searching for a sign, a signal.  Then I noticed she was rubbing her hands.  Hers were minuscule and cold, like two ice cubes.  With my big hands I warmed hers, all the while my eyes still fixed in hers.  She thanked me, I think, but by that time I was in outer space, by that time I only had her in mind, by that time my ears had stopped working so that my eyes could function better and register every inch of her face.  By that time I was leaning in for the kill, by that time—

‏4 ½ months later

‏– I was ready to leave her.  I love her.  She hates me.  What the fuck?  How did we get here?  Does she love me?  Do I hate her?  I’m completely a coté de la plaque.  If this was a test, I failed miserably.  One minute the switch was on, the next it had been turned off.  And neither Hercule Poirot nor Columbo could solve the mystery.  One day she has an orgasm, the next day a fucking spasm, of which I am the victim.  It bothers me, it irritates me, it … excites me?  Why do I still love her?  Why do I still want to be with her?  Nothing is perfect anymore, yesterday everything was.  What’s love?  Am I in love?  I feel like a kid who just learned the magic of question to encounter the hell of uncertainty, and keeps asking questions about everything, wanting to know everything.   I’m mad, she cries, her eyes scintillating – has she ever been this beautiful?  But at the same time, has she ever been this repulsive?  My toy doesn’t grow, it doesn’t feel.  Numbness.  My mind: ambivalent.  Ambiguous, too.  Where are we going?  Certainly not back to Amsterdam, not like this.  Amsterdam!  What joy!  Mushrooms, Disney, California, in Germany, one-armed kid playing soccer.  I remember the couch, too, where I first met her.  I firstly met her in school, but I firstly met her tongue on that couch, I contoured her body there, her body, which I first saw at her place, me naked, her naked, sweat pouring, nervous sweat, of course, because it was March and cold and I was a virgin and about to have sex for the first time, and again if it had been a test, then I failed miserably, because again my toy didn’t grow, and I took the test again the next day: humiliation, annihilating defeat, test failed again, what is wrong with me?  Third time’s the charm, though, and the third time I found the way in the tunnel.  It was my first time driving.  Did I like it, did it disgust me?  I think about it all the time now, so what do you think?  Her (broken) bed, her couch, her kitchen, her bathroom (failed attempt), Trocadéro, the movie theatre, Amsterdam (damn Amsterdam, it’s hauntingly everywhere), museum of eroticism (failed attempt), her mom’s couch, her mom’s bed (in front of a construction worker), the bus (where only my fingers did the trick); and I want to leave her?  Why, again?  Maybe because she brings me too much joy, and too much is not good, too much is overdose, and drugs are bad, you die from an overdose, but drugs are good, she taught me that, but she didn’t teach me enough, this can’t be over, I still have so much to learn.  She might be the best teacher I’ve ever had.  What’s sure, anyways, is that I never played so much with my toy thinking about a teacher like I have with her.  I hate her.  I don’t attract her.  She’s jealous of my family, I’m jealous of her friends.  Wanna trade?  I’ll pitch in my greedy thief of a grandmother in the bargain.  Secrets.  Strange word.  Meaningless words.  How can I talk of secrets when I’ve told her everything, told her that I hate her, that I love her, that she irritates me, that she’s the shining star in my sky, that when I close my eyes I see her smiling face, that I see her holding my children, our children, in our house, in our country, whichever country, it doesn’t matter, whichever house, it doesn’t matter.  As long as there’s a sofa!

Spain||Short story.text:
‏	A wedding in Spain.  Sounded like a good idea: a week away from the heat of the blazing sun suffocating Parisians and the heat of the fading love corrupting my mind.  A week away from everyday routines, from my parents, from Amélie; a week with my sister, my brother, a week with strangers, a week of practicing Spanish., a week of tapas, tortillas, of churros and cheap stores.  I was excited!
‏	The church.  The priest, the altar, the wedding dress, the joy.  Too much joy is depressing, especially when it’s everywhere except in your heart.  And my heart was confused, unsure of where it stood.  Was I in love?  Was she in love?  I was scared; my heart didn’t beat but trembled.  Every second I had to myself was spent thinking terrifying thoughts: would she cheat on me, would I cheat on her, would we break up, would we stay together?
‏	Eva stared Nicholas straight in the eyes as she repeated the priest’s sermon that she would stay with her love, for better and for worse, for eternity.  I remembered Las Vegas, the countdown.  How everyday I would lie saying we were getting closer and closer to a fake wedding date, which we both loathed.  We both pretended to be happy not to vex the other.  Why is love made up of so many stupid lies?  And why are lies sometimes good?  
‏	Eva said ‘yes.’  Another lie perpetrated by love?  Or a willing answer coming from the heart?  Rendezvous in a few years, either in a divorce courtroom or the fairytale ending of a big family happily ever-after.  I wondered about Amélie, whether this day would ever come for us.

Train Station||Short story.text: ‏I’m waiting, anxious, walking back and forth, quick paces.  Very quick.  I take out my phone to check the time.  I sit, get up.  Check the phone.  Fucking time.  Sometimes, it just goes too slow.  Sometimes, you just want to fast forward to the good times, fast forward past the bad times.  Fast forward to the train sweeping in the station, passengers invading the platform like bees storming out of their severed nest.  Then in the middle of the crowd, even though it’s as impossible as finding a needle in a hay stack, you see her, a glitter among the bland, the queen of the bees.  My princess.  She sees you, runs, arms are thrown wide open.  And that smile, that damn killer smile.  Whenever you see it, you want to cry.  Whenever you see it, you can’t help but think how stupid you were to have let her go away.  At the same time, you can’t help but think how good it is to see her again.  I feel her breasts squeezed against my chest, her arms clutched around my neck, her breath batting against my face.

Truth||Short story.text:
It all began a long time ago; it all became interesting a few years ago; it all happened, really, as I will tell it, because from now on I will tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth, so help me God.
	I am an atheist; I have long dirty hair; they used to be golden blond when I was younger but over the years they’ve darkened and grown to the point that they now cover my eyes.  My parents want me to cut it, because they don’t want their son to look like a joint-smoking hippie; my girlfriend wants me to keep it long, so that I look as cool as the joint-smoking hippie that I am turning into.  I don’t know what to do, so I do nothing, and every day, inch by inch, my hair grows, and my parents’ exasperation grows, and so does my girlfriend’s satisfaction.  Whatever.
	It’s been three years, not since my last haircut (thank God), but since my family and I moved back to France.  Our last year in the US was also my first (and only real) year in college, at Boston University.  I spent the first semester at the Holiday Inn, because, as the Igou family motto goes, “Do everything at the last minute.”  You could even add, “If you can’t, don’t even do it.”  And so, my housing application to BU was never sent.  A week before classes started, I took a train by myself to Boston, to go to orientation.  The dorms were full, so I was given a room, along with 80 other students (whose families must have the same motto as mine) at the Holiday Inn, in Brookline, a ten minute walk from the BU campus.  Those days, Lady Luck still watched my back, and the Holiday Inn experience had more than its shares of advantages.  My roommate, Ted, had lost his mother over the summer, from cancer.  We never really talked, only once in a while, to make arrangements.  We agreed that on Wednesdays he would get the TV to watch West Wing, and I would get in on Thursdays for 24.  Then, during the Thanksgiving break, he broke.  He cracked.  I guess it must have come from seeing family members.  I don’t know.  All I know is that he never came back, and so I was handed a hotel room to myself.  Cable TV, shower, cleaning service.  In college.  I lived like a king.  Like the king of kings, the one with the golden throne above all the other thrones.  I put the two single beds next to each other, got myself a queen-size bed.  That was my point of view, first semester.
	The other point of view, the one from my parents, I only had glimpses of.  Those glimpses came when I checked my bank account balance, which always remained around $0.  Because that year, that’s when the Igou stock market crashed, that’s when our Black Tuesday occurred.  That year, my parents borrowed money from friends to pay the $18 000 tuition.
	Second semester, things went downhill.  My parents were broke, and simply did not pay BU.  I was broke, so drowned into poker to make some money; it turned out Lady Luck also watched my back that semester, because I made a shit load of money.  The first half of that semester, I spent it in real dorms.  I shared a room with an Italian-American that could easily have gotten a role in The Sopranos.  He was the creepiest guy I’ve ever met; what made him uncanny was that he told the most absurd stories, yet in the end, fixing him in the eyes, you always wondered.
	I remember I dined with him and two other friends on Valentine’s Day in a cozy Italian restaurant on Newbury Street.  Heart-shaped candles blazing on every table and a chandelier chained high up from the ceiling were the sole source of light in the dimly-lit room; indistinct lovers’ whispers mixed with the hasty footsteps of waiters and the clanking of dishes being served echoed like sweet music.  While the other three ordered over-priced meals, I was fed with bread because I was too broke for anything above being free.  Bread, like the poor Romans in the Coliseum that needed to be fed before the show.  They were entertained by gladiators, I by a horror tale.
	Paul’s story, said beaming with that creepy grin of his that made him look like a fat, Soprano’s version of the Grinch: “I have a sister.  She had a boyfriend, once.  One day, she comes home cryin’, runnin’ straight to her room, without even saying hi to me or my da’.  I’m her big brother, you know, so I do what big brothers do.  I go to her room.  It was locked, but I had a copy of her key, so I pull it out and open the door.  She was lyin’ on her bed, her head buried in her pillow.  For a long time she wouldn’t tell me what was wrong, but eventually she let me know.”
	Paul took a sip from his glass of red wine, then pushed on.  “It turned out her boyfriend, a faggot named Jake, had called her a cunt.  I don’t know why he did, and I don’t give a flyin’ fuck.  No one should treat his girlfriend like that.  I was pissed, all right.  So I phoned my cousin Kev.  The next day, we waited for Jake at his place.  We asked him to take a drive with us.  He looked scared, but he came.  Kev’s a big guy, and Jake’s a fucking midget of a faggot.”
	I’m 6’1, yet I always felt small next to Paul.  I couldn’t even imagine what his beast of a cousin must have been like.  Paul stopped his story for a few seconds; his raviolis were getting cold.  After a nice assault on his plate, which was almost half emptied after just a few raids of his fork, Paul continued.  “We brought him to my uncle’s shop, to the basement.”  Then he stopped, fixed us each in the eyes for a few seconds, one by one.  “We sat him on a chair by a wooden table.  I told him to put his hand flat on the table.  He did.  He was fidgeting, probably pissed his pants, too.  But he put his hand out flat on the table.  Then my cousin took out the hammer.  I still remember the glint in the little faggot’s eyes, the terror that swept across his face, when he saw the hammer.  The dumb fuck understood immediately what we were gonna do to him.  I told him not to move his hand, otherwise it’d only get worse.  I took the hammer and started to swing.  He pulled his hand back.”
	I looked at the other two people around the table, Erin and his girlfriend.  I can’t remember her name.  Not even what she looks like.  All I remember about Erin is that he was the only other atheist I knew at BU.  Atheist or not, though, we were both big believers of Paul’s stories.  His girlfriend seemed to dig it, too.
	“There was only one thing to do for him to stop pulling his hand away.  We gave him a Quarter-Jesus.”
	“What’s that?” one of us asked, though I don’t remember who it was – it doesn’t matter anyways, we were an audience, the three of us only one unit.
	“Well, Jesus got nailed four times.  Jake got a quarter of what Jesus got.”
	“Are you fucking serious?” asked Erin’s girlfriend, mouth gaped open wider than the length of a football field.
	Kevin didn’t reply directly to her question, which was one of the creepy habits he had that made us believe his stories actually were true.  “There was blood everywhere, and the faggot screamed like a little faggot that he is.  He never saw my sister again, never called her a cunt again.  My point is, you gotta do what you gotta do to teach people to respect each other.  Sometime you gotta do it the easy way, sometime you gotta do it the hard way.”
	I don’ know Paul’s religious affiliations, but he would have been a great Christian, always ready to give great morals.  Only problem is, those morals seemed to apply to everyone on Earth but him, because the hand-nailing-out-for-justice Paul was also a woman-beating Paul.
I remember once he told me: “I taught my girlfriend a lesson when that bitch showed her face in my club without me.  Fuckin’ slut.”  Whatever.
Needless to say, it wasn’t such bad news when I got a letter telling me I would be kicked out of my room by Spring Break if my parents didn’t pay the second semester tuition.  I liked Paul, but I mostly feared him, and would definitely not miss him and his bone-chilling stories.
I would have loved moving out under a torching sun, but I guess it was around that time that Lady Luck grew tired of me, and so I did it under a pouring rain.  I dreadfully dragged my drenched luggage and dripping long hair across town, using the T.  My sister’s apartment, my new home, was on Huntington Ave. in the Northeastern U. campus.  I slept in a ragged, putrid couch in a small windowless room that also served as the kitchen and thus exerted diversified smells from my sister and her three roommates’ dinners, which combined to form a blockbuster of a reeking smell.  I say reeking, but the mice that peopled my room probably thought otherwise.
After Melancholic Ted and Creepy Paul, I met the Algerian Twins, my sister’s roommates.  The third one, Dasha, a Ukrainian girl, was as visible as a ghost, always absent or locked in her room.  But Nassim and Salem’s door was always open.  They were Muslims, and always told me religious stories, secretly confident they would eventually convert me.  Don’t worry, I remain an atheist to this very day.  But the twins were also the nicest people I have ever met.
One day, after a strenuous, marathon-like 40 minute walk under a snow storm from the BU campus back to my sister’s apartment, carrying an overloaded backpack full of books that weighted 200 lbs and were worth $200, I entered my bedroom/common room/kitchen to find an unshaved man with blond hair dirtier and longer than mine, wearing clothes more tattered than my sleeping couch, which he was sitting on, eating a soup.  Truth be told (because I promised I would tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth), I was scared shitless, but I think the guy was even more scared than me, like a small defenseless animal in front of a bigger animal; he jumped, dropped his bowl of soup all over my couch (damn it, I thought) and ran into Nassim and Salem’s room.
A few seconds later, while I was still in shock, the twins and the mysterious stranger all came out of the room.
“Hey, ma biche, ça va?” asked one of the twins, though I could never tell which one was Salem and which one was the other.
“Uh, yeah, I’m good,” I replied, but fixing the stranger.  Somehow, I was sure I had seen him before, but I couldn’t remember when and where.  “What about you guys?”
“We’re good,” replied the other twin, which, for the sake of the story, I’ll call Salem.  “This is our friend, Frank.  Frank, this is Thomas.”
I said hi, and Frank said hi back.
“Frank lives on the street.  It’s pretty cold today, so we invited him up for a soup, and to let him watch some TV.”
I didn’t know what to say; I think I stupidly uttered something like: “Oh, that’s nice.”
Anyhow, the twins are the nicest people I’ve ever met.  They welcomed me in their apartment, even though Dasha, the third roommate, had vetoed it.  But democracy rules in Boston.
I remember, also, toward the end of the semester; my parents were still broke, and so they couldn’t send us money to pay the rent.  My sister, afraid, tried to avoid the twins.  Whenever she wanted to leave her room, she slightly opened her door so that it stood ajar, then she peaked out like a special ops agent, scouting the room for any Algerians.  When the coast was clear, she would run out the apartment.  If the coast wasn’t clear, she would abruptly close the door.
Of course, I slept in the common room, so I would have been an easy prey to the twins’ incessant badgering for their rent.  But they never did that, because they understood my parents’ situation.  They only told me that they knew my sister was hiding from them, that they could see the door partially opening to scout the room for them, and they told me to tell her she didn’t have to do that.  She didn’t, because they were the nicest people I’ve ever met, and they paid our rent without saying a word, like it was the most normal thing.  Personally, I think they did it because to them it was the Muslim thing to do.  “Love thy neighbor and love thy roommate’s brother that sleeps on the dirty couch in thy apartment, and if he can’t, pay his rent, and if he has no money, take him out to the restaurant for his birthday.”
	What I also remember from them, is their obsession with girls.  They kept commenting on them, all the time.  It was pretty shocking, because during these times, they seemed almost out of character, as if they had put on a disguise.  Once, a friend of my sister, named Kate, came over, and as she walked away to my sister’s room, Salem made a noise similar to the one trucks make when they’re backing out.
	Then he said, to justify his act, “Her ass is bigger than a truck.”
	College was definitely a strange experience for me.  It also reinforced a growing sentiment that I lived in an unconventional family.  We had a motto we applied to the word, as I’ve mentioned before, but it wasn’t only that.  For example, most other kids are accompanied to college by their parents.  I wasn’t.  I was lucky enough to have been driven to the train station.  It wasn’t that my parents didn’t love us; it’s just that they didn’t care about traditions.  Especially American traditions.
	I remember one of the few times my mother did come up to Boston to visit, for a weekend.  She came by herself, in an old flamboyant red Volvo.  She took my sister and I out for lunch, near Newbury Street, which is impossible to park, even for such a small car.  My sister suggested we leave the car in the McDonald’s parking lot, which wasn’t far from where we intended to lunch.  My mother was reluctant, but my sister insisted, tired of waiting, assuring us nothing would happen, that “my friends do it all the time, and they always get their cars back.”  So my mother agreed.
	The restaurant we went to apparently had won an award of the year the previous year, and it served Indian food, which we all liked for its spiciness.  A waiter wearing a turban and a wide smile warmly welcomed us into a restaurant as empty as a beach in winter.  A bit shocking, for an award of the year winner.  Anyway, this allowed us to choose the best table, by a window on the upper floor that offered a view on a busy Newbury Street.

TV||Short story.text:
When I was asked by my history teacher what I thought was the greatest invention of the past two millenniums to do a project on, TV sprang to mind.  Was it because the satanic device had created a generation of couch potatoes?  No, because when she asked me for more precision, I didn’t talk to her about the Simpsons, or MTV, or Lost – I mentioned the 1960’s and 70’s, the Golden Age of Television.  What would TV in the 60’s and 70’s have to do with history, you might ponder.  Where to start, I want to say.
	In the early 1960’s around 80% of households in America had a TV, and the population of the USA stood approximately at 180 million people.  This meant that, not only did TV shows had an immense impact on American culture, but also that television in general became the first medium through which the average citizen became a live witness of history in the making.
	If we want to talk about the evolution of television since its creation, then one has to consider the 1960s and 70s as a big a testing field, television executives as scientists, and the viewers as rats being experimented on.  And what better field to experiment on than politics?  Thus, in 1960, the new big black box that stood in 80% of households bestowed its first televised political debate between young, charismatic and good-looking candidate John F. Kennedy, and sweaty, nervous Richard Nixon.  The Democrat had better prepared his appearance, and seemed calm and relax, while his opponent had refused to put make-up on, and emerged tense.  On television, at least.  Because according to polls taken from those who listened to the debate on the radio, they tended to think that the Republican candidate had come out on top.  The difference of opinions between radio listeners and television viewers is the first example where looks and appearances had an effect on the public.  Prior to television, political speeches and campaigns were reported in newspapers and on the radio, making the actual looks of politicians insignificant.
	In the end, John F. Kennedy won the presidential election by the slightest of margin in American history, until the 2000 elections between Bush and Gore.  And Richard Nixon refused to debate his opponents on national television when he ran again for office in 1968 and 1972.  He won both elections.  Although these facts don’t prove with certitude that, since 1960, television doesn’t have a great influence on politics, it’s undeniable that it does have the power to sway an election.  Thanks to the two experimental rats that were Nixon and Kennedy, politicians since then have been aware of television’s power, and due to this have hired whole teams committed only to work on their image.

15 :28 Melody

	Second thoughts.  She didn’t want to admit it, but that’s what lingered in her mind as she surfed the net.  Melody’s pale face, which seemed like cream buttered on, was inches away from the fizzling screen, yet her mind was miles and miles away.  To Larchmont, New York.  And its Autumn.  Always orchestrated by a concert of colors and sounds: red, green, and crunchy yellow leaves dangling on dying branches, then tumbled by gushing wind while birds chirped and squirrels darted around in search for food.
	Second thoughts, because it was a month today she’d been in Paris, and she was starting to regret it.  Autumn’s concert in Paris was unicolored, dead leaves everywhere, fat pigeons bombing the sidewalks with shit, cars honking incessantly, and a thick and ever-present grey cloud looming above that, at free will, battered the city with rain.
	Beyond the weather though, what she detested most about the city was the loneliness.  It had been her decision to move to Paris after graduating college, and she was sure it was the right choice, but it was rough having no one to talk to.  All her life she had always been surrounded by numerous friends.  Now, all that surrounded her, suffocating her, were four decaying walls and a tiny, cracked window that gave her a view of Parisian rooftops and very chilly nights.
	She found an interesting ad on the site she was visiting, and clicked on it.  Band Looking for Male or Female Singer.  She read the rest of the description, then copied the email address. You feel depressed, decomposed.
Hope is your only ally,
But then time goes by,
And reality becomes your worst enemy,
Because you know together you can’t be!
And your heart is hurt deeply,
Because you know how amazing she can be!
Together you can’t be,
How happy can you be?
No matter how much you cry,
She always says bye,
And that’s the reason why,
Hope is a lie.

It hurts to think about her,

She’s a glimmer of light that fills your heart;
You’re a lonely bird in search of a herd!
